860736.long_answer: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II (HEMPAS) is the most prevalent form of CDA, and it is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SEC23B gene, which encodes a core component of the COPII vesicle coat essential for ER-to-Golgi protein trafficking in developing erythroblasts.

203782.long_answer: Ring chromosomes were first identified in 1926 by geneticist Lilian Vaughan Morgan, who described a ring-shaped X chromosome in Drosophila melanogaster. Her work provided the earliest documentation of chromosomes whose ends had fused to form a circular structure.

186159.long_answer: Fondaparinux is a fully synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin III and selectively inhibits factor Xa. Because it lacks the larger heparin backbone, it does not form the heparin-PF4 complexes that trigger heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), making it an effective and widely used alternative anticoagulant for patients with HIT.

951000.long_answer: Yes.  In hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (HypoPP) attacks are precipitated by any factor that lowers circulating potassium or promotes an intracellular shift of potassium.  Classical recognised dietary triggers include large carbohydrate loads, but authoritative reviews (e.g., GeneReviews, Medscape, UpToDate) also list high-sodium (high-salt) intake as a precipitating factor.  A sodium load increases distal tubular sodium delivery, stimulating renal potassium secretion; it can therefore lower serum K⁺ and favour the fall in extracellular potassium that sets off an attack.  For this reason standard preventative advice for patients with HypoPP is to limit both simple carbohydrates and excess dietary salt, and some clinicians recommend a modest low-sodium diet (<2 g Na/day).  Thus, while reduced salt is most commonly emphasised for hypertension and heart disease, it is also relevant for people with hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.

570726.long_answer: Primary hyperoxaluria type II is caused by pathogenic variants in the GRHPR gene, which encodes the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase. This enzyme possesses D-glycerate dehydrogenase (hydroxypyruvate reductase) activity, catalyzing the NAD(P)H-dependent reduction of hydroxypyruvate to D-glycerate and glyoxylate to glycolate. Loss-of-function mutations in GRHPR impair this activity, leading to excessive glyoxylate and oxalate accumulation characteristic of primary hyperoxaluria. Therefore, an enzyme with D-glycerate dehydrogenase activity is indeed implicated in primary hyperoxaluria when mutated.

788056.long_answer: Zika virus, which has been linked to a surge in congenital microcephaly, is primarily transmitted to humans by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes—particularly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus—making Aedes the recognized vector genus for this virus.

594097.long_answer: Polydactyly is the presence of one or more extra digits on the hands and/or feet. It is the most common congenital malformation of the limbs and has been linked to mutations in at least 39 different genes involved in limb patterning (e.g., GLI3, ZRS enhancer of SHH). British actress Gemma Christina Arterton has publicly stated that she was born with extra fingers, which were surgically removed shortly after birth, illustrating this condition.

824992.long_answer: The BK virus small T antigen binds directly to the cellular serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A). This interaction inhibits PP2A’s normal regulatory activity, leading to abnormal phosphorylation of key cell-cycle regulators (e.g., retinoblastoma pathway components) and thereby drives unscheduled progression through the cell cycle.

583649.long_answer: Nephroblastoma (Wilms’ tumour) was first described by the German surgeon Max Wilms. Wilms completed his medical studies at the University of Bonn and was awarded his medical doctorate (Dr med) in 1890, five years before beginning the investigative work that led to his classic 1899 monograph on the ‘mixed tumours’ of the kidney.

892125.long_answer: British psychiatrist Dr Lorna Wing (1928–2014) helped found the National Autistic Society in the early 1960s and, in a 1976 publication, was the first to introduce and use the term “Asperger syndrome” in the English-language medical literature, bringing Hans Asperger’s original 1944 description to wider clinical attention.

937463.long_answer: Scheuermann disease, also called juvenile kyphosis, is a form of vertebral osteochondritis in which growth‐plate disturbance leads to anterior wedging of several thoracic or thoracolumbar vertebral bodies. This uneven vertebral growth produces a rigid kyphotic curve that typically first becomes apparent during the adolescent growth spurt.

240486.long_answer: Shulman’s syndrome, better known as eosinophilic fasciitis, is usually idiopathic but has been linked to a variety of external triggers (strenuous exercise, infections, medications and supplements). During the late-1980s an epidemic of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) and several cases of classic eosinophilic fasciitis were traced to ingestion of over-the-counter L-tryptophan preparations that were later found to be contaminated. Case reports and small series published in the rheumatology and dermatology literature (e.g., Arch Dermatol 1991; Mayo Clin Proc 1990; Arthritis Rheum 1991) documented patients who developed the characteristic skin induration, fascial thickening, peripheral eosinophilia and tissue biopsies diagnostic of Shulman’s syndrome after taking L-tryptophan, with improvement after the supplement was discontinued and immunosuppressive therapy initiated. Because of these observations, authoritative reviews list L-tryptophan ingestion as a recognized, albeit uncommon, precipitating factor for eosinophilic fasciitis. Thus, according to established biomedical consensus, Shulman’s syndrome can indeed be related to (i.e., triggered by) L-tryptophan exposure.

252465.long_answer: Whipple’s disease is a rare systemic infection produced by the Gram-positive actinomycete Tropheryma whipplei. The organism infiltrates the small-intestinal mucosa, leading to villous blunting and lymphatic obstruction that cause steatorrhea, weight loss, and other malabsorption features mimicking celiac disease. Because the pathogen disseminates, extra-intestinal manifestations such as arthritis, neurologic, cardiac, and ocular involvement are also common. Histologically, periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive macrophages packed with the bacillus are characteristic, confirming that Tropheryma whipplei infection underlies the disorder.

805719.long_answer: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder in which autoreactive lymphocytes progressively destroy thyroid tissue, leading to chronic hypothyroidism. Reduced thyroid hormone production disrupts hair growth cycles; a classic clinical clue is madarosis—loss of hair from the outer third of the eyebrows—seen in longstanding hypothyroidism caused most commonly by Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

906796.long_answer: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome (MDS) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutations in nuclear genes that govern mtDNA replication or nucleotide metabolism (e.g., POLG, TK2, DGUOK, MPV17). Because the defective genes are nuclear, transmission follows an autosomal recessive, not maternal, pattern. The defining laboratory and pathological feature is a marked loss of mitochondrial DNA—often >80–90% reduction—in the affected tissues (muscle, liver, brain), leading to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and the clinical manifestations of the disease.

581932.long_answer: Feingold syndrome type 1 is an autosomal-dominant malformation disorder characterized by microcephaly, digital anomalies and learning difficulties. The condition results from heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions of the MYCN gene located on chromosome 2p24; disruption of MYCN impairs its role in embryonic development, accounting for the syndrome’s clinical features.

882911.long_answer: Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside extracted from foxglove plants, which belong to the genus Digitalis (e.g., Digitalis purpurea). William Withering’s 1785 monograph, “An Account of the Foxglove,” first detailed the plant’s medicinal and toxic effects, linking Digitalis ingestion to the characteristic manifestations of digoxin poisoning.

699828.long_answer: Phorbol esters (e.g., PMA) are potent agonists that bind to and activate protein kinase C (PKC). Experimental activation of PKC in adipose tissue promotes adipocyte proliferation and vascularization, producing angiolipomas—small, frequently painful subcutaneous lipoma-like nodules. Hence, PKC is the kinase whose phorbol-ester-mediated activation is linked to formation of these painful lipomas.

697601.long_answer: Theodor von Leber first reported Leber congenital amaurosis in 1869, describing children with severe, early-onset blindness, nystagmus and a markedly reduced or absent electroretinogram. This autosomal-inherited retinal dystrophy, now known as Leber congenital amaurosis, is characterized by congenital or early-infantile vision loss due to primary retinal photoreceptor dysfunction.

459602.long_answer: The most frequent brain vascular malformation is a cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM), in which arteries connect directly to veins without an intervening capillary bed. This high-flow shunt predisposes the lesion to rupture and is a leading cause of non-traumatic intracranial hemorrhage in young adults.

951796.long_answer: In granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis can destroy the nasal septal cartilage, causing loss of dorsal support and collapse of the nasal bridge, known as a saddle-nose deformity. Augmentation rhinoplasty restores the nasal dorsum and corrects this characteristic deformity.

335637.long_answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener’s granulomatosis) is an ANCA-associated small- to medium-vessel autoimmune vasculitis that frequently causes destructive granulomatous inflammation of the nasal septal cartilage. This leads to collapse of the cartilaginous dorsum and the characteristic saddle nose deformity, making GPA a well-documented etiologic factor in such nasal bridge loss.

614145.long_answer: The three pneumoconioses encountered most frequently worldwide are silicosis (from inhaling crystalline silica), coal-workers’ pneumoconiosis (from coal dust), and asbestosis (from asbestos fibres). Ground baryte ore consists chiefly of barium sulfate; inhalation of its dust can lead to a much rarer condition called baritosis, a benign form of pneumoconiosis. None of the common forms—silicosis, coal-workers’ pneumoconiosis, or asbestosis—arise from baryte exposure. Therefore, exposure to ground baryte ore is not responsible for any of the top three most common types of pneumoconiosis.

916878.long_answer: The hypothalamic hamartoma of the tuber cinereum characteristically produces gelastic seizures—brief, stereotyped bursts of inappropriate laughter. The term comes from the Greek word "gelos," meaning laughter, reflecting the seizure’s hallmark ictal laughter episodes.

351044.long_answer:
Although the two disorders have very different pathophysiology, they share several non-specific clinical manifestations. Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) typically presents with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, profuse sweating (diaphoresis), fatigue, nausea and a feeling of impending doom. Lymphomas, on the other hand, most classically cause painless lymph-node enlargement, but B-symptoms such as unexplained fever, drenching night-sweats, profound fatigue and unintentional weight loss are also part of the accepted symptom complex. Thus: 
• Fatigue is a recognised constitutional symptom in both lymphoma and AMI.
• Sweating occurs in both conditions—the "night-sweats" of lymphoma and the acute diaphoresis of an infarction.
• Dyspnoea/shortness of breath can accompany either disease (in AMI because of acute heart dysfunction; in lymphoma because of anaemia, large mediastinal masses or pleural effusions).

Because at least some symptoms (fatigue, sweating, dyspnoea) are observed in both conditions, the correct answer is "yes."

186082.long_answer: Cyclopia is an extremely rare congenital malformation— a severe form of holoprosencephaly—named after the one-eyed Cyclops of Greek mythology. Affected embryos develop a single midline ocular structure and an absent or non-functional nose, often replaced by a proboscis. The defect is usually incompatible with life: most pregnancies end in spontaneous miscarriage, and live-born infants typically die within hours or days postpartum.

858693.long_answer: Behr syndrome, an early-onset optic atrophy syndrome, is frequently accompanied by cerebellar dysfunction. The hallmark neurological sign is ataxia—impaired voluntary coordination of gait and limb movements—reflecting involvement of cerebellar pathways that commonly occurs in this disorder.

275151.long_answer: Adrenal insufficiency results from inadequate production of adrenal corticosteroids (primarily cortisol, often aldosterone). The resulting symptoms—fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, adrenal crisis, etc.—are due to hormonal deficiency, not infection. Standard therapy is physiologic replacement with glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone, prednisone) and, when needed, mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone) plus stress-dose steroids during illness. Antibiotics have no direct effect on the underlying endocrine defect or its manifestations; they are only indicated if a separate bacterial infection is present. Therefore, symptoms of adrenal insufficiency themselves are not treatable with antibiotics.

199357.long_answer: Autoimmune Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) involves immune-mediated destruction of the adrenal cortex, greatly reducing synthesis of glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). The resulting cortisol and aldosterone deficiency impairs vascular tone and sodium-water balance, so patients are prone to severe, life-threatening hypotension, especially during stress (adrenal crisis).

521240.long_answer:
Alexander disease is a leukodystrophy caused by dominant mutations in the gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). The neuropathologic hallmark of the disorder is the accumulation of Rosenthal fibers within astrocytes. Biochemical and immunohistochemical studies of Rosenthal fibers have consistently shown that, in addition to mutant GFAP, they contain several stress-response and cytoskeletal–associated proteins. Among the most repeatedly documented constituents are: 
• Heat-shock protein 27 (HSP27), a small heat-shock protein that accumulates as part of the cellular stress response.
• Ubiquitin, reflecting the engagement of the ubiquitin–proteasome degradation pathway in response to misfolded or aggregated proteins.
• Synemin, an intermediate-filament–associated protein that colocalizes with GFAP in Rosenthal fibers.
Multiple independent neuropathology studies have demonstrated immunoreactivity for HSP27, ubiquitin, and synemin in Rosenthal fibers from brains of patients with Alexander disease. Hence, these three proteins are indeed recognized molecular markers associated with the disease process.

248374.long_answer: Rhabdomyolysis is a syndrome in which massive skeletal-muscle fiber destruction releases large amounts of myoglobin, creatine kinase, potassium, and other intracellular contents into the circulation. The filtered myoglobin pigments darken the urine (myoglobinuria) and can precipitate within renal tubules, causing acute tubular necrosis and acute kidney injury.

832203.long_answer: Premature ovarian failure, also called primary ovarian insufficiency, is defined by the partial or complete loss of ovarian function before the age of 40. It leads to hypo-estrogenism and elevated gonadotropins, resulting in secondary amenorrhea and infertility.

757070.long_answer: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency manifests only in individuals who are homozygous for pathogenic variants in the BCHE gene—i.e., they inherit one mutant allele from each parent. This requirement for two mutant copies, with carriers (heterozygotes) typically unaffected, is the defining feature of an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

268734.long_answer: I’m sorry – I’m unable to identify, with confidence, a specific syndrome that matches all the details provided (first described in 1973 at the Abraham Lincoln School of Medicine, autosomal-dominant with variable expression, and later giving rise to a “cerebrofacioarticular syndrome” subset). Available reference material does not document a well-accepted syndrome fitting this exact description.

468323.long_answer: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by severe restriction of energy intake that leads to a body weight significantly below normal, an intense, irrational fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a distorted perception of body shape or size. Although individuals are commonly underweight, they remain preoccupied with perceived physical flaws—particularly believing they are overweight—and engage in behaviors aimed at preventing weight gain.

180573.long_answer: 5α-Reductase type 2 deficiency is caused by mutations in the SRD5A2 gene, which encodes the steroid 5-α-reductase type 2 enzyme. The mature human SRD5A2 protein consists of 254 amino acids.

188963.long_answer: Nephrocalcinosis is usually driven by persistent hypercalcemia (serum calcium typically > 2.6–2.7 mmol/L) and/or marked hypercalciuria, as seen in disorders such as primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis, distal renal tubular acidosis, and certain genetic tubulopathies. A serum calcium concentration of 2.4 mmol/L lies squarely within the normal reference range for total calcium in adults (≈ 2.15–2.55 mmol/L). At this physiologic level there is no established pathophysiologic mechanism by which calcium would precipitate in renal tissue or appreciably increase urinary calcium excretion beyond normal limits. Therefore, a serum calcium of 2.4 mmol/L, by itself, would not be considered a contributing factor to the development of nephrocalcinosis.

977705.long_answer: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is caused by pathogenic variants in the RMRP gene and is frequently accompanied by an immunodeficiency in which circulating lymphocyte counts—particularly T-cells—are markedly reduced. This reduction of lymphocytes is termed lymphopenia (or lymphocytopenia), the immunological condition defined by abnormally low blood lymphocyte levels and classically reported in CHH patients.

877079.long_answer: Hemoglobinopathies such as sickle-cell disease and the thalassemias commonly involve the spleen. In sickle-cell disease, sickling of red blood cells can trigger acute splenic sequestration crises early in life and repeated vaso-occlusion eventually leads to functional autosplenectomy. In β- and α-thalassemia, chronic hemolysis and extramedullary hematopoiesis produce persistent splenomegaly; many patients ultimately require splenectomy. These well-documented phenomena show that disorders centered on abnormal hemoglobin structure or production can and often do affect splenic size and function.

335018.long_answer: Hashimoto's thyroiditis destroys thyroid tissue, leading to deficient production of thyroxine (T4). The standard treatment for the resulting hypothyroidism is lifelong hormone replacement with levothyroxine, a synthetic form of T4 that restores normal serum thyroid hormone levels and alleviates symptoms.

848910.long_answer: Ichthyosis vulgaris is an autosomal semi-dominant form of ichthyosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene. This variant accounts for more than 95 % of all ichthyosis cases, making it by far the most common presentation of the disorder.

960617.long_answer: Septic shock is the most severe form of infection-induced organ dysfunction. It is defined as sepsis with persistent hypotension that does not resolve after adequate intravenous fluid resuscitation and typically requires vasopressor support. This condition carries high mortality because of profound circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities.

614094.long_answer: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the commonest sex-chromosome aneuploidy in males. Affected men have one or more extra X chromosomes, leading to testicular dysgenesis with small, poorly functioning testes, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and consequent infertility. Elevated estradiol relative to testosterone promotes gynecomastia, which is observed in a substantial proportion of these patients.

705666.long_answer: The psychiatric disorder most characteristically linked to persistent psychosis—particularly auditory hallucinations—is schizophrenia. In DSM-5 criteria, the presence of hallucinations (usually voices), delusions, or disorganized thinking for at least one month is central to the diagnosis. While other conditions can produce psychotic symptoms, schizophrenia is the prototypical and most common mental disorder where auditory hallucinations are a core, defining feature.

528434.long_answer: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. A father contributes his Y chromosome to his sons and his single X chromosome to his daughters. Because the mutated dystrophin gene responsible for Duchenne muscular dystrophy resides on the X chromosome, an affected father’s pathogenic X chromosome can be transmitted only to daughters, who will become carriers (or, very rarely, manifest disease if they have X-inactivation skewing or another X abnormality). Sons receive the father’s Y chromosome and therefore do not inherit their father’s X-linked mutation. Thus, fathers with Duchenne muscular dystrophy cannot pass the X-linked recessive trait to their sons under normal patterns of human inheritance.

336838.long_answer: Interrupted aortic arch (IAA) is itself a congenital malformation of the cardiovascular system; it occurs when the aortic arch is not completely formed during fetal development, creating a discontinuity between the ascending and descending aorta. Because it results from abnormal embryologic development and is present at birth, IAA is classified as a birth defect (congenital heart defect). In addition, IAA is frequently found in association with other congenital anomalies such as ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and chromosomal disorders like the 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome. Hence, by definition and by its clinical associations, interrupted aortic arch is linked to birth defects.

660933.long_answer: Hyperprolactinemia raises serum prolactin to a level that suppresses hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion. This reduces pituitary LH and FSH release, leading to hypo-estrogenism in women. Estrogen deficiency can produce classic vasomotor symptoms—hot flashes—as well as menstrual disturbances, vaginal dryness, and decreased libido. Although hot flashes are not the most common presentation (amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea and galactorrhea are more typical), they are a recognized consequence of the estrogen deficit caused by chronic hyperprolactinemia and are documented in endocrinology and gynecology references (e.g., UpToDate, Endocrine Society guidelines). Therefore, hyperprolactinemia can indeed cause hot flashes in women.

312123.long_answer: Chronically high prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release, which lowers LH and FSH secretion and, consequently, ovarian estrogen production. The resulting hypoestrogenism (a menopause-like, low-estrogen state) leads to vasomotor instability, making the thermoregulatory center more sensitive and causing symptoms such as hot flashes.

852613.long_answer: Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, is classically maintained in rodent populations and transmitted to new hosts by the bites of infected fleas (e.g., Xenopsylla cheopis). When a flea feeds on a bacteremic rodent, Y. pestis multiplies in the flea’s mid-gut and can block its proventriculus. Subsequent feeding attempts lead the flea to regurgitate bacteria into the bite site, inoculating the pathogen into the skin of a human or other mammal. This flea-borne route is the primary mechanism underlying most naturally occurring cases of bubonic plague in humans and is well documented in epidemiologic investigations and experimental studies. Therefore, a flea that has fed on an infected rodent can indeed transmit Yersinia pestis to a human through its bite.

768787.long_answer: The Oriental rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis, is the principal vector of Yersinia pestis to humans. This flea commonly infests commensal rats, and when infected, Y. pestis forms a biofilm that blocks the flea’s proventriculus. The blockage causes the flea to regurgitate contaminated blood into each new bite, efficiently transmitting the bacterium to human hosts. Historical and epidemiological studies identify X. cheopis as the main driver of bubonic plague outbreaks in urban settings.

271547.long_answer: Scurvy, caused by a deficiency of vitamin C, leads to defective collagen synthesis and consequent fragility of blood vessels. This vascular fragility commonly produces petechiae and perifollicular purpura—small red or purple spots on the skin that result from minor bleeding under the skin. These cutaneous signs are well-documented hallmark features of scurvy in clinical literature and are part of the classic diagnostic description of the disease.

514187.long_answer: Scurvy is the classic deficiency disease that arises from insufficient vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis; without adequate collagen, blood vessel walls become fragile, leading to capillary hemorrhages that appear as petechiae and larger bruises, along with gum bleeding and impaired wound healing.

118949.long_answer: Systemic scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) is well-recognized to produce dystrophic calcification of the skin and subcutaneous soft tissues, known clinically as calcinosis cutis. Calcinosis is one of the classical features of the limited cutaneous form (the “C” in the CREST acronym: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia), but it can also be seen in diffuse disease. These calcium deposits arise in areas of chronic tissue injury and fibrosis and may present as firm nodules, plaques, or larger masses within the soft tissues. Hence, there is established biomedical consensus that systemic scleroderma is associated with the formation of calcium deposits in soft tissue.

910403.long_answer: PAX2 is a paired-box transcription factor that directs early embryonic cell-lineage specification, coordinates the morphogenesis of organs such as the eye and kidney, and patterns regions of the developing central nervous system. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in PAX2 cause renal-coloboma syndrome, in which optic nerve/ocular coloboma is a defining feature, underscoring its established link to coloboma.

327315.long_answer: PAX2 encodes the paired-box transcription factor Pax2, which is crucial for patterning of the midbrain–hindbrain (isthmic) boundary during embryogenesis. Loss-of-function mutations in PAX2 disrupt optic fissure closure, leading to optic nerve coloboma and the renal–coloboma (Papillorenal) syndrome, establishing the gene’s association with coloboma.

924334.long_answer: Gerodermia osteodysplastica is inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion, most commonly due to biallelic pathogenic variants in the GORAB gene. In autosomal-recessive disorders, clinical disease generally occurs only when both copies of the gene carry deleterious mutations, whereas heterozygous carriers (one mutated allele, one normal allele) are typically unaffected. Therefore, two copies of the deleterious allele are required for the disease to manifest.

178064.long_answer: Holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the HLCS gene. Since the mid-1990s, case reports and mutation surveys have accumulated more than two dozen distinct disease-causing variants. Reviews and databases such as OMIM, ClinVar, and HGMD list well over 30 different pathogenic or likely-pathogenic HLCS mutations (missense, nonsense, splice-site, small deletions/insertions) that disrupt attachment of biotin to carboxylases. Because the number of documented pathogenic HLCS variants clearly exceeds 20, the statement that there are ‘fewer than 20 known mutations’ is not consistent with the established literature.

757673.long_answer: In ductal-dependent congenital heart defects such as tricuspid atresia, continuous intravenous infusion of Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) is given to relax the smooth muscle of the ductus arteriosus. This prevents postnatal closure, maintaining a vital pathway for pulmonary or systemic blood flow until definitive surgical correction or shunt placement can be performed.

320479.long_answer: Serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D (25-OHD) concentrations of about 30–50 ng/mL (75–125 nmol/L) are generally considered vitamin-D-sufficient by most bone-health authorities (e.g., Endocrine Society, National Osteoporosis Foundation, International Osteoporosis Foundation). Observational studies consistently show that individuals whose 25-OHD levels fall below this range—particularly below 20 ng/mL—have lower bone-mineral density and a higher incidence of osteoporosis and fragility fractures. Meta-analyses of cohort studies and randomized trials indicate that raising 25-OHD into the 30 ng/mL or higher range improves calcium absorption, suppresses secondary hyperparathyroidism, and is associated with better bone mineralization, translating into a reduced risk of osteopenia/osteoporosis relative to vitamin-D-deficient individuals. While optimal targets can vary slightly between guidelines (the U.S. IOM considers ≥20 ng/mL adequate for most), the weight of evidence supports the conclusion that maintaining 25-OHD in the 30–50 ng/mL range correlates with a lower risk of osteoporosis compared with lower concentrations.

804444.long_answer: Cocaine, the substance responsible for prenatal cocaine exposure (PCE), is classified by the U.S. Controlled Substances Act as a Schedule II controlled substance. Schedule II drugs have a high potential for abuse but also accepted, restricted medical uses (e.g., as a topical anesthetic in otolaryngology), which places cocaine in this regulatory category.

398262.long_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis infection is called the “silent epidemic” because most cases are asymptomatic. A first-line treatment is the broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic doxycycline, which is given for seven days. The same drug is also widely prescribed as chemoprophylaxis against Plasmodium species in travelers to malaria-endemic regions, making doxycycline the antibiotic that fulfills both roles.

867818.long_answer: Cushing’s syndrome can be iatrogenic (exogenous) when a person receives pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids. Cortisol-like medications—such as oral prednisolone, intravenous methylprednisolone, and even high-dose or prolonged-use inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone, budesonide)—are mainstays in the treatment of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Chronic or high-dose exposure to these synthetic glucocorticoids suppresses the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and raises systemic glucocorticoid levels, producing the classical features of Cushing’s syndrome (moon face, truncal obesity, striae, proximal muscle weakness, osteoporosis, glucose intolerance, etc.). This phenomenon is well documented in clinical guidelines and pharmacology texts and is recognized by regulatory agencies as a potential adverse effect of both systemic and inhaled corticosteroids used for asthma and COPD. Therefore, the statement is supported by established biomedical consensus.

456140.long_answer: Iatrogenic (exogenous) Cushing’s syndrome is overwhelmingly due to chronic administration of systemic glucocorticoids; oral prednisone—the most widely prescribed glucocorticoid for inflammatory and autoimmune disorders such as asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus—accounts for the majority of these cases. Prolonged prednisone therapy raises circulating glucocorticoid levels, suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and produces the characteristic features of Cushing’s syndrome.

597964.long_answer: Perimyositis simply refers to inflammation of the perimysium, the connective-tissue sheath that surrounds muscle fascicles. Like other forms of myositis, this inflammation can arise from a variety of mechanisms—autoimmune (e.g., dermatomyositis, polymyositis), metabolic, drug-induced, or traumatic—as well as infectious (bacterial, viral, parasitic) causes. Because many documented cases of perimyositis occur in the setting of systemic autoimmune inflammatory myopathies with no detectable pathogen, infection is not an obligatory component. Therefore, it is incorrect to state that perimyositis always involves an infection.

929075.long_answer: When a pilonidal cyst becomes acutely infected and forms an abscess, the standard first-line treatment is a minor procedure called incision and drainage. Under local anesthesia, a small cut is made over the cyst to open it, release the accumulated pus, and decompress the cavity, which rapidly relieves pain and allows the infection to resolve. This simple office-based intervention is widely recommended in surgical guidelines before considering more extensive excisional surgery.

118939.long_answer: Most Lassa mammarenavirus infections are either entirely asymptomatic or cause only mild, non-specific illness. Epidemiological studies estimate that roughly 80% of infected individuals do not develop the classic, clinically recognizable Lassa fever. Only a minority (≈20%) progress to severe, symptomatic disease. Therefore, it is not typical for people to exhibit notable symptoms when infected with Lassa mammarenavirus.

318011.long_answer: Desferal is the trade name for deferoxamine (desferrioxamine), an iron-chelating drug. Chronic transfusion therapy for patients with β-thalassemia major leads to progressive iron overload, which must be controlled to prevent cardiac, hepatic and endocrine complications. For decades, subcutaneous or intravenous deferoxamine (Desferal) has been the standard and most widely used chelating agent for this purpose. Although newer oral chelators such as deferasirox and deferiprone are now available, international guidelines (e.g., WHO, TIF, AHA) continue to list Desferal as a first-line or alternative therapy, and it remains in common clinical use worldwide. Therefore, the statement that Desferal is commonly used as a chelating agent in the treatment of β-thalassemia is correct and consistent with established medical consensus.

318755.long_answer: Patients with beta-thalassemia major accumulate excess iron from chronic transfusions; the standard therapy to remove this iron is the chelating agent deferoxamine. Administered intravenously (or subcutaneously), deferoxamine binds free ferric iron to form ferrioxamine, which is then excreted in urine and bile, thereby lowering body iron stores and preventing organ damage.

137247.long_answer: For transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) the only FDA-approved therapy is tafamidis. In the phase-3 ATTR-ACT trial and in the prescribing information, the adverse events occurring ≥5 % and more often than with placebo were diarrhea, urinary-tract infection, and vaginal infection; no other side effects were consistently more frequent. Thus these three represent the common side effects of medications used to treat ATTR-CM.

564362.long_answer: Cinchonism is the constellation of toxic effects produced by large or prolonged doses of quinine (and related cinchona alkaloids). The alkaloid quinine was first successfully isolated from Cinchona bark in 1820 by the French chemists Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph-Bienaimé Caventou. This date is well documented in the history of pharmacology and marks the introduction of a purified antimalarial agent. Therefore, the statement that the medication which causes cinchonism was first isolated in 1820 is accurate.

477818.long_answer: Bacterial dysentery (classically caused by Shigella species) is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. The ‘Five Fs’—fingers, flies, fields, fluids, and food—describe the ways fecal matter can contaminate hands, vectors, soil, water, or meals, allowing pathogens to enter the mouth and infect new hosts.

212619.long_answer: Praziquantel is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic that increases calcium permeability of helminth membranes, causing rapid paralysis and death of the parasite. It is the first-line drug against all human Schistosoma species (schistosomiasis) and is also highly effective in single oral doses against cestode infections, including the dwarf tapeworm Hymenolepis nana and the rat tapeworm H. diminuta. Therefore, the same medication—praziquantel—is recommended for both conditions.

241841.long_answer: In Panayiotopoulos syndrome, autonomic seizures frequently begin with nausea—a diffuse epigastric unease that gives the child a strong urge to vomit. This symptom precedes or accompanies the characteristic gagging and actual vomiting seen during the seizures, and it is therefore the recognized autonomic manifestation involving a feeling of unease with an urge to vomit.

826431.long_answer: Panayiotopoulos syndrome, a benign childhood autonomic epilepsy, typically presents between 3–6 years of age with autonomic seizures marked by nausea, retching, and profuse vomiting, often accompanied by pallor and other autonomic signs. These characteristic ictal vomiting episodes distinguish it from other pediatric seizure syndromes.

535718.long_answer: The PTH1R gene encodes the classical parathyroid hormone 1 receptor, a G-protein–coupled receptor for parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide that controls calcium ion balance in bone and kidney. Activating mutations in PTH1R are the established cause of Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.

292484.long_answer: Fibromyalgia is considered a central sensitization syndrome because the key abnormality lies in heightened pain processing within the central nervous system—particularly the spinal cord dorsal horn and brain pain-modulating regions—rather than in peripheral tissues or nerves.

576547.long_answer: Schindler disease is caused by an inherited deficiency of the lysosomal exoglycosidase α-N-acetylgalactosaminidase (also called nagalase). In contrast, the same enzyme’s activity is markedly elevated in the blood of many cancer patients, where circulating α-N-acetylgalactosaminidase has been used as a tumor burden and progression marker. Thus, this enzyme both accumulates in cancer sera and is lacking in individuals with Schindler disease.

801430.long_answer: Minocycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic. All systemic tetracyclines, including minocycline, are contraindicated during pregnancy because they cross the placenta and can deposit in developing fetal bones and teeth, leading to permanent tooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, and inhibition of skeletal growth. The drug has historically carried FDA pregnancy category D (positive evidence of human fetal risk). Dermatology and obstetric guidelines therefore recommend that pregnant patients with rosacea avoid minocycline and other tetracyclines. Safer alternatives for rosacea during pregnancy include topical azelaic acid, topical metronidazole, and (when needed) certain macrolide antibiotics such as oral erythromycin. Consequently, minocycline is not considered suitable for treating rosacea in pregnant women.

353709.long_answer: Minocycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic that exists as conventional oral preparations and as a 1.5 % topical foam (marketed, e.g., as Zilxi) specifically approved for inflammatory rosacea. Beyond its antimicrobial activity, low-dose oral minocycline exerts anti-inflammatory effects and has been employed as a disease-modifying agent in rheumatoid arthritis, making it the tetracycline that fulfills both clinical uses.

401525.long_answer: Lou Gehrig’s disease is the common name for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a neurodegenerative disorder grouped with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and Parkinson’s disease. ALS is defined by the progressive degeneration and death of both upper motor neurons in the cerebral cortex and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and eventual paralysis.

687489.long_answer: Panayiotopoulos syndrome is an idiopathic childhood‐onset epilepsy characterized by predominantly autonomic seizures. The typical ictal picture begins with an ill-defined, diffuse feeling of malaise or epigastric/abdominal ‘unease’, rapidly followed by prominent autonomic signs such as nausea, retching, and actual vomiting. Large clinical series and the original descriptions by Panayiotopoulos report that more than two-thirds of seizures include nausea and vomiting, and that a vague, uncomfortable sensation (‘sickness’, ‘unease’) often precedes these gastrointestinal symptoms. Therefore, a diffuse sensation of unease accompanied by an urge to vomit is indeed a recognized and characteristic symptom of Panayiotopoulos syndrome.

522424.long_answer: Panayiotopoulos syndrome—also called benign childhood epilepsy with occipital paroxysms (Panayiotopoulos type)—is a benign focal epilepsy of childhood characterized by very long seizures dominated by autonomic symptoms such as nausea, retching, and profuse vomiting. Because these prolonged seizures can mimic gastroenteritis, migraine, or encephalitis, the condition is frequently misdiagnosed.

988010.long_answer: Indometacin and ibuprofen are both non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  All NSAIDs can potentially raise blood pressure through renal sodium and water retention, so hypertension is listed in their prescribing information as a possible cardiovascular adverse reaction.  However, in regulatory summaries (e.g., FDA labels, European SmPC, British National Formulary) hypertension is not classified as a “common” (≥1 % or ≥1/100) adverse effect for either drug.  For indometacin hypertension is usually described as ‘uncommon’ or ‘rare’; for ibuprofen it is reported as ‘rare’, ‘uncommon’, or ‘frequency not known,’ with gastrointestinal complaints, headache and rash being the common events instead.  Therefore, hypertension is not a common adverse effect for ibuprofen, and it is not consistently common for indometacin, so the two drugs do not share hypertension as a common adverse event.  Hence the statement is incorrect.

778929.long_answer: Indometacin (indomethacin) received U.S. FDA approval in 1965 as the prescription drug Indocin, whereas ibuprofen was not approved in the United States until 1974 (later becoming OTC in 1984). Therefore, indometacin was approved for medical use in the United States earlier than ibuprofen.

795804.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) is a group of rare, genetically-determined neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by prenatal or very early-life underdevelopment of the cerebellum and pons. Because these brain structures are critical for coordination, balance, muscle tone, and motor learning, children with PCH typically show profound global developmental delay. Most affected patients exhibit severe hypotonia, poor head control, and marked delay or absence of gross-motor milestones; many never achieve independent sitting or walking. Consequently, higher-level motor skills that build on basic ambulation—such as running, jumping, sliding, or swimming—are invariably delayed and often never reached. This consensus is well documented across clinical case series and reviews of PCH subtypes. Therefore, it is correct to state that a patient with pontocerebellar hypoplasia will experience delayed development in those skills.

596265.long_answer: After an acute myocardial infarction (heart attack), a range of mechanical and hemodynamic complications can develop. Cardiogenic shock is an early, life-threatening complication that arises when extensive myocardial damage impairs the heart’s pumping ability, leading to severe hypotension and systemic hypoperfusion. Ventricular aneurysm is a later structural complication in which infarcted ventricular wall tissue becomes thin and bulges outward during systole; it can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, or thrombus formation. Both conditions are well-documented, textbook complications of myocardial infarction, confirming the statement as correct.

533485.long_answer: Mutations in the WFS1 gene can indeed produce a form of nonsyndromic sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA6/14/38) that is characteristically limited to the low-frequency range, so affected individuals have trouble hearing low‐pitched sounds. However, nonsyndromic deafness does not make up three-quarters of all hearing-loss cases. Most hearing loss worldwide is acquired (e.g., age-related presbycusis, noise exposure, ototoxic drugs, infections). Among the genetically determined cases, roughly 70 % are nonsyndromic and 30 % are syndromic, but when all causes are considered, nonsyndromic genetic deafness represents only a minority of total hearing loss. Therefore the statement that nonsyndromic deafness both causes low-tone loss in WFS1 patients and “constitutes 75 % of all hearing loss cases” is partly correct on the first point and incorrect on the second, so overall it is not accurate.

754736.long_answer: Mutations in the WFS1 gene cause the autosomal-dominant form of nonsyndromic deafness DFNA6/14/38, which is typified by loss of hearing at low frequencies (e.g., trouble detecting the “m” in “moon”). WFS1 encodes wolframin, an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that is also critical for pancreatic β-cell function; intact WFS1 helps regulate insulin secretion and, consequently, blood glucose levels. Thus WFS1 links low-frequency hearing loss with glucose-control physiology.

247758.long_answer: Minimally differentiated acute myeloblastic leukemia (also called AML-M0 in the FAB classification) is classified under acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a group of myeloid-lineage blood cancers. Like other forms of AML, the disease is defined by clonal proliferation of immature myeloid precursor cells (blasts) that accumulate rapidly in the bone marrow and frequently spill over into the peripheral blood. The high burden of these abnormal blasts crowds out normal hematopoietic cells, leading to impaired production of functional red cells, white cells, and platelets. This pathophysiology matches the description given in the question, so the statement is consistent with established hematology consensus.

136660.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive overgrowth disorder genetically distinct from Simpson-Golabi-Behmel and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes is Perlman syndrome. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DIS3L2 gene, which encodes a 3′-5′ exoribonuclease that degrades uridylated RNAs. DIS3L2 is situated on the long arm of chromosome 2 (region 2q37), making chromosome 2 the locus of the pathogenic gene.

524170.long_answer: Keratolytic agents—such as salicylic acid, lactic acid, glycolic acid, and high-concentration urea—are routinely used to soften and remove the excess keratin that forms calluses. The same agents are part of standard dermatologic therapy for keratosis pilaris, where they help dissolve follicular keratin plugs and smooth the skin’s surface. Clinical guidelines and dermatology textbooks list topical keratolytics as first-line or adjunctive treatments for keratosis pilaris, supporting their effectiveness in both conditions. Thus, keratolytic products that work for calluses are also effective, and commonly recommended, for treating keratosis pilaris.

467635.long_answer: Conduritol B epoxide (CBE) is a cyclitol epoxide that covalently binds to the catalytic site of acid β-glucocerebrosidase, the lysosomal hydrolase that degrades glucocerebroside. This irreversible inhibition prevents substrate cleavage, and experimental administration of CBE reproduces the enzymatic deficiency seen in Gaucher’s disease.

491322.long_answer:
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is the first-line antiviral recommended by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the World Health Organization (WHO) and most national obstetric-infectious-disease guidelines for treatment of suspected or confirmed influenza, including the 2009 pandemic H1N1 (so-called “swine influenza”), in pregnant women.  

Safety: Although classified as FDA pregnancy category C, more than a decade of post-marketing surveillance, pregnancy exposure registries, and large observational studies involving several thousand exposed pregnancies have found no signal for increased congenital malformations, miscarriage, stillbirth, or other adverse fetal outcomes when oseltamivir is used at therapeutic doses. Animal studies show no teratogenic effects at exposures several-fold higher than those used clinically. The most common maternal adverse effects are mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting), which are manageable and not harmful to the fetus.  

Effectiveness: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor active against influenza A and B viruses, including the 2009 H1N1 strain. Randomized trials in non-pregnant adults and extensive observational data in pregnant patients demonstrate that starting therapy within 48 h of symptom onset shortens illness duration, reduces fever, and, most importantly, lowers the risk of severe complications, hospitalisation, pneumonia and mortality. Because pregnancy itself is a strong risk factor for severe influenza, the absolute benefit in this population is high.  

Guideline consensus: Current CDC, ACOG, RCOG and WHO guidance all state that the benefits of treating pregnant women with oseltamivir for suspected or confirmed influenza far outweigh potential risks, and treatment should not be withheld because of pregnancy.  

Therefore, based on established scientific and clinical consensus, Tamiflu is considered both safe and effective for a pregnant woman presenting with fever and cough due to swine influenza infection.

717130.long_answer: Anton syndrome (also called visual anosognosia) is classically produced by bilateral damage to the occipital lobes and, in many cases, associated injury to visual association pathways extending into the parietal or temporal cortex. The cortical destruction causes complete loss of visual perception (cortical blindness), and the accompanying disconnection of awareness networks leads patients to deny their deficit. Thus, the syndrome is intrinsically linked to structural brain injury—most frequently ischemic stroke, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, traumatic brain injury, or encephalitis affecting the visual cortices. Therefore, patients with Anton syndrome do indeed have demonstrable physiological (structural) damage to specific brain regions.

518487.long_answer: Malakoplakia is characteristically linked to infections by coliforms such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella, which belong to the Gram-negative group. Gram-negative bacteria do not retain the crystal violet–iodine complex during the decolorization step of Gram staining; instead they take up the counterstain (safranin) and appear pink. This staining property and their frequent isolation from malakoplakia lesions make Gram-negative bacteria the correct classification.

932511.long_answer: In newborns with high or complex anorectal malformations, surgeons commonly perform a colostomy within the first 24 hours after birth. In this operation, the colon is brought through the abdominal wall to create a stoma, providing an alternative pathway for feces to leave the body while protecting the malformed distal rectum until definitive repair can be done.

276421.long_answer: Calamine lotion (a topical preparation containing zinc oxide and ferric oxide) is widely used to relieve pruritus, mild inflammation, and irritation associated with contact dermatitis, insect bites, and other superficial skin disturbances. Its mechanism is primarily protective and antipruritic: it forms a soothing barrier on the skin, provides a mild astringent effect, and can reduce itching. Because it is applied topically and has negligible systemic absorption, calamine is considered safe for use during pregnancy; it is not associated with teratogenicity or other fetal risks in the medical literature and is routinely recommended as a first-line, non-pharmacologic measure for pruritic dermatoses in pregnant patients. Therefore, using calamine lotion to alleviate the itching and irritation of contact dermatitis in a pregnant woman is consistent with established dermatologic and obstetric practice.

667129.long_answer: Erythema refers to the reddish discoloration of skin that results from vasodilation and increased blood flow in superficial capillaries. This hallmark finding is commonly observed in conditions such as erythromelalgia, where episodic vasodilation produces intense warmth, redness, and pain in the affected extremities.

447998.long_answer: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) produces a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur that is classically loudest at the left lower sternal border because blood flows from the high-pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle throughout systole. This left-to-right shunt across the interventricular septum is the most common congenital heart lesion associated with such a murmur.

974607.long_answer:
Cabergoline is a dopamine-agonist of the ergot class and is the first-line drug for shrinking a prolactinoma and normalising serum prolactin.  From a hepatic-safety standpoint, cabergoline is considered to have a very low rate of clinically important liver injury.  Post-marketing surveillance and the LiverTox/NIH database list only rare, usually mild, transient elevations of aminotransferases and extremely uncommon case reports of clinically apparent hepatitis.  No consistent pattern of cholestatic liver injury has been described and cabergoline is not classified as hepatotoxic.

The prescribing information does not list hepatic or cholestatic disease as a contraindication.  Pharmacokinetic studies show that in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A or B) exposure to cabergoline increases modestly (≈30–40 %), but no dose adjustment is required; the advice is simply to use the lowest effective dose and monitor liver tests if there is pre-existing liver disease.

Therefore, in a patient who already has cholestasis but requires treatment for a proven prolactinoma, standard clinical guidance supports the use of cabergoline, provided that baseline and periodic liver-function tests are obtained and other potential causes of cholestasis are addressed.  In short, current scientific and regulatory consensus indicates that cabergoline can be used safely—with routine monitoring—in patients with cholestasis.

634256.long_answer: Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH) is a rare, usually autosomal-dominant genodermatosis caused most often by pathogenic variants in the ADAR gene. Clinically it presents in childhood with a mixture of hyper- and hypopigmented macules distributed mainly on the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet, sometimes extending to the face and forearms. Because the hallmark manifestations involve the skin’s pigmentation and distribution of lesions, it is classified among inherited pigmentary skin disorders. All major dermatology and genetic-disease references (e.g., OMIM, Orphanet, Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology) describe DSH as a cutaneous condition. Therefore, it is indeed considered a type of skin condition.

942304.long_answer: Spondylolisthesis is the forward (or occasionally backward) slipping of one vertebral body over the one below it. It involves the vertebrae themselves, not the inter-vertebral disc. The popular term “slipped disc” refers to a herniated or prolapsed inter-vertebral disc, in which disc material bulges or extrudes beyond its normal confines. Therefore, spondylolisthesis is not what is commonly meant by a slipped disc—two distinct conditions with different pathoanatomy, causes, and treatments.

753789.long_answer: Cystic hygroma is the older clinical term for a congenital macrocystic lymphatic malformation. In the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) classification, lymphatic malformations are one of the major categories of vascular malformations (alongside capillary, venous, arteriovenous, etc.). Therefore, by current accepted nomenclature, a cystic hygroma is indeed a type of vascular malformation (specifically a lymphatic malformation).

482281.long_answer: The lymphatic malformation termed a cystic hygroma (literally a “water tumor”) is most commonly detected by prenatal ultrasound in the second trimester. Such second-trimester cystic hygromas are strongly associated with monosomy X, or Turner syndrome (45,X), reflecting the characteristic lymphatic outflow obstruction seen in this chromosomal disorder.

988122.long_answer: Fox–Fordyce disease involves apocrine sweat glands, which remain essentially inactive until they are stimulated by rising sex hormones at puberty; the disease commonly manifests once these glands first become functional during adolescence.

702504.long_answer:
Fainting (syncope) is a well-described clinical manifestation of each condition.  
• Pulmonary hypertension, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension or advanced chronic thrombo-embolic disease, can limit the ability of the right heart to increase output during exertion. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure leads to exertional dizziness or overt syncope, and guidelines list syncope as a classic symptom of moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypertension.  
• Tachycardia—especially pathologic forms such as supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, or atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response—can abruptly reduce ventricular filling time and cardiac output. This drop in cerebral perfusion commonly produces presyncope or frank syncope, which is why fainting is a key warning symptom in patients with rapid heart rhythms.  
Therefore, fainting is recognized in the medical literature as a possible symptom of both pulmonary hypertension and tachycardia.

100223.long_answer: The extensor digitorum brevis is an intrinsic dorsal foot muscle whose tendon slips insert into the bases of the middle phalanges of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th toes, producing their extension at the metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. Anatomically it is supplied by the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve, and in many individuals receives additional motor fibers from the accessory deep peroneal nerve, making it the only foot muscle routinely innervated by both of these nerves.

187696.long_answer: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory agent that disrupts microtubule assembly to blunt neutrophil chemotaxis. It is recommended for treatment and prophylaxis of acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout), and it is the standard lifelong therapy for familial Mediterranean fever, where it prevents febrile serositis attacks and secondary amyloidosis.

194351.long_answer: Livedoid vasculopathy (formerly called livedoid vasculitis) presents with recurrent, painful ulcers on the lower legs that heal leaving porcelain-white, atrophic ‘atrophie blanche’ scars. It was historically regarded as a form of small-vessel vasculitis, but is now understood to be a thrombotic microvascular disorder.

150011.long_answer: Livedoid vasculopathy is now regarded as a primary thrombotic vasculopathy: histology shows fibrin thrombi and hyalinized vessel walls with little or no leukocytoclastic inflammation, and clinical response is best to anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy rather than anti-inflammatory drugs. Therefore it is not categorized as an inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis but as a disorder of cutaneous microvascular thrombosis.

233227.long_answer: In hydrocephalus the stretched or compressed sixth cranial (abducens) nerve, which innervates the lateral rectus muscle that produces outward gaze, can be injured. This results in a focal neurological deficit known as abducens (VI) nerve palsy, characterized by impaired eye abduction and horizontal diplopia.

600200.long_answer: Congenital heart defects (CHDs)—such as ventricular or atrial septal defects, outflow-tract obstructions, coronary artery anomalies, or valve malformations—can produce cardiovascular complications including myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, or ventricular hypertrophy. All of these pathophysiological changes may manifest clinically as chest pain, particularly in older children or adults who have survived with a CHD or have undergone partial repair. Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis is a skeletal dysplasia that is well documented to be accompanied, in some patients, by a variety of CHDs. Therefore, if an individual with osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis has an associated congenital heart defect, that heart defect can indeed be a source of chest pain. The statement is consistent with established clinical knowledge.

819301.long_answer: The PNKD gene (formerly MR-1), whose mutations cause paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia, is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 2 (region 2q32–q35).

745330.long_answer: The tumor-suppressor gene TP53, which encodes the p53 protein known as the “guardian of the genome,” is frequently mutated by ultraviolet (especially UV-B)‐induced DNA damage. These UV-signature mutations accumulate in keratinocytes of sun-exposed skin, driving the dysplastic changes that manifest clinically as actinic keratoses and can progress to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

803330.long_answer: Retinoschisin, encoded by the X-linked RS1 gene, is a secreted cell-adhesion protein whose absence or mutation causes X-linked juvenile retinoschisis. Functional studies show that retinoschisin binds to photoreceptors and bipolar cells to maintain cell-cell adhesion and laminar architecture; without it, the retinal layers split and disorganize. Thus retinoschisin is indispensable for proper cellular organization of the retina.

771463.long_answer: Standard therapies used to control acne rosacea are not uniformly safe during pregnancy. Several first-line or escalation drugs have well-documented risks to the fetus: oral tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) can impair fetal bone and tooth development and are contraindicated; oral isotretinoin is highly teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated; some topical vasoconstrictors (brimonidine, oxymetazoline) and topical ivermectin lack adequate safety data and are generally avoided. Although a few agents such as topical metronidazole or azelaic acid are considered relatively low risk (FDA pregnancy category B), treatment choices must be individualized and many commonly used rosacea drugs cannot be given safely. Therefore the statement that "typical treatment drugs are always safe for pregnant women" is incorrect.

343388.long_answer:
Sarcoglycan genes (e.g., SGCA, SGCB, SGCG, SGCD, SGCE, SGCZ) encode the sarcoglycan proteins that assemble with dystrophin, dystroglycans, and other partners to form the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in skeletal and cardiac muscle. This complex links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix, thereby stabilizing both the cytoskeleton and the sarcolemma during muscle contraction. Loss-of-function mutations in sarcoglycan genes weaken this structural linkage and lead to membrane fragility, which is why they cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.   

The second part of the statement is also accurate: the cytoskeleton (actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments together with associated motor proteins) not only provides structural support but drives intracellular transport, organelle positioning, vesicle trafficking, and overall movement of cellular contents. Thus, saying that the cytoskeleton "facilitates motion of the cellular contents" is fully consistent with established cell-biology knowledge.   

Because both components of the statement are supported by well-accepted scientific consensus, it is NOT incorrect to say them.

949678.long_answer: Maternal intake of the sedative-anticonvulsant phenytoin (a hydantoin derivative) during pregnancy can cause fetal hydantoin syndrome. This teratogenic disorder is characterized by craniofacial anomalies such as orbital hypertelorism, broad and depressed nasal bridge, epicanthal folds, growth deficiency and limb defects, all resulting from phenytoin’s interference with embryonic neural-crest development.

654842.long_answer: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13: the fetus possesses three copies of chromosome 13. This chromosomal abnormality produces a characteristic constellation of congenital defects, and first-trimester ultrasound frequently shows cystic hygroma among its early markers.

585995.long_answer: Blue cone monochromacy is an X-linked inherited cone photoreceptor disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the long- (OPN1LW) and medium- (OPN1MW) wavelength-sensitive opsin genes. As a result, the L- and M-cones are absent or non-functional, leaving only the short-wavelength (S, “blue”) cones and rods intact. The primary defect therefore resides in the cone photoreceptors themselves. Retinal ganglion cells are post-synaptic neurons that relay visual information from all photoreceptors to the brain; they are not the site of the genetic or cellular defect that produces blue cone monochromacy. Consequently, retinal ganglion cells are not responsible for the disease.

874494.long_answer: Sézary syndrome is recognized as the leukemic, systemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, whereas classic mycosis fungoides is primarily a skin-limited disease. The diagnostic triad of Sézary syndrome consists of: (1) diffuse erythroderma, (2) generalized lymphadenopathy, and (3) significant numbers of clonally malignant CD4-positive T cells (Sézary cells) detectable in the peripheral blood. These blood and systemic manifestations distinguish it from mycosis fungoides, which usually presents with patch- or plaque-stage skin lesions without leukemic involvement early in its course. Therefore, the statement accurately reflects the established clinical distinction between Sézary syndrome and mycosis fungoides.

590744.long_answer: Noonan syndrome is a RASopathy caused by germ-line mutations in RAS/MAPK pathway genes such as PTPN11, SOS1, KRAS or RAF1. Clinically it presents with short stature, webbed neck, hypertelorism (wide-spaced eyes), low-set posteriorly rotated ears and other characteristic facial features. Because the same signaling pathway regulates hematopoietic proliferation, affected individuals have an increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and other leukemias, linking the syndrome to a leukemia predisposition.

897493.long_answer: An adrenal cortical adenoma is a common benign tumour of the adrenal cortex, incidentally detected in roughly 5–10 % of autopsies. When the adenoma arises from the zona glomerulosa and autonomously secretes aldosterone, it produces primary hyperaldosteronism, known clinically as Conn’s syndrome.

556401.long_answer: Vasopressin, often called antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is normally secreted in higher amounts at night to concentrate urine. In many children with nocturnal enuresis this nocturnal surge is inadequate, so less water is reabsorbed in the kidneys, resulting in increased overnight urine volume and bed-wetting.

117978.long_answer: Propionic acidemia is an autosomal recessive organic acidemia caused by deficiency of the biotin-dependent enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase (encoded by PCCA and PCCB genes). Loss of this enzyme blocks conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA, leading to accumulation of propionic acid and secondary elevations of glycine accompanied by metabolic acidosis and ketosis (‘ketotic hyperglycinemia’). The presence of ketosis distinguishes propionic acidemia from glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia), which is due to defects in the glycine cleavage system rather than propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

631767.long_answer: In cystinuria, urinary cystine derives from the metabolism of the essential amino acid methionine; therefore, dietary restriction of methionine-rich protein is recommended along with hydration, citrate, and low-salt intake to lower urinary cystine concentration and reduce stone formation.

753451.long_answer: Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is the extracorporeal circulation technique used during open-heart surgery to take over the pumping and oxygenating functions of the heart and lungs. Exposure of blood to the artificial circuit triggers a systemic inflammatory response, complement activation, and endothelial injury, making CPB an established indirect (extrapulmonary) risk factor for developing acute respiratory distress syndrome.

851254.long_answer: After SARS-CoV-2 infection, some paediatric patients develop a Kawasaki-like hyperinflammatory condition officially termed Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C, also called PIMS-TS). It is characterized by fever, systemic inflammation, and involvement of multiple organs, and was first recognized during the COVID-19 pandemic as a post-infectious immune response distinct from classic Kawasaki disease.

110394.long_answer: Jaundice is the yellow discoloration of skin and sclerae that occurs when serum total bilirubin rises above ~3 mg/dL. It commonly develops in chronic, progressive hepatobiliary diseases such as cirrhosis or primary sclerosing cholangitis affecting the liver and gallbladder ducts, reflecting impaired bilirubin metabolism and excretion.

734312.long_answer: Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) results from deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase, which normally catalyzes the hydrolysis of terminal unsulfated α-L-iduronosidic linkages in glycosaminoglycans such as dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Loss of this hydrolase causes accumulation of these GAGs, producing the characteristic clinical features of the disorder.

694212.long_answer: Canavan disease is a leukodystrophy in which the brain’s white-matter myelin breaks down. The myelin sheath in the central nervous system is produced by oligodendrocytes; therefore, the degenerating material responsible for Canavan disease is formed by oligodendrocyte cells.

661293.long_answer: Canavan disease is an autosomal-recessive leukodystrophy caused by mutations in the ASPA gene that eliminate or greatly reduce activity of the enzyme aspartoacylase. Loss of this enzyme prevents normal catabolism of N-acetylaspartate in the brain, leading to its accumulation, osmotic swelling, and profound deterioration of myelin. The resultant spongy degeneration of white matter produces the severe neurodevelopmental impairment that characterizes this leukodystrophy.

260422.long_answer: In 2018 the World Health Organization (WHO) added the term “Disease X” to its R&D Blueprint list of priority pathogens. The designation serves as a place-holder for a future, currently unknown infectious agent that could cause a serious international epidemic—analogous to how the term “X-ray” once denoted an unexplained form of radiation. By including Disease X, WHO highlights the need for flexible preparedness and research capabilities even when the exact pathogen has not yet been identified.

988327.long_answer: Tracheobronchomegaly (also called Mounier-Kuhn syndrome) is generally classified as a congenital anomaly of the trachea and main bronchi. Pathologic studies show deficient or absent elastic fibers and smooth-muscle elements in the airway walls that are present from birth, leading to marked dilation of the tracheobronchial tree. Because it arises from abnormal development of the respiratory tract and is present (even if undiagnosed) at birth, it is regarded in the medical literature as a congenital condition—that is, a birth defect.

405530.long_answer: The disorder is Social anxiety disorder (social phobia), defined by marked fear or anxiety during social interactions or performance situations. Epidemiologic studies show that about two-thirds (≈66%) of affected individuals meet criteria for at least one additional psychiatric condition, and clinical research consistently reports a notable comorbidity with body dysmorphic disorder, which frequently emerges in socially anxious patients preoccupied with perceived appearance flaws.

918710.long_answer: In AAA (Allgrove) syndrome, the earliest clinical manifestation is often alacrima—markedly reduced or absent tear secretion. This tear-production defect can be objectively confirmed with a Schirmer's test, which measures tear wetting of filter paper; patients with alacrima show little to no wetting, supporting the diagnosis.

126941.long_answer: Mutations in the BLM gene, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase, lead to Bloom syndrome—a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by genomic instability, growth deficiency, sun-sensitive skin rash, immunodeficiency, and a markedly elevated cancer risk.

295356.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy commonly involves severe autonomic failure, and one hallmark sign is orthostatic hypotension—an excessive drop in blood pressure when moving from supine to upright. A tilt-table test provokes this postural change under controlled conditions, allowing clinicians to document the characteristic fall in systolic (≥20 mm Hg) and/or diastolic (≥10 mm Hg) pressure that confirms autonomic dysfunction in MSA.

475130.long_answer: The “hot cross bun” sign—cruciform T2-hyperintensity in the pons due to degeneration of pontocerebellar fibers—is a classic MRI feature of multiple system atrophy (especially the cerebellar subtype, MSA-C). MSA is a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy that typically presents with prominent autonomic failure (dysautonomia) such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary and bowel dysfunction, linking the imaging finding to the clinical feature in the question.

536132.long_answer: Epidermal nevus syndrome is a congenital multisystem disorder characterized by epidermal nevi together with neurological abnormalities such as seizures, intellectual disability, and structural brain malformations; these manifestations reflect involvement of the central nervous system.

281973.long_answer: Dercum’s disease (adiposis dolorosa) is characterized by chronic, often severe pain in multiple lipomatous fatty deposits. Case series, reviews and expert consensus uniformly describe this pain as poorly responsive to standard non-opioid analgesics. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been tried frequently, but the published literature reports little or no sustained relief. Most reviews therefore consider the pain 'refractory' to NSAIDs and recommend alternative measures (e.g., lidocaine infusions, liposuction, interferon-α, low-dose naltrexone, neuromodulators, or surgical excision) when simple analgesics fail. Hence, the best-supported consensus is that the pain associated with Dercum’s disease does not meaningfully respond to NSAID therapy.

548483.long_answer: Chondromalacia patellae is the histopathologic term for softening and degeneration of the articular cartilage on the undersurface of the patella.  In everyday clinical use, however, many clinicians loosely apply the term to describe the broader clinical picture of anterior knee pain or patellofemoral pain syndrome—pain that arises from abnormal tracking or mechanical stress between the kneecap (patella) and the femur.  Although purists reserve “chondromalacia” for documented cartilage changes and prefer “patellofemoral pain syndrome” for idiopathic anterior knee pain, the two terms are often used interchangeably in practice.  Therefore, the statement that chondromalacia patellae is sometimes used synonymously with knee pain related to patella-femur problems is accurate.

561736.long_answer: Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD) arises in people with Parkinson’s disease—the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer’s. About one-third of Parkinson’s patients eventually develop this dementia. Together with Dementia with Lewy bodies, PDD forms the two recognized clinical subtypes of Lewy body dementia, both characterized by α-synuclein Lewy body pathology in brain regions governing cognition and movement.

545632.long_answer: Anterior horn cell diseases classically include amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), and poliomyelitis/other viral anterior horn cell infections. Spinal muscular atrophy is a genetically determined disorder caused in almost all cases by homozygous deletions or other loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 (Survival Motor Neuron 1) gene on chromosome 5q13. Therefore, among the principal anterior horn diseases, SMA is indeed associated with mutation of the SMN1 gene, making the statement correct.

784532.long_answer: Henry Molaison—long studied under the abbreviation "H.M."—underwent a bilateral medial temporal lobe resection (including most of the hippocampi) in 1953 to relieve intractable epilepsy. The surgery cured much of his seizures but left him with profound anterograde amnesia (inability to form new explicit memories) and graded retrograde amnesia for events preceding the operation. His case was pivotal in demonstrating the critical role of the medial temporal lobe, especially the hippocampus, in declarative memory formation.

679190.long_answer: Fetal karyotype analysis for suspected trisomy-8 is most commonly performed on cells obtained by amniocentesis or chorionic-villus sampling (CVS). In the case of amniocentesis—the procedure in which a needle is passed through the maternal abdominal wall and uterus to withdraw amniotic fluid—the needle has to penetrate the fetal membranes (the chorion and the amnion) in order to reach the amniotic cavity and aspirate the fluid that contains fetal cells. Therefore, when trisomy 8 is being diagnosed by amniocentesis, the needle does indeed puncture the amnion.

330697.long_answer: Craniosynostosis is defined as the premature (early) fusion of one or more cranial sutures. When it involves the metopic suture, the suture closes earlier than normal and produces trigonocephaly. A persistent (or un-fused) metopic suture is the converse situation: the metopic suture remains open beyond the age at which it normally fuses (usually by 6–8 years of age) and is considered a normal anatomic variant, not a pathologic condition. Therefore, craniosynostosis is associated with early closure—not persistence—of the metopic suture. Hence, a persistent metopic suture is not associated with craniosynostosis.

993780.long_answer: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a mesangial proliferative form of glomerulonephritis characterized by episodic gross or microscopic hematuria that often follows an upper respiratory tract infection. Because both IgA nephropathy and thin basement membrane disease can present with otherwise unexplained hematuria, clinicians must differentiate between them to guide prognosis and management.

623852.long_answer: Needle electromyography (EMG) is a diagnostic procedure in which fine needle electrodes are inserted into muscle tissue and an electromyograph records the electrical activity at rest and during contraction.
