This test is routinely recommended in suspected myositis because characteristic patterns—such as spontaneous fibrillation potentials and short-duration, low-amplitude motor unit action potentials—help confirm muscle inflammation and differentiate it from neuropathic disorders.

990890.long_answer: Human chromosome 7 is approximately 159 million base pairs long and was the chromosome found to be present in two copies inherited solely from the mother in the landmark 1988 report of maternal uniparental disomy, the first documented case of UPD in humans.

256489.long_answer: Post-transfusion purpura is most effectively managed with high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), a pooled mixture of IgG antibodies collected from thousands of donors. IVIG modulates immune responses and is widely used for diverse autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, making it the standard therapy for this condition.

195446.long_answer: Lhermitte–Duclos disease, also termed dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma, is a rare, slow-growing lesion of the cerebellum characterized by hypertrophic ganglion cells that expand the cerebellar cortex. It is often regarded as a hamartomatous rather than a true neoplastic process and shows strong association with Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome).

170022.long_answer: Naxos disease is an autosomal-recessive syndrome caused by mutations in the desmosomal protein plakoglobin. It combines diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and woolly hair with the inherited cardiac disorder arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (also called arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia), characterized by fibro-fatty replacement of right ventricular myocardium and ventricular arrhythmias.

228887.long_answer: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is a clonal/myeloproliferative neoplasm in which malignant precursor cells drive persistent, marked eosinophilia (>1.5 × 10⁹ cells/L). Because the eosinophils arise from a primary (intrinsic) genetic abnormality—such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB or FGFR1 rearrangements—HES is often termed primary hypereosinophilia. This malignant, clonal process is clearly distinguished from the far more common secondary (reactive) eosinophilia seen in allergic diseases or parasitic infections.

141686.long_answer: The small reef-dwelling rabbitfish Siganus spinus ranges widely across the Indo-Pacific and is notorious for occasionally causing ichthyoallyeinotoxism—an intoxication that produces drunkenness-like or hallucinogenic symptoms in people who eat its flesh. Because of this effect it earned the popular nickname “the fish that inebriates.”

740975.long_answer: Seckel syndrome type 1 has been linked to biallelic mutations in the ATR gene. ATR is located on human chromosome 3q23 and encodes the large serine/threonine-protein kinase ATR (ATM- and Rad3-related), a key regulator of the DNA damage response. Defective ATR signaling impairs replication-stress checkpoints, leading to the growth retardation, microcephaly and neurodevelopmental defects characteristic of this form of Seckel syndrome.

225638.long_answer: Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome is classically caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC16A2 gene, which encodes the thyroid-hormone transporter MCT8. Independent studies of families with X-linked leukoencephalopathy (characterised by hypomyelination on MRI) have identified missense and nonsense mutations in the same SLC16A2 gene, demonstrating that loss of MCT8 function underlies both AHDS and this form of X-linked white-matter disease.

515597.long_answer: The CYP7B1 gene, located on chromosome 8q21, encodes the enzyme 25-hydroxycholesterol 7-α-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450 7B1). Loss-of-function mutations in CYP7B1 cause the autosomal-recessive form of hereditary spastic paraplegia known as SPG5A.

293076.long_answer: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. It has no definitive cure and, according to the 2020 Atlas of MS, about 2.8 million people worldwide were living with the condition that year. Optic neuritis—an inflammatory attack on the optic nerve causing sudden vision loss or pain—is one of the most common presenting manifestations of MS and frequently occurs during disease relapses.

713935.long_answer: Central nervous system malignant rhabdoid tumours (also called atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumours) that carry loss of the INI1/hSNF5 tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 22 most often arise in the posterior fossa, characteristically in the lateral posterior fossa at the cerebellopontine angle rather than the midline vermis or fourth ventricle.

847556.long_answer: Malignant rhabdoid tumor was first described in 1978 by Beckwith and Palmer as a rhabdomyosarcomatoid (rhabdoid) variant of Wilms tumor of the kidney. Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) was later recognized as a distinct central-nervous-system entity in 1996 (e.g., Biggs et al., Brain Pathology 6:381-391, 1996). The interval between 1978 and 1996 is therefore 18 years.

726206.long_answer: The laryngeal ventricle is a small mucosa-lined recess situated between the true (vocal) and false (vestibular) vocal folds. From its anterior aspect arises a blind-ending pouch called the laryngeal saccule (also known as the appendix of the ventricle). When this ventricle–saccule complex dilates and becomes air-filled, it forms a laryngocele. Clinically, a laryngocele is defined as an abnormal, air-containing out-pouching of the laryngeal saccule or ventricle that can extend internally within the larynx or externally through the thyrohyoid membrane. Therefore, dilatation of the laryngeal ventricle (or its saccule) is indeed associated with, and essentially constitutes, the condition termed laryngocele.

479239.long_answer: Cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion) is associated with congenital heart defects in roughly one-third of affected infants. Among the cardiac anomalies reported, ventricular septal defects (a defect in the wall dividing the left and right ventricles) are one of the most frequently observed lesions, along with patent ductus arteriosus and atrial septal defects. Therefore, a defect in the ventricular septum is indeed considered a common finding in cri du chat syndrome.

536294.long_answer: During myocardial ischemia or an acute myocardial infarction, the deprivation of oxygen and metabolic substrates rapidly alters the electrophysiologic properties of heart muscle. Ischemic cardiomyocytes develop ATP-dependent ion-channel dysfunction, acidosis, and membrane depolarization, which raise the resting membrane potential and inactivate fast sodium channels. As a result, the affected region becomes partially or completely unexcitable (unresponsive) to incoming or externally delivered electrical stimuli. The mixture of unexcitable tissue and surviving but slowed-conduction fibers sets up zones of conduction block and heterogeneous refractoriness. These changes are well-recognized substrates for serious, sometimes fatal, ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Hence, established cardiac electrophysiology and clinical evidence support that ischemia or heart attack can render cardiac tissue unresponsive to stimuli and thereby predispose to life-threatening arrhythmias.

575712.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the OCTN2 (SLC22A5) carnitine transporter. The defect prevents adequate uptake of carnitine into cells and re-absorption of carnitine in the kidney, leading to markedly reduced intracellular carnitine stores. Carnitine is required for the carnitine shuttle that transfers long-chain fatty acyl-CoA molecules from the cytosol into mitochondria, the organelles where β-oxidation and most cellular ATP generation occur. Without sufficient carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot be moved into mitochondria in normal amounts, so mitochondrial β-oxidation – and therefore ATP production from fatty acids – is severely impaired. This mechanistic link is the basis for the characteristic hypoketotic hypoglycemia, myopathy, and cardiomyopathy seen in the disorder. Hence, the statement accurately describes the pathogenic consequence of systemic primary carnitine deficiency.

446401.long_answer: Mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD, also known as hyper-IgD syndrome) is an autoinflammatory disorder that typically manifests with recurrent febrile attacks. In clinical practice MKD itself is considered in the differential diagnosis of a patient who presents with ‘fever of unknown origin’ (FUO) or with periodic fevers. The converse is not true: “fever of unknown origin” is not a specific disease entity that is listed among the conditions clinicians must distinguish from MKD; rather, it is a descriptive clinical category that often leads physicians to include MKD as a possible underlying cause. Therefore stating that ‘fever of unknown origin is part of the differential diagnosis of mevalonate kinase deficiency’ reverses the accepted relationship and is not in line with established medical usage.

191338.long_answer: The anticholinergic chemical-warfare incapacitating agent 3-Quinuclidinyl benzilate, code-named BZ, was tested by the U.S. Army in the late 1960s. Military reports noted that volunteer subjects under the drug’s prolonged delirium not only hallucinated but also began to adopt and reinforce each other’s hallucinations and delusional ideas, a presentation explicitly compared to folie à deux (shared psychosis). These observations led investigators to describe BZ as capable of producing a ‘shared psychotic-like’ state among exposed individuals.

779207.long_answer: Klein-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type III) is Waardenburg syndrome accompanied by various congenital musculoskeletal anomalies of the upper limbs and shoulder girdle. Published clinical descriptions list abnormalities such as hypoplasia of the scapular muscles, humeroscapular dysplasia and ‘scapula alata’ or ‘winged scapula.’  A winged scapula presents clinically as a medial scapular border that protrudes straight out from the back when the patient pushes against resistance.  Therefore, a scapula whose medial border sticks out (winged scapula) is indeed one of the skeletal manifestations that can be seen in Klein-Waardenburg syndrome.

983488.long_answer: In familial hypercholesterolemia, mutations in the LDL receptor prevent the normal clathrin-coated pit binding and internalization of LDL particles. This defect specifically disrupts receptor-mediated endocytosis—the selective uptake pathway that normally brings LDL–receptor complexes into hepatocytes—leading to elevated plasma LDL levels.

304370.long_answer: Autosomal dominant multiple epiphyseal dysplasia can result from heterozygous mutations in the COL9A2 gene, which encodes the α2 chain of type IX collagen. COL9A2 is located on chromosome 1p34, and defects in this collagen subunit impair cartilage extracellular matrix integrity, leading to the disordered epiphyseal ossification that characterises the disease.

829711.long_answer: The human TP53 gene encodes the tumor suppressor protein p53. The reference (canonical) isoform—UniProt entry P04637-1—consists of exactly 393 amino acid residues, spanning the N-terminal transactivation domain, central DNA-binding domain, and C-terminal tetramerization and regulatory regions.

808942.long_answer: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE) syndrome is classically associated with a diffuse, symmetric leukoencephalopathy—i.e., involvement of the cerebral white matter—visible as high-signal areas on T2-weighted or FLAIR MRI. This white-matter change is considered one of the radiologic hallmarks of the disorder and is present in the vast majority of documented cases. Therefore, the statement that MNGIE does not affect the white matter of the brain is incorrect and contradicts established clinical and imaging evidence.

656727.long_answer: In familial dysautonomia (Riley–Day syndrome), impaired swallowing coordination and frequent vomiting lead to recurrent aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents. This material carries bacteria into the distal airways, producing aspiration pneumonia—an inflammatory lung condition in which the alveoli become infected and inflamed.

220313.long_answer: Human cytomegalovirus (CMV), a betaherpesvirus categorized within the TORCH group of congenital infections, is the leading viral cause of sensorineural hearing loss in newborns. Transplacental CMV transmission can damage the developing inner ear, resulting in permanent deafness.

236369.long_answer: Chronic hyperglycaemia in diabetes causes microvascular injury and autonomic neuropathy that reduce penile arterial inflow and cavernous nerve function, leading to erectile dysfunction. When lifestyle measures, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, and other conservative options fail, the definitive surgical remedy is implantation of a penile prosthesis, making erectile dysfunction the form of sexual dysfunction most characteristically managed with such implants.

877413.long_answer: Clinical trials such as the MiG (Metformin in Gestational diabetes) study and subsequent meta-analyses show that metformin therapy in pregnant women with diabetes results in lower mean birth weight and a significantly reduced incidence of fetal macrosomia compared with insulin treatment, making metformin more effective than insulin at preventing macrosomia.

108902.long_answer: Yes. In normal purine catabolism, the enzyme xanthine oxidoreductase (also called xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase) catalyzes the final step: conversion of xanthine to uric acid, the principal breakdown product of purine nucleotides. Type I hereditary xanthinuria is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the XDH gene that encodes this enzyme. The resulting enzyme deficiency blocks the xanthine-to-uric-acid reaction, leading to accumulation of xanthine, very low serum/urine uric acid, and the clinical picture of Type I xanthinuria. Thus, a deficiency of the enzyme responsible for converting xanthine into the final purine breakdown product directly causes Type I xanthinuria.

863701.long_answer: Punctate inner choroidopathy (PIC) is a white-dot inflammatory choroiditis that typically occurs in young, moderately to highly myopic women. Unlike related entities such as multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis, PIC shows little to no inflammation in the anterior chamber or vitreous, making this absence of intraocular inflammation a distinguishing clinical feature.

356637.long_answer: Cowden syndrome is an autosomal-dominant PTEN-hamartoma tumor syndrome caused by germ-line mutations in the PTEN tumor-suppressor gene located at chromosome 10q23.3. Clinically, it features multiple hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract and characteristic mucocutaneous lesions such as trichilemmomas. This contrasts with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, which involves STK11 (LKB1) mutations on chromosome 19.

162538.long_answer: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is strongly paraneoplastic in women, and about 50 % of affected female patients harbor an ovarian teratoma— a germ-cell tumor (usually a mature cystic teratoma) that characteristically contains ectoderm-derived tissues such as hair, teeth, or bone. Removal of the ovarian teratoma often improves or cures the encephalitis, underscoring the causal association.

988326.long_answer: LGMD D5 is produced by pathogenic variants in COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3. These three genes encode the α-chains of type VI collagen, and the same genes also cause collagen VI-related myopathies such as Bethlem myopathy and Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy. Thus, the diseases involve variants of type VI collagen.

607348.long_answer: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by abnormal thickening of the myocardium, which can impair ventricular filling and increase left-sided filling pressures. This hemodynamic disturbance often leads to exertional or even resting shortness of breath (dyspnea). Dyspnea, along with chest pain, exercise intolerance, syncope/presyncope, and palpitations, is among the most frequently reported symptoms in patients with HCM and is well-documented in cardiology guidelines and textbooks. Therefore, dyspnea is indeed a recognized symptom of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

992994.long_answer: Mutations in the β-myosin heavy chain gene (MYH7) located on chromosome 14 are a classic autosomal-dominant cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. This inherited myocardial disorder produces left-ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, which often manifest clinically as exertional dyspnea—the symptom the American Thoracic Society defines as a ‘subjective experience of breathing discomfort.’

936698.long_answer: Hypertension that arises from a demonstrable narrowing of one or both renal arteries (renal artery stenosis) is considered secondary hypertension. In this setting, reduced renal perfusion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, driving systemic blood-pressure elevation. Because the hypertension has a specific, identifiable cause—the vascular lesion of the renal artery—it is classified under the category of secondary (as opposed to primary or essential) hypertension in standard clinical guidelines.

498019.long_answer: Growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas raise circulating growth hormone, which in turn drives the liver and other tissues to produce excess insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). Chronically elevated IGF-1 stimulates proliferation of bone and soft tissues. In children and adolescents this can cause generalized stature increase (gigantism); in adults, whose epiphyseal growth plates are closed, it produces acromegaly, characterized by disproportionate enlargement of specific body parts such as the hands, feet, jaw, nose, and soft tissues. The tumor need not be invasive for this endocrine effect to occur; a hormonally active but non-invasive pituitary adenoma is sufficient to elevate IGF-1 and produce the described excessive, localized growth. Therefore, a patient with elevated IGF-1 from a non-invasive pituitary tumor can indeed experience excessive growth of certain body parts.

213329.long_answer: Acromegaly is almost always caused by a benign, non-metastasizing pituitary adenoma arising from somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary. This growth hormone–secreting (somatotropin) adenoma autonomously releases excess GH, leading to sustained IGF-1 elevation and the characteristic overgrowth of soft tissues and bones seen in acromegaly.

734848.long_answer: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes) is a maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA disorder. Mutations—most commonly the A3243G mutation in the mt-tRNALeu(UUR) gene—impair oxidative phosphorylation, leading to encephalopathy with recurrent stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, and myopathy.

688754.long_answer: Motile nodal cilia located on the cells of the embryonic primitive node create a left-directed fluid flow that breaks bilateral symmetry and establishes normal left–right body orientation. In primary ciliary dyskinesia these nodal cilia can be immotile or dyskinetic, disrupting the leftward flow, which randomizes laterality and can result in complete situs inversus.

437476.long_answer: Tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome) is defined by an anatomic, congenital or acquired dilation of the trachea and main bronchi caused by deficiency of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the airway wall. Because its primary abnormality is a fixed morphological enlargement of the airways, it is classified as a structural disorder rather than a functional disorder, which would involve reversible or dynamic physiologic changes without permanent anatomic alteration.

205314.long_answer: Crohn’s disease produces chronic transmural inflammation and fibrosis of the intestinal wall. When the inflammatory or fibrotic process obstructs or distorts the intestinal and mesenteric lymphatic vessels, the upstream lymphatics become dilated; this pathologic dilatation is termed secondary (acquired) intestinal lymphangiectasia. Although not as common as strictures, fistulas, abscesses, or extra-intestinal manifestations, secondary lymphangiectasia with consequent protein-losing enteropathy is a well-documented, recognised complication of Crohn’s disease in the gastro-enterology literature. Therefore, secondary lymphangiectasia can legitimately be listed among the potential complications of Crohn’s disease.

945783.long_answer: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is an opportunistic demyelinating disease caused by reactivation of JC virus in the setting of severe cellular immunodeficiency. Before the widespread availability of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), PML was one of the more common CNS opportunistic infections seen in people with AIDS. The risk of PML rises sharply when CD4⁺ T-cell counts fall below ~100 cells/µL, a condition typical of individuals with longstanding, untreated HIV infection. Multiple epidemiologic studies from the pre-HAART era showed that 3–7% of untreated AIDS patients developed PML, and autopsy data demonstrated even higher rates of subclinical JC virus–related brain lesions. With modern ART, the incidence of PML in HIV-infected persons has fallen dramatically, underscoring the link between uncontrolled HIV replication, profound immunosuppression, and susceptibility to PML. Therefore, untreated HIV-positive individuals, especially those with prolonged disease and low CD4 counts, are indeed highly susceptible to PML.

204623.long_answer: In Triple-A (Allgrove) syndrome, failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter—the muscle ring at the junction of the oesophagus and stomach—to relax and open normally is termed achalasia. This impaired relaxation obstructs passage of food and is a cardinal feature of the syndrome alongside alacrima and adrenal insufficiency.

875275.long_answer: Nitrous oxide (commonly called “laughing gas”) is administered by dentists for its anxiolytic and analgesic-anaesthetic properties, where it is regulated as a medical gas. Outside this setting it is also misused as a recreational inhalant—obtained from whipped-cream chargers or gas cartridges—and thus is grouped with other household or industrial products that are inhaled for their psychoactive effects.

395068.long_answer: Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal-recessive disorder in which mutations in nucleotide-excision-repair genes prevent efficient removal of UV-induced DNA photoproducts. The resulting accumulation of DNA damage causes a dramatic increase in the incidence of skin cancers, particularly melanoma, in affected individuals.

191063.long_answer: Ovarian cancer, particularly epithelial ovarian carcinoma, is notorious for presenting with nonspecific symptoms such as persistent pelvic or abdominal pain and bloating. Because it is usually diagnosed at an advanced stage and lacks an effective population-wide screening test, ovarian cancer accounts for the greatest number of deaths among all gynecologic (female reproductive system) malignancies, giving it the highest mortality rate in this category.

859459.long_answer: The extracellular deposits (drusen) that build up in age-related macular degeneration contain amyloid-β (β-amyloid) peptide. This is the same misfolded protein that constitutes the senile plaques characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease, indicating a biochemical overlap between the two conditions.

900133.long_answer: German epidemiologists such as Fritz Lickint first demonstrated a strong statistical association between cigarette smoking and lung cancer in the late 1920s-early 1930s. Subsequent research confirmed that carcinogens in tobacco smoke (e.g., polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines) induce genetic mutations that drive malignant transformation of bronchial epithelial cells, making smoking the dominant risk factor for this cancer. According to the World Health Organization’s Global Cancer Observatory, lung cancer was responsible for about 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2020, more than any other cancer type.

935787.long_answer: Mutations in the α-spectrin gene lead to membrane-unstable erythrocytes that are preferentially trapped and destroyed in the spleen’s reticuloendothelial system. Splenectomy removes the primary site of premature red-cell sequestration and destruction, thereby decreasing hemolysis and improving anemia in severe autosomal-recessive spectrin-deficiency disorders.

240972.long_answer: In hereditary angioedema, deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor permits unchecked kallikrein activity, generating excessive bradykinin. Bradykinin is a vasoactive peptide that increases vascular permeability and causes the swelling characteristic of the disorder. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), also known as kininase II, normally degrades bradykinin; therefore, ACE inhibition or C1 inhibitor deficiency both lead to elevated bradykinin levels.

662146.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) normally degrades the vasoactive peptide bradykinin. ACE inhibitors block this enzymatic activity, causing bradykinin to accumulate. Elevated bradykinin increases vascular permeability and vasodilation, which can precipitate ACE-inhibitor–induced angioedema.

378797.long_answer: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits microtubule polymerization in neutrophils and other inflammatory cells. Although it does not lower serum uric acid, it is a standard therapy for controlling the clinical manifestations that arise from hyperuricemia, most notably the acute and recurrent inflammatory attacks of gout. Current rheumatology guidelines (e.g., American College of Rheumatology, European League Against Rheumatism) recommend colchicine for the treatment of acute gout flares and for flare prophylaxis when urate-lowering drugs are started. Thus, while colchicine does not treat the underlying hyperuricemia, it is indeed used to manage the symptoms caused by it.

515614.long_answer: Cirrhosis is characterized not only by fibrotic architectural change but also by a state of chronic, systemic inflammation. Numerous studies show that patients with compensated and especially de-compensated cirrhosis have elevated circulating levels and hepatic expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6, and interleukin-1β. Kupffer-cell activation by gut-derived endotoxin, hepatocyte injury, and activation of hepatic stellate cells all drive overproduction of these cytokines. Raised TNF-α correlates with portal hypertension, encephalopathy, infection risk, and overall Child-Pugh/MELD severity. Hence, abnormal (typically increased) activity of inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, is a well-recognized and common finding in cirrhosis according to the current biomedical literature.

217353.long_answer: A thrombus that forms in the deep veins of the leg (deep-vein thrombosis) can dislodge and travel through the venous circulation, pass through the right side of the heart, and lodge in the pulmonary arteries. This obstruction of pulmonary blood flow is called a pulmonary embolism, a potentially life-threatening condition causing acute dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxemia, and hemodynamic compromise.

547846.long_answer: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) results from autosomal-recessive mutations in the PYGM gene, which encodes the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase. The PYGM gene is situated on the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q13), so chromosome 11 is the chromosomal location involved in this disorder.

852076.long_answer: In myoglobinuria, the pigment detected in the urine is myoglobin, an oxygen-binding heme protein normally confined within striated skeletal muscle fibres. When these skeletal muscle cells are injured or undergo necrosis (as in trauma, rhabdomyolysis, burns, ischemia), myoglobin is released into the circulation and subsequently filtered by the kidneys, leading to its appearance in urine.

324754.long_answer: Shapiro syndrome is an exceedingly rare disorder in which hypothalamic dysfunction leads to recurrent, spontaneous bouts of profound hypothermia (often <35 °C) accompanied by profuse sweating. First described in 1958 as a triad that also included agenesis of the corpus callosum, the core manifestations are the paroxysmal hypothermia and hyperhidrosis driven by disturbed thermoregulatory centers in the hypothalamus. Because autoimmune encephalitis can also produce episodic autonomic instability (temperature dysregulation, diaphoresis), Shapiro syndrome may clinically mimic that condition, but it is a distinct, non-inflammatory entity.

964710.long_answer: Pneumoconiosis is a group of chronic lung diseases caused by inhalation of inorganic dusts such as asbestos and crystalline silica. Ship-breaking (ship demolition) exposes workers to large quantities of asbestos insulation, refractory materials, silica-containing blasting grit, and other respirable mineral dusts that accumulate when old vessels are cut, stripped and sand-blasted. Multiple epidemiologic surveys from major ship-breaking yards in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkey have documented high airborne asbestos and silica concentrations well above occupational limits and have reported excess prevalence of asbestosis, silicosis and mixed-dust pneumoconiosis among demolition workers. On this basis, international occupational-health agencies (e.g., ILO, WHO) list ship demolition as a job category with a recognized risk for pneumoconiosis. Therefore, working in the ship demolition industry is indeed commonly associated with pneumoconiosis.

149319.long_answer: Ship-breaking commonly involves cutting and dismantling older vessels that contain asbestos insulation and fireproofing. Inhalation of asbestos fibers leads to the fibrotic pneumoconiosis known as asbestosis, characterized by diffuse interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques, and an increased risk of mesothelioma and lung carcinoma. Thus, asbestosis is the pneumoconiosis of greatest concern for ship-breaking workers.

192672.long_answer: Magnetic-resonance imaging (MRI) produces pictures of internal organs by applying strong static magnetic fields, rapidly switched magnetic-field gradients, and radio-frequency pulses. MRI is one of several standard imaging modalities that can reveal the right-to-left reversal of thoracic and abdominal organs characteristic of situs inversus. Although plain chest/abdominal radiographs, ultrasound, or CT scans are more commonly used first, MRI is fully capable of confirming the anatomic mirror-image arrangement. Therefore, saying that diagnosing situs inversus involves generating images with strong magnetic fields, magnetic-field gradients, and radio waves is consistent with established medical practice and is not incorrect.

177071.long_answer:
The term “arbovirus” is a contraction of “arthropod-borne virus” and is conventionally applied to any virus whose natural transmission cycle involves blood-feeding arthropods such as mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies or midges. This definition is standard in virology and public-health literature.

A substantial subset of arboviruses is neurotropic: West Nile virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Tick-borne encephalitis virus, Eastern and Western equine encephalitis viruses, and others are well-documented causes of viral encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) or meningo-encephalitis in humans and animals. While not every arbovirus is neuroinvasive, the group as a whole clearly possesses the capacity to cause brain inflammation, fulfilling the statement that such viruses "have the potential" to do so.

Therefore, both parts of the question reflect established scientific consensus.

760458.long_answer: Repeated transfusions in alpha-thalassemia deliver far more iron than the body can excrete, leading to toxic iron overload. The standard management is iron chelation therapy—typically with agents such as deferoxamine, deferasirox, or deferiprone—which binds excess iron so it can be eliminated, preventing cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine complications.

367313.long_answer: Glutaric acidemia type II (also called multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, MADD) is almost always produced by loss-of-function mutations in one of three genes: ETFA, ETFB (which encode the α- and β-subunits of electron-transfer flavoprotein, ETF) or ETFDH (which encodes ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase, also called ETF dehydrogenase, ETF-QO).  ETF and ETF-QO are FAD-containing flavoproteins that reside on the matrix side of the inner mitochondrial membrane, where they relay electrons from dozens of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases to the respiratory chain.  Disruption of these flavoproteins impairs multiple dehydrogenase activities and leads to the characteristic accumulation of glutaric acid and other organic acids seen in glutaric acidemia type II.  Thus, mutations in flavoproteins located on the matrix face of the inner mitochondrial membrane are indeed the recognized molecular cause of glutaric acidemia type II.

984694.long_answer: The described presentation matches Dercum’s disease (adiposis dolorosa), a rare adipose-tissue disorder marked by numerous subcutaneous lipomas that are chronically painful. These lipomas appear on the trunk and limbs, the pain is often burning or aching, and standard analgesics usually give little or no relief—features that distinguish the condition from ordinary, painless lipomatosis.

952612.long_answer: Glanzmann's thrombasthenia is an inherited platelet-function disorder in which platelets lack functional glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, so they are already unable to aggregate normally and affected individuals are prone to mucocutaneous and surgical bleeding. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen reversibly inhibit cyclo-oxygenase-1 in platelets, lowering thromboxane A₂ production and further impairing platelet aggregation for the life of the drug’s effect. Because any additional drug-induced platelet dysfunction can significantly increase bleeding risk in patients whose platelets are already defective, clinical guidelines and hematology texts recommend that people with congenital platelet-function disorders, including Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen whenever possible. Therefore it is correct that a person with Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia should avoid ibuprofen because it inhibits platelet aggregation.

364309.long_answer: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is characterized by uncontrolled activation of cytotoxic T-cells and macrophages that engulf (phagocytose) erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets in the bone marrow, spleen, and liver. This pathologic hemophagocytosis, along with the high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, causes peripheral cytopenias (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), not an overproduction of blood cells. Bone-marrow examinations in HLH typically show active macrophages ingesting hematopoietic elements, and laboratory criteria for the disease include bicytopenia or pancytopenia. Therefore, HLH leads to depletion—not increased production—of cellular blood components.

437264.long_answer: Fissured tongue (also called scrotal tongue) frequently co-exists with geographic tongue; studies show 30–50 % of individuals with geographic tongue have fissured tongue as well. While geographic tongue can appear at any age, fissured tongue is an acquired condition whose prevalence increases progressively with advancing age, making it more common in older adults.

515493.long_answer: Rituximab is a chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that received its first FDA approval in 1997 for the treatment of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. By depleting CD20-positive B lymphocytes, rituximab reduces production of the pathogenic anti-ADAMTS13 auto-antibodies that underlie acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Consequently, after standard therapy with plasma exchange and corticosteroids, rituximab is commonly added in refractory or relapsing TTP to hasten remission and decrease relapse rates.

507683.long_answer: The LIS1 gene (official symbol PAFAH1B1) resides at 17p13.3. It encodes a regulatory subunit of platelet-activating-factor acetylhydrolase that is essential for proper neuronal migration. Deletions involving LIS1 produce the classical lissencephaly seen in Miller-Dieker syndrome, and point mutations in the same gene can lead to milder cortical malformations such as pachygyria.

529354.long_answer: Bevacizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A). It was first licensed for systemic use in solid tumours such as metastatic colorectal, lung and renal cancers. Because the same VEGF-A–driven neovascularisation underlies ocular diseases, intravitreal bevacizumab is now widely employed (off-label) as an anti-VEGF treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, neovascular age-related macular degeneration and related retinal disorders.

206657.long_answer: Schizophreniform disorder, defined by psychotic symptoms persisting for at least one month but less than six months, is managed in the same way as schizophrenia. The standard pharmacologic treatment is a course of antipsychotic drugs—especially second-generation (atypical) agents such as risperidone or olanzapine—which antagonize dopamine D2 receptors (and often serotonin 5-HT2A receptors) to alleviate hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking.

854304.long_answer: Blepharospasm is most effectively managed by local injections of botulinum toxin type A, a serotype of the Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin. BoNT-A reversibly blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction of the orbicularis oculi, reducing the involuntary eyelid spasms. Owing to its potency, predictable duration of action, and extensive clinical evidence, BoNT-A is considered the first-line treatment for this focal dystonia.

795535.long_answer: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease that develops almost exclusively in pre-term infants who have required oxygen supplementation and/or positive-pressure ventilation. The two strongest, well-established risk factors are (1) prematurity and (2) exposure to supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation for a sustained period. Although the incidence of BPD drops sharply with increasing gestational age and is most common in infants born <32 weeks, late-preterm infants (34-36 weeks) who still require respiratory support have a markedly higher likelihood of developing BPD than late-preterm infants who breathe room air from birth or than term infants. Current consensus definitions (NICHD/AAP) actually diagnose BPD on the basis of a continued need for supplemental oxygen for ≥28 days, with severity assessed at 36 weeks post-menstrual age or 56 days post-natal age for babies born ≥32 weeks. Therefore, a neonate delivered at 36 weeks who already needs supplemental oxygen meets two key risk criteria—prematurity and oxygen exposure—and is indeed considered at increased risk for developing bronchopulmonary dysplasia, even though the absolute risk is lower than that of extremely pre-term infants.

507964.long_answer: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease that develops in preterm infants—typically those born before 37 weeks’ gestation—who have required prolonged mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Repeated ventilator-induced lung injury and oxygen toxicity interfere with normal alveolar and pulmonary vascular development, leading to persistent respiratory morbidity characteristic of BPD.

763753.long_answer: The anterior-horn motor neuron disease described is spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). Virtually all classic 5q-linked SMA cases result from homozygous deletion or loss-of-function mutation of the Survival Motor Neuron 1 gene (SMN1) on chromosome 5q13. Loss of SMN1 protein leads to degeneration of anterior horn cells, progressive muscle wasting, and, in its severe infantile form (SMA type 1), is the leading genetic cause of death in infancy if untreated.

601508.long_answer: Hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy (also called hereditary brachial plexus neuropathy) is an autosomal-dominant neuralgic syndrome that clinically mimics acute brachial neuritis/Parsonage–Turner syndrome. It is specifically linked to point mutations or copy-number alterations of the SEPT9 gene on chromosome 17q25, which distinguishes it genetically from the sporadic form of brachial neuritis.

402244.long_answer: Moyamoya disease type 2 is caused by pathogenic variants in the RNF213 gene, which maps to chromosome 17q25.3. RNF213 encodes ring-finger protein 213; the recurrent missense variant p.Arg4810Lys and other loss-of-function changes in this gene segregate with the familial form of Moyamoya and are strongly enriched in sporadic cases, establishing RNF213 as the causal gene for the type 2 subtype.

456442.long_answer: Both myocarditis (inflammation of cardiac muscle) and pericarditis (inflammation of the fibrous pericardial sac) are most frequently attributed to viral infections. Among these, enteroviruses—particularly Coxsackie B virus—are the single most common identified cause in epidemiologic and clinical studies, accounting for the majority of presumed ‘idiopathic’ myopericardial inflammations.

560227.long_answer: Toxoplasma gondii is the protozoan parasite responsible for toxoplasmosis. In immunocompromised individuals, reactivation of latent infection often manifests as chorioretinitis. When the parasite is transmitted transplacentally during pregnancy, congenital toxoplasmosis can result, classically presenting with hydrocephalus and intracranial (cerebral) calcifications, along with chorioretinitis. These hallmark associations make Toxoplasma gondii the definitive answer.

551712.long_answer: Bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobe—including the hippocampus and adjacent cortical areas—impairs the brain’s ability to consolidate new declarative memories. Classic evidence from patient H.M. showed that after this surgery he could not form new long-term memories, though most previously stored memories remained intact. This inability to lay down new memories is characteristic of anterograde amnesia.

321794.long_answer: Diabetic retinopathy, particularly in its non-proliferative stage, is marked by the formation of retinal microaneurysms—tiny outpouchings of capillary walls visible on fundoscopic exam. Progressive capillary leakage and ischemia can lead to macular edema, neovascularization, and eventual vision loss, making diabetic retinopathy one of the foremost causes of blindness worldwide.

410582.long_answer: Pneumonic plague is caused by Yersinia pestis. This organism is a small, Gram-negative, non-motile bacterium that appears as a short rod with rounded ends and shows characteristic bipolar (“safety-pin”) staining. Because it has a shape intermediate between cocci (spherical) and bacilli (rod-shaped), it is classically classified as a coccobacillus. Hence, the bacterium responsible for pneumonic plague is indeed a coccobacillus.

556909.long_answer: The 48,XXXY syndrome is a rarer variant of Klinefelter syndrome in which males carry two extra X chromosomes, giving a total karyotype of 48 chromosomes (XXXY). Epidemiological data show it occurs in roughly 1 in 50,000 male births, distinguishing it from the classic 47,XXY Klinefelter presentation and other, even rarer, polysomy variants.

170420.long_answer: In essential thrombocythemia, about 50–60 % of patients carry the activating V617F point mutation in the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene. JAK2 is a member of the Janus kinase family, and the V617F substitution constitutively activates the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, driving the myeloproliferative phenotype characteristic of the disease.

217889.long_answer: After surgical removal of papillary or follicular thyroid cancer, patients commonly receive radioactive iodine ablation with iodine-131. This β- and γ-emitting isotope is selectively taken up by residual thyroid tissue and metastatic thyroid cells via the sodium-iodide symporter, enabling targeted destruction of remaining malignant cells while sparing most other tissues.

170561.long_answer: Cimetidine is an H2-receptor antagonist that was first licensed in the United Kingdom in 1976. By inhibiting histamine-stimulated gastric acid secretion it is effective for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Large observational studies and pregnancy-exposure registries have shown no increase in congenital malformations or adverse fetal outcomes, so cimetidine is considered safe for use during pregnancy when GERD requires pharmacologic therapy.

829022.long_answer: H2 receptor antagonists (e.g., ranitidine, famotidine) competitively block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion and relieving gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) symptoms in roughly 40 % of patients. Although effective, they have been largely superseded by the more potent acid-suppressive proton pump inhibitors.

420185.long_answer: Alexandrium tamarense is a toxic marine dinoflagellate that produces saxitoxins, potent neurotoxins that block voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle. When these toxins accumulate in bivalve shellfish and are ingested by humans, they cause the clinical syndrome known as paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP).

256580.long_answer: Saxitoxin-producing dinoflagellates (e.g., Alexandrium species) bioaccumulate in filter-feeding bivalve mollusks. When humans ingest these contaminated shellfish, the saxitoxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, leading to the characteristic neurologic and potentially paralytic symptoms of Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP), one of the four recognized shellfish-poisoning syndromes.

657453.long_answer: Mycosis fungoides is the prototypical and most frequent variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). CTCLs arise from skin-homing mature CD4⁺ T lymphocytes and together comprise only about 2 % of all lymphoid malignancies (non-Hodgkin lymphomas). Therefore, the lymphoma subtype of which mycosis fungoides is the commonest form is cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

326868.long_answer: Hemophilia A is caused by pathogenic variants in the F8 gene on the X-chromosome. A genetically normal 46,XY male possesses only one X chromosome, so for every X-linked locus he carries a single allele; by definition he is hemizygous. If that lone F8 allele is mutant, and if there is no somatic mosaicism (i.e., the mutation is present in all his cells), he must be hemizygous for the mutation. In the absence of additional X chromosomes (e.g., XXY) or mosaicism, there is no way for a man to be heterozygous or homozygous for two different F8 alleles. Therefore, a man with hemophilia A necessarily carries the mutant gene in hemizygous state.

722697.long_answer: Mutations in the TYR gene disrupt the activity of tyrosinase, the enzyme that catalyzes the first steps of melanin biosynthesis from tyrosine. Without functional tyrosinase, melanocytes cannot produce melanin, leading to the characteristic hypopigmentation of oculocutaneous albinism.

528519.long_answer: Tricho-hepato-enteric syndrome is produced by recessive mutations in two genes: TTC37 and SKIV2L. The great majority of documented patients carry mutations in TTC37, which is situated on chromosome 5 (cytogenetic band 5q). SKIV2L, responsible for a smaller subset of cases, resides on chromosome 6. Therefore, the chromosome associated with the gene found in more patients is chromosome 5.

267930.long_answer: Grover’s disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) is defined histologically by acantholysis—the breakdown of desmosomal connections that leads to loss of cohesion between adjacent keratinocytes. This acantholytic change produces the characteristic suprabasal clefts and dyscohesive keratinocytes seen on biopsy, making acantholysis the key microscopic hallmark of the disorder.

830311.long_answer: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (dominant form) can result from heterozygous mutations in COL9A2. COL9A2 encodes the α2(IX) chain of type IX collagen; this particular α-chain uniquely carries a covalently linked chondroitin-sulfate glycosaminoglycan side chain. Disruption of this glycosylated collagen chain impairs cartilage matrix integrity, producing the characteristic skeletal abnormalities of autosomal-dominant MED.

561990.long_answer: In more than 80 % of cases, primary hyperparathyroidism is produced by a solitary parathyroid adenoma—a benign tumor arising in one parathyroid gland. The autonomous over-secretion of parathyroid hormone by this single adenoma leads to hypercalcaemia and the clinical syndrome known as primary hyperparathyroidism.

244100.long_answer: The leading cause of short bowel syndrome (SBS) in the neonatal period is surgical resection following necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Extensive clinical and epidemiologic studies show that NEC occurs predominantly in premature infants, especially those with very-low birth weight (VLBW, <1500 g). Prematurity and VLBW are consistently cited as the strongest, most well-established risk factors for NEC, with incidence rates rising as gestational age and birth weight decrease. Because NEC is the principal precipitating disease that ultimately leads to SBS in this age group, factors that increase the risk of NEC—namely prematurity and very low birth weight—thereby also serve as indirect risk factors for developing SBS. Therefore, prematurity and VLBW are indeed recognized risk factors for the most common cause of short bowel syndrome in infants.

649859.long_answer: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a severe inflammatory and ischemic disease of the neonatal intestine that occurs predominantly in premature or very-low-birth-weight infants. The bowel wall becomes necrotic and may perforate, often necessitating surgical resection of affected segments of small intestine. Extensive resection can leave the infant with insufficient functional bowel length, resulting in short bowel syndrome.

849629.long_answer: Bacterial vaginosis is the leading cause of vaginitis. When 10% potassium hydroxide (a base) is added to a sample of vaginal discharge on a slide, the alkaline pH releases volatile amines produced by overgrowing anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Gardnerella vaginalis), generating the characteristic "fishy" odor known as the positive whiff (amine) test.

670816.long_answer: Plasmodium species (e.g., P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae) are unicellular eukaryotic parasites that belong to the phylum Apicomplexa, classically categorized as protozoa. When an infected Anopheles mosquito takes a blood meal, it injects Plasmodium sporozoites into the human bloodstream, initiating malaria. Because the causative organism is a protozoan and the disease process results from its establishment and replication in human tissues, this event is, by definition, a protozoan infection.

351583.long_answer: Inhalation of freshly formed zinc oxide fumes during welding galvanized steel produces the self-limited condition known as metal fume fever. According to occupational-medicine texts, CDC/NIOSH guidelines, and UpToDate reviews, symptoms (fever, chills, myalgias, cough, malaise) usually begin 3–10 hours after exposure and resolve spontaneously within 24–48 hours once the worker is removed from the environment. While some individuals may start feeling better after about 12 hours, complete resolution by 12 hours is not the typical or expected course; most cases take roughly a day or two to clear. Therefore, the statement that symptoms “typically resolve within 12 hours” is not consistent with the established consensus.

915811.long_answer: ‘Zinc shakes’ or ‘zinc chills’ is the colloquial name for metal fume fever, an acute, self-limited influenza-like illness that occurs after inhalation of zinc oxide fumes (or other metal oxide fumes) produced during welding, galvanizing, or metal cutting. Symptoms—fever, chills, malaise, myalgia, and cough—typically begin 4–12 h after exposure as the inhaled metal oxide particles induce cytokine release in the lungs.

458288.long_answer: The substance described is the extracellular matrix (ECM) of connective tissues, whose major organic component is collagen and whose mineral phase in bone contains hydroxy-apatite. Prolidase (peptidase D) is the cytosolic exopeptidase that cleaves iminodipeptides containing C-terminal proline or hydroxyproline, thereby recycling these amino acids for new collagen synthesis and permitting complete degradation of old collagen. In prolidase deficiency, this step is blocked: collagen breakdown products accumulate, free proline/hydroxyproline supply for new collagen is reduced, and post-translational processing of collagen is disturbed. The result is defective remodeling and turnover of the ECM. Clinically, individuals with prolidase deficiency present with chronic, poorly healing skin ulcers, recurrent infections, and other signs of impaired connective-tissue repair. Hence, prolidase deficiency does indeed disrupt the metabolism of the extracellular matrix and leads to impaired wound healing.

855148.long_answer: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan parasite that infects the female genital tract, producing the sexually transmitted disease trichomoniasis. Infection typically manifests as vaginitis with a frothy, malodorous discharge and can extend to involve the cervix, leading to cervicitis. Its established role in causing both vaginitis and cervicitis is well documented in gynecologic and infectious-disease literature.

102429.long_answer: Triple-A syndrome is caused by mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the nuclear pore complex protein ALADIN. The AAAS gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 12q13 on human chromosome 12.

792997.long_answer: The GYG1 gene on chromosome 3 encodes glycogenin-1, the self-glucosylating protein that primes glycogen synthesis. Loss-of-function mutations or deficiency of glycogenin-1 leads to Glycogen storage disease type XV (GSD-XV), a rare glycogenosis characterized by abnormal muscle glycogen accumulation and associated myopathy.

585280.long_answer:
Bevacizumab (a VEGF-A monoclonal antibody) is indeed recognized for producing a toxic, dose-related form of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), typically manifesting as renal-predominant injury with hypertension, proteinuria and kidney-limited microangiopathic hemolysis. This entity is mechanistically linked to endothelial damage from VEGF blockade and does not involve severe ADAMTS13 deficiency or an immune reaction against ADAMTS13.

True thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is defined by systemic TMA in the setting of marked ADAMTS13 activity <10 %, usually because of autoantibody inhibition (acquired TTP) or an inherited enzyme defect. Drugs that are well documented to induce immune-mediated TTP include quinine, ticlopidine, clopidogrel, cyclosporine, mitomycin-C, interferon and a few others. Bevacizumab is not on that list, and large pharmacovigilance series, clinical trials and post-marketing surveillance have not shown a consistent association with ADAMTS13-deficient TTP.

Isolated case reports occasionally label bevacizumab-related systemic TMA as "TTP," but when ADAMTS13 activity is measured it is usually normal or only mildly reduced, indicating that the pathologic process is not true TTP but rather a VEGF-inhibitor, renal-predominant TMA. Therefore, although bevacizumab unquestionably causes TMA, the current scientific consensus does not support the claim that it predisposes patients to genuine thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

In summary, bevacizumab causes a VEGF-inhibitor toxic TMA, not ADAMTS13-deficient TTP; hence it is not considered to predispose patients to TTP.

797581.long_answer: Alström syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the ALMS1 gene. The canonical ALMS1 transcript (e.g., NM_015120) spans roughly 224 kb on chromosome 2p13 and is composed of 23 exons, which together encode a 4,169-amino-acid protein. Thus, the gene responsible for Alström syndrome contains 23 exons.

834351.long_answer: Sarcoidosis was first reported in 1877 by the English physician Jonathan Hutchinson. It is defined by the formation of non-caseating granulomas—abnormal aggregates of macrophages (often epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells)—that most commonly manifest initially in the lungs, intrathoracic lymph nodes, or skin.

284693.long_answer: Rombo syndrome predisposes patients to basal cell carcinoma, which classically appears as a painless, shiny, raised (pearly) skin lesion. The standard way to establish the diagnosis of a suspected basal cell carcinoma is a shave biopsy: a superficial tangential removal of the lesion that provides adequate tissue for histopathologic confirmation while being quick, low-morbidity, and appropriate for non-pigmented, non-melanoma skin cancers.

806942.long_answer: Rombo syndrome is a rare genodermatosis characterized by cutaneous atrophoderma, telangiectasias, and milia. A well-documented complication of this condition is the early and frequent development of multiple basal cell carcinomas, making this form of non-melanoma skin cancer a hallmark risk for affected individuals.

844836.long_answer: Hereditary spastic paraplegia was first clearly delineated in the late-19th century by the German neurologist Adolph von Strümpell, whose 1880s descriptions of families with progressive spastic weakness of the lower limbs led to the eponym Strümpell–Lorrain disease (the other name honoring the French neurologist Maurice Lorrain).

448599.long_answer: In July 2022 the U.S. FDA granted approval for topical ruxolitinib 1.5 % cream (a selective JAK1/2 inhibitor, marketed as Opzelura) specifically for the treatment of non-segmental vitiligo in patients ≥12 years of age. This made ruxolitinib the first pharmacotherapy formally approved—rather than used off-label—to induce repigmentation in vitiligo, based on phase III trials showing significant restoration of facial and total body pigmentation via inhibition of the JAK-STAT-mediated IFN-γ signaling that drives melanocyte loss.

797118.long_answer: Fanconi–Bickel syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC2A2 gene, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT2. GLUT2 is a facilitative (passive) glucose transporter found in liver, kidney, intestine and pancreatic β-cells. Its transport activity depends solely on the trans-membrane glucose concentration gradient; it is not recruited to or activated at the membrane by insulin. In contrast, the insulin-responsive transporter is GLUT4, not GLUT2. Therefore, the protein associated with Fanconi–Bickel syndrome (GLUT2) performs facilitated diffusion independently of insulin.

336682.long_answer: Yes. Positron-emission tomography (PET)—usually performed as integrated PET/CT—uses radiotracers such as 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose to depict areas of increased glucose metabolism. Malignant cells typically have higher metabolic activity than normal tissues, so FDG-PET highlights primary lung tumors as well as metastatic deposits in lymph nodes, bone, adrenal glands, brain, and other organs. International lung-cancer staging guidelines (e.g., NCCN, ACCP, ESMO) recommend FDG-PET/CT for initial staging and for detecting distant metastases in patients with suspected or confirmed lung cancer. Numerous studies show that PET imaging improves the accuracy of metastatic detection compared with anatomic imaging alone and influences treatment planning. Hence, an imaging technique that employs radiotracers to visualize metabolic changes is indeed used routinely to locate metastases in lung-cancer patients.

516385.long_answer: Folliculitis decalvans is often treated with a dual-antibiotic regimen consisting of the lincosamide antibiotic clindamycin together with rifampicin. Clindamycin, a well-established lincosamide active against Staphylococcus aureus, is recommended because it penetrates follicular tissue and, when combined with rifampicin, helps eradicate bacterial colonisation and reduce the chronic inflammatory response characteristic of this scarring scalp disorder.

498978.long_answer: Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) first converts the viral SARS-CoV-2 RNA in the specimen into complementary DNA with reverse transcriptase, then uses repeated thermal cycling of DNA polymerase to exponentially amplify that cDNA. The presence of amplified product, assessed at the end-point, provides a non-quantitative diagnostic indication of the virus.

618369.long_answer: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a non-steroidal synthetic estrogen that was prescribed from the 1940s to the 1970s to treat female hypogonadism and to prevent miscarriage. Epidemiologic studies later showed that in-utero exposure to DES markedly increases the risk of clear-cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina and cervix, as well as structural and fertility problems in both female and male offspring. Owing to these serious reproductive health complications, therapeutic use of DES for hypogonadism and other pregnancy-related indications was discontinued.

829235.long_answer: Fifth disease is caused by human parvovirus B19, a member of the Parvoviridae family. Parvoviruses possess a small, non-enveloped capsid with icosahedral (T=1) symmetry. A regular icosahedron is composed of 20 identical equilateral triangular faces; therefore, the capsid of parvovirus B19—and thus of the virus causing fifth disease—has 20 equilateral triangular faces.

648481.long_answer: It is not inappropriate to consider impaired nutrient (particularly fat) absorption in the gastrointestinal tract as a possible cause of hypolipoproteinemia. Serum lipoprotein levels depend on adequate intestinal uptake of dietary lipids and fat-soluble nutrients and on their subsequent assembly into chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoproteins. Conditions that interfere with this process—such as generalized malabsorption syndromes (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn’s disease with extensive small-bowel involvement, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency), short-bowel syndrome, or specific genetic disorders like abetalipoproteinemia and homozygous hypobetalipoproteinemia—are well-documented to produce markedly reduced plasma concentrations of cholesterol- and triglyceride-containing lipoproteins. Malnutrition resulting from chronic malabsorption can also secondarily lower lipoprotein levels. Therefore, evaluating gastrointestinal malabsorption as an etiologic factor is consistent with established medical knowledge, and labeling it “inappropriate” would be incorrect.

687399.long_answer: When dietary triglycerides are not adequately digested or absorbed, the unabsorbed fats remain in the intestinal lumen and are excreted in the stool. This produces steatorrhea—bulky, pale, foul-smelling stools that contain excess fat— the characteristic fecal abnormality seen in triglyceride malabsorption.

253662.long_answer: Disturbances of taste perception (dysgeusia, ageusia, or hypogeusia) are listed in otolaryngology texts and surgical consent forms as a recognised, though infrequent, complication of tonsillectomy. They are thought to arise from traction or inadvertent injury to the lingual branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve or from post-operative inflammation. Large clinical series place the incidence well below 1 %, and most cases resolve within weeks to months, underscoring that it is uncommon but nevertheless a documented risk. Therefore the statement is consistent with established medical consensus.

857118.long_answer: Syringocystadenoma papilliferum, a benign adnexal skin tumour, characteristically shows a dense stromal infiltrate of antibody-secreting white blood cells—plasma cells—beneath its papillary projections.

490038.long_answer: Rapid gastric emptying (also referred to as dumping syndrome) is a recognized, although less common, postoperative problem after Nissen (laparoscopic or open) fundoplication. Numerous case series and reviews—especially in the pediatric literature but also in adults—document symptomatic rapid gastric emptying that arises after an antireflux fundoplication, typically attributed to loss of the proximal gastric reservoir, altered fundal compliance, or vagal-nerve injury during the operation. Therefore, stating that rapid gastric emptying is "not a complication" of the Nissen procedure is incorrect; it is an established, if infrequent, complication.

892309.long_answer: After a Nissen fundoplication some patients develop dumping syndrome, a rapid-gastric-emptying complication in which chyme is propelled too quickly from the stomach into the duodenum. Loss of normal pyloric regulation (often from vagal nerve or anatomic changes during the wrap) leads to post-prandial tachycardia, diaphoresis, abdominal cramping and hypoglycaemia characteristic of this syndrome.

912403.long_answer: Alopecia areata is widely recognized as an autoimmune disease. In this disorder, cytotoxic T-lymphocytes and other immune cells erroneously target the bulb of actively growing (anagen) hair follicles. The immune attack disrupts the normal hair cycle, causing premature shedding and resulting in patchy or more extensive hair loss. This pathophysiology is supported by histologic studies showing peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrates, clinical response to immunosuppressive therapies, and genetic associations with other autoimmune conditions. Therefore, the statement accurately reflects established scientific consensus.

662971.long_answer: Roger Altounyan discovered sodium cromoglycate (cromolyn sodium) in 1965. This chromone derivative stabilizes mast cell membranes, preventing degranulation and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Ophthalmic preparations of sodium cromoglycate are routinely prescribed to treat allergic conjunctivitis.

244210.long_answer: Erythroplakia is a red, velvety mucosal lesion of the oral cavity. Histologic studies show that more than 90 % of erythroplakias already harbor severe epithelial dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or frankly invasive cancer at the time of biopsy, and virtually all of these malignant changes are of the squamous cell type. Therefore, erythroplakia is most commonly associated with development of oral squamous cell carcinoma.

152455.long_answer: The condition known as fibular aplasia–ectrodactyly syndrome (also called fibular aplasia or hypoplasia with ectrodactyly/syndactyly) is an autosomal-dominant limb-malformation disorder with reduced penetrance. Affected individuals show complete or partial absence of the fibula and variably present split hand/foot (ectrodactyly), brachydactyly, or syndactyly of the digits, fitting all the features listed in the question.

730123.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is classified among the seronegative spondyloarthritides, meaning that characteristic autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor (RF) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are typically absent. The standard diagnostic approach to AS relies on clinical features (inflammatory back pain, reduced spinal mobility), imaging of the sacro-iliac joints and spine (plain radiography or MRI), and genetic testing for HLA-B27. While ANA testing is routinely ordered when evaluating systemic autoimmune connective-tissue diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, it is not considered useful or recommended for diagnosing AS. Therefore, antinuclear antibodies are not commonly used as diagnostic markers for ankylosing spondylitis.

793861.long_answer: Carnitine is required for shuttling long-chain fatty acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane; without it, these substrates cannot reach the mitochondrial matrix, the subcompartment where β-oxidation normally occurs. Consequently, systemic primary carnitine deficiency blocks fatty-acid oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix.

921251.long_answer: Primary Raynaud’s phenomenon is an idiopathic condition in which no associated systemic disorder or provoking factor can be identified. When Raynaud’s episodes occur in the setting of an underlying disease or pathophysiologic trigger—such as cryoglobulinemia, connective-tissue disorders, vasculitis, hematologic abnormalities, certain drugs, etc.—the condition is classified as secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon. Cryoglobulinemia involves circulating immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold and can cause vascular occlusion and vasospasm, directly providing an identifiable cause for the Raynaud’s attacks. Therefore, Raynaud’s due to cryoglobulinemia is unequivocally categorized as secondary, not primary, Raynaud’s phenomenon.

145230.long_answer: In neuromyotonia, peripheral motor nerves are hyper-excitable, leading to sudden depolarisations that activate single α-motor neurons. This produces brief, spontaneous contractions of individual motor units—clinically observed as fasciculations, which are a hallmark finding in this condition.

974988.long_answer: The claim that it is false that bone-morphogenetic-protein (BMP) mutations can cause anophthalmia is itself incorrect. Multiple members of the BMP gene family (notably BMP4 and BMP7) are critical regulators of early eye development. Heterozygous loss-of-function or missense mutations in BMP4 have been repeatedly reported in patients presenting with anophthalmia, microphthalmia, or the broader MAC (microphthalmia–anophthalmia–coloboma) spectrum (e.g., Bakrania et al., 2008; Reis et al., 2011; Fleurisson et al., 2019). Similar associations, supported by animal models and limited human data, exist for BMP7. The consensus in developmental genetics is therefore that BMP mutations are a recognised, though relatively infrequent, monogenic cause of anophthalmia. Consequently, stating that “mutations of the bone morphogenetic protein cannot cause anophthalmia” is contradicted by established evidence.

223602.long_answer: Ochoa syndrome, also called urofacial syndrome (UFS), is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by a distinctive inverted facial expression and severe functional bladder outflow obstruction. Genetic studies in multiple, independently affected families have shown that loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene (Heparanase-2) segregate with the disease. Because HPSE2 was the first gene in which pathogenic variants were identified for this condition, the locus is referred to in OMIM as UFS1. A second, rarer locus (LRIG2; UFS2) has subsequently been described, but the involvement of HPSE2 remains well-established and widely accepted in the biomedical literature. Therefore, the claim that Ochoa syndrome is believed to be caused by mutations in the HPSE2 (UFS1) gene is true; saying it is false would be incorrect.

506698.long_answer: Petrea Jacobsen first described a familial unbalanced reciprocal translocation that removed the distal long-arm segment (q23-qter) of chromosome 11. This 11q deletion—now recognised as Jacobsen syndrome—is the critical cytogenetic abnormality; the other partner chromosome can vary, but the defining lesion always involves chromosome 11.

637872.long_answer: Yes. 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase (HMG-CoA lyase) catalyzes the final, committed step of hepatic ketogenesis: the cleavage of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria. The acetoacetate formed can (1) be reduced by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase to β-hydroxybutyrate or (2) undergo spontaneous decarboxylation to acetone. Thus HMG-CoA lyase is indispensable for the endogenous production of all three major ketone bodies—acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone. Clinical evidence supports this: individuals with inherited HMG-CoA lyase deficiency are unable to generate ketone bodies and develop hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting. Therefore, the statement accurately reflects established biochemical knowledge.

948373.long_answer: Cervical spine disorders that limit motion, meningeal irritation from subarachnoid hemorrhage, and meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis all characteristically produce nuchal rigidity—painful stiffness of the neck that restricts flexion or other movements.

280733.long_answer: According to the Jones criteria, which are the internationally accepted diagnostic guidelines for acute rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea—historically called “St. Vitus’s dance”—is listed as one of the five major manifestations. The full set of major criteria consists of carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea (St. Vitus’s dance), erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules. Therefore, St. Vitus’s dance is indeed a major Jones criterion used in the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

446178.long_answer: The condition is Dercum's disease (adiposis dolorosa), first reported in 1892 by Dr. Francis Xavier Dercum, a neurologist who later served on President Woodrow Wilson’s medical team. It predominantly affects women beginning in the third decade of life and is marked by numerous painful fatty tumors (lipomas) distributed over the trunk and limbs, often accompanied by generalized obesity, weakness, and fatigue.

204604.long_answer: Dissociated vertical deviation (DVD) is a form of strabismus in which one eye slowly drifts upward (often with excyclotorsion and abduction) when visual attention is relaxed or the eye is occluded. Because DVD causes an elevated eye position that can resemble the hypertropia seen with inferior oblique overaction, it is frequently misdiagnosed as such. Unlike true inferior oblique overaction, DVD is a dissociated misalignment, not linked to specific gaze directions, and the deviation increases when the fixing eye is switched or the non-fixing eye is covered.

170603.long_answer: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia stems from enzymatic defects in cortisol biosynthesis, a process that normally occurs in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. Impaired cortisol production in this cortical layer leads to excess ACTH stimulation and adrenal hyperplasia, making the zona fasciculata the adrenal region classically associated with the disorder.

547554.long_answer: Potocki–Lupski syndrome results from a duplication of the 17p11.2 chromosomal region that increases the dosage of the RAI1 (Retinoic-acid-induced 1) gene. Conversely, Smith–Magenis syndrome arises when the same 17p11.2 segment is deleted or when RAI1 itself is mutated, reducing its dosage. Thus, altered copy number of the single gene RAI1 can lead to either disorder, making it the gene common to both syndromes.

602046.long_answer: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infects epithelial tissues; low-risk types (especially HPV-6 and HPV-11) are responsible for laryngeal papillomatosis, while persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic types (notably HPV-16 and HPV-18) is the established etiologic agent for virtually all cases of cervical cancer.

674555.long_answer: Bevacizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A), thereby inhibiting tumor angiogenesis. Originally approved by the U.S. FDA for metastatic colorectal cancer, subsequent clinical studies demonstrated that systemic or intralesional bevacizumab can shrink vestibular schwannomas and lead to measurable hearing improvement in patients with Neurofibromatosis type II, making it the leading anti-angiogenic therapy investigated for this disorder.

988439.long_answer: Follicular lymphoma, a common indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, classically shows neoplastic small cleaved (centrocytic) cells, carries the t(14;18)(q32;q21) IgH-BCL2 translocation, and consequently overexpresses the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2.

994776.long_answer: The standard and only proven therapy to prevent and treat Treponema pallidum infection acquired in utero or at birth (congenital syphilis) is intramuscular benzathine penicillin G. This long-acting form of penicillin eradicates T. pallidum in the mother, crosses the placenta to treat the fetus, and is likewise used in neonates; no alternative antibiotic has shown comparable efficacy, making benzathine penicillin G the universally recommended drug of choice.

237388.long_answer: The CLCN7 gene encodes the chloride channel 7 that is critical for osteoclast acidification of the resorption lacuna. Heterozygous missense mutations in CLCN7 account for the great majority of reported cases of autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (also called Albers-Schönberg disease). While biallelic CLCN7 defects can cause rarer recessive forms, most CLCN7‐related osteopetrosis presents as the milder, adult-onset autosomal dominant type II.

743668.long_answer: The Ex Utero Intrapartum Treatment (EXIT) procedure is a specialized form of cesarean delivery in which the fetus is partially delivered while uteroplacental circulation is deliberately maintained. This allows surgeons and anesthesiologists time to secure the newborn’s airway (e.g., via intubation, bronchoscopy, or tracheostomy) before the umbilical cord is clamped. EXIT is the standard approach when congenital lung masses such as congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) compress or obstruct the airway, preventing effective breathing immediately after birth.

476622.long_answer: Histoplasmosis is a pulmonary and systemic mycosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum, which proliferates in soil enriched with bat or bird droppings—animal excrement (guano) historically spread on fields as fertilizer. Inhalation of the airborne microconidia primarily affects the lungs, and a recognized chronic complication of this infection is fibrosing mediastinitis, a dense fibrotic reaction in the mediastinum.

977418.long_answer: Mutations in the KCNJ5 gene, which encodes the G-protein–activated inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir3.4, are the recognized cause of familial hyperaldosteronism type III. These gain-of-function or selectivity-altering mutations increase sodium influx in adrenal zona glomerulosa cells, stimulating aldosterone over-production and primary aldosteronism. The same gene is expressed in cardiac tissue; loss of selective potassium conductance there prolongs the action-potential repolarization phase, producing the cardiac electrophysiologic phenotype classified as Long QT syndrome type 13.

469559.long_answer: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a herpesvirus that can trigger infectious mononucleosis; a proportion of patients develop a post-infectious chronic fatigue syndrome. Separately, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma characteristically contains EBV-positive B-cell immunoblasts, and EBV infection is considered a contributory factor in its pathogenesis. Thus, EBV is the virus linked to both post-infectious chronic fatigue syndrome and angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma.

680429.long_answer: Salla disease is a form of free sialic-acid storage disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC17A5 gene. SLC17A5 encodes the lysosomal membrane transporter ‘sialin,’ which normally exports free sialic acid from lysosomes to the cytosol. Defective or absent sialin prevents this efflux, leading to intralysosomal accumulation of sialic acid that characterises Salla disease patients.

805703.long_answer:
3MC syndrome (encompassing Michels, Malpuech, Mingarelli and Carnevale syndromes) is characterised by a constellation of variable craniofacial, skeletal, genital and neuro-developmental anomalies that result from recessive variants in MASP1 or COLEC11.
