Typical craniofacial findings include high-arched or arched eyebrows, ptosis with blepharophimosis, telecanthus, cleft lip/palate, anterior-or unicoronal craniosynostosis, a broad nasal bridge and ear anomalies.   

While unilateral coronal craniosynostosis can produce cranial–facial asymmetry in some affected individuals, this feature is not present in every case and is not part of the obligatory diagnostic criteria. Published case series and reviews describe many patients with 3MC syndrome who have symmetric craniofacial structures. Therefore the statement that asymmetry of the neurocranium and the facial skull is **always** present in 3MC syndrome (or in Michels syndrome) is not supported by the established medical literature.

682446.long_answer: The amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide that forms the characteristic cerebral plaques in Alzheimer’s disease is also a major constituent of the drusen deposits that accumulate beneath the retina in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Detection of Aβ in these ocular deposits links the two disorders pathologically and has led researchers to dub AMD the “Alzheimer’s of the eye.”

412086.long_answer: The GSS gene encodes glutathione synthetase, the enzyme that catalyzes the final step in the de-novo synthesis of glutathione (γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine). Glutathione is the most abundant non-protein thiol found in animal cells and is essential for redox homeostasis, detoxification, and many cellular processes. In the autosomal-recessive disorder known as glutathione synthetase deficiency, pathogenic variants in the GSS gene markedly reduce or abolish enzyme activity. This enzymatic block prevents the efficient conversion of γ-glutamylcysteine to glutathione, leading to severely diminished intracellular glutathione levels. Consequently, the disorder directly hinders the production of the most abundant non-protein thiol in animal cells. Hence, the statement is supported by established biochemical and clinical evidence.

747397.long_answer: Renovascular hypertension arises when one or both renal arteries become narrowed (renal artery stenosis), most commonly from atherosclerotic plaques in older adults or fibromuscular dysplasia in younger patients. The diminished renal perfusion stimulates renin release, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which elevates systemic blood pressure and produces this form of secondary hypertension.

803556.long_answer: Fanconi–Bickel syndrome (glycogen storage disease type XI) results from loss-of-function mutations in the SLC2A2 gene, which encodes the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT2. Defective GLUT2 impairs glucose and galactose transport in hepatocytes, pancreatic β-cells, and renal proximal tubules, leading to the characteristic hepatorenal glycogen accumulation, proximal renal tubular dysfunction, and dysregulated glucose homeostasis seen in this disorder.

994467.long_answer: Ellis-van Creveld (EVC) syndrome is classified among the human ciliopathies. The two genes most commonly mutated in the disorder—EVC and EVC2 (LIMBIN)—encode proteins that localize to the basal body/transition zone of the primary cilium and are required for proper Hedgehog signal transduction through the ciliary compartment. Loss-of-function variants in these genes disrupt primary cilium structure and signaling, which underlies the skeletal dysplasia, polydactyly, and other developmental abnormalities characteristic of the syndrome. Thus, defects in the structure and function of the primary cilium are central to the pathogenesis of Ellis-van Creveld syndrome.

950879.long_answer: Among the pneumoconioses, inhalation of asbestos fibers produces asbestosis, a fibrosing lung disease. Asbestos exposure is strongly linked to the later development of malignant mesothelioma of the pleura and peritoneum, making asbestosis the pneumoconiosis that can progress to mesothelioma.

393178.long_answer: The description "an imaging technique that employs a rotating X-ray tube and a row of detectors" corresponds to computed tomography (CT). When iodinated intravenous contrast is administered, CT is well-established for visualizing intracranial meningiomas. These tumors are typically extra-axial, frequently calcified or hyperdense on non-contrast scans, and they characteristically show strong, homogeneous enhancement after contrast because of their rich vascular supply and intact blood-brain barrier. Contrast-enhanced CT therefore reliably delineates meningioma margins, dural attachment, mass effect, and bony involvement. This is standard, consensus clinical practice, so the statement is correct.

398767.long_answer: Azathioprine is a purine-analog immunosuppressant first synthesized in 1957 by Hitchings and Elion. It is a pro-drug of 6-mercaptopurine that inhibits de novo purine synthesis, leading to dose-dependent bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia). Because it allows reduction of corticosteroid dosage while providing systemic immunosuppression, azathioprine is commonly employed as a steroid-sparing agent in autoimmune conditions, including severe, relapsing polychondritis.

551819.long_answer: Botulinum toxin type A is a potent neurotoxic protein produced by Clostridium botulinum. When injected locally into the orbicularis oculi muscles, it blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, transiently weakening the muscle fibers. This chemodenervation relieves the intermittent, involuntary spasms and contractions characteristic of bilateral blepharospasm (eyelid muscle dystonia), making botulinum toxin A the standard therapeutic agent for this condition.

188198.long_answer: NMNAT2 (nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase-2) is the brain-enriched member of the NMNAT enzyme family. It must be continuously transported into axons; when NMNAT2 levels drop, the loss of its NAD⁺-synthesizing activity triggers the SARM1 pathway and initiates Wallerian-like axonal degeneration, a mechanism implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

151462.long_answer: The pandemic that devastated Eurasia between 1346 and 1353 is known as the Black Death. Historical, genetic, and epidemiological evidence shows it was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, the same pathogen that produces bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic plague forms.

171046.long_answer: Van der Woude syndrome (VWS) is classically inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner. Most affected families carry heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the IRF6 gene (and less commonly GRHL3). Because the disorder is autosomal dominant, possession of a single mutated allele (one copy) is sufficient to produce the clinical phenotype of VWS, although expressivity can be variable. Therefore, a single mutated copy of the gene can indeed cause Van der Woude syndrome.

806815.long_answer: Arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene. VPS33B encodes a member of the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) domain protein family that regulates vesicle trafficking and membrane fusion. Disruption of this Sec1-domain protein impairs intracellular vesicular transport, leading to the multisystem manifestations characteristic of ARC syndrome.

951432.long_answer: The severe end of the benign fasciculation/peripheral nerve hyper-excitability spectrum is Isaacs’ syndrome (acquired neuromyotonia). It is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies against the voltage-gated K⁺-channel complex that cause continuous muscle-fiber activity, fasciculations, cramps and stiffness. Because it is immune-mediated, patients are often treated with immunosuppressive or immunomodulating therapies such as plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin or corticosteroids, unlike the milder benign fasciculation syndrome that usually needs only reassurance or symptomatic therapy.

150243.long_answer: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (also called marfanoid craniosynostosis syndrome) is a rare congenital multiple-anomaly disorder produced by heterozygous mutations in the SKI gene on chromosome 1p36. Affected individuals show craniosynostosis, marfanoid habitus, arachnodactyly—extremely long, slender “spider fingers”—and other connective-tissue and skeletal abnormalities. The association of SKI gene mutations with this characteristic phenotype is well established in the medical genetics literature, making Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome the correct answer.

331013.long_answer: The SERPINA1 gene, situated on chromosome 14q32, encodes the serine-protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT). AAT’s main physiological role is to neutralize neutrophil elastase and related proteases. When AAT is deficient, elastase activity in connective-tissue–rich organs, including the aortic wall, is left unchecked, leading to excessive degradation of elastin fibers. This accelerated elastin breakdown weakens the aortic media and has been associated with a higher incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysm formation. Thus, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can promote pathological elastin loss in the aorta and elevate AAA risk.

568641.long_answer: Absent tibia-polydactyly-arachnoid cyst syndrome presents with limb malformations similar to those seen in disorders caused by mutations in the HOXD gene cluster on chromosome 2q31. Because of this phenotypic overlap, researchers analysed the coding sequence of the chromosome-2 homeobox gene HOXD13 in affected patients. Sequencing revealed no pathogenic variants, demonstrating that HOXD13 is not abnormal in individuals with this syndrome.

260402.long_answer: The single most frequent large-scale mitochondrial DNA rearrangement in both chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) and Kearns–Sayre syndrome is the 4,977-base-pair (≈4.9-kb) deletion that spans nucleotide positions ~8,470–13,447 of the mitochondrial genome. This “common deletion” is detected in roughly one-third of CPEO cases and is the predominant deletion reported in Kearns–Sayre syndrome, making it the hallmark molecular lesion of these disorders.

796223.long_answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), the current name for Wegener’s granulomatosis, is an ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis. Besides affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys, GPA can involve ocular tissues; granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels in the eye frequently manifests as uveitis—an inflammation of the pigmented uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, choroid). Hence, GPA is a recognized autoimmune cause of uveitis.

830404.long_answer: Mutations in the Indian hedgehog (IHH) gene—an essential component of the Hedgehog signaling pathway—cause the congenital skeletal disorder known as Brachydactyly type A1. Affected individuals are born with abnormally short fingers and/or toes because the middle phalanges fail to develop properly. Thus, Brachydactyly type A1 is the congenital syndrome linked directly to Hedgehog pathway dysfunction.

746202.long_answer: Familial intestinal polyatresia syndrome (FIPA) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A gene. TTC7A normally restrains the RhoA/ROCK (Rho-associated co-iled-coil-containing protein kinase) pathway. When TTC7A is defective, RhoA becomes hyper-activated, which in turn increases ROCK kinase activity. Elevated ROCK signaling perturbs the organization of the actin cytoskeleton, leading to failure of apical-basal polarity in intestinal epithelial cells. Restoration of polarity in experimental models can be achieved by pharmacologic inhibition of ROCK, confirming that excessive ROCK activity is the proximal driver of the polarity defect. Therefore, FIPA is indeed associated with increased Rho kinase activity that disrupts epithelial polarity.

663513.long_answer: The SCN4A gene encodes the Nav1.4 voltage-gated sodium channel in skeletal muscle. Mutations that cause hypokalemic periodic paralysis impair this channel, preventing the normal influx of the predominant extracellular cation—sodium (Na+)—across the muscle-cell membrane during depolarization, leading to episodic muscle weakness.

313741.long_answer: James R. Lupski, M.D., Ph.D., currently holds the Cullen Foundation Endowed Chair in Molecular Genetics at Baylor College of Medicine. Together with Dr. Lorraine Potocki, he was the first to delineate the microduplication syndrome now known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome (17p11.2 microduplication) in the mid-1990s. Therefore the statement that the physician who presently occupies the Cullen Endowed Chair at BCM was the first to describe Potocki-Lupski syndrome is factually correct, not incorrect.

770213.long_answer: Potocki–Lupski syndrome is a rare microduplication of chromosome 17p11.2. One of its namesakes is Dr. James R. Lupski, a professor of molecular and human genetics at Baylor College of Medicine. Dr. Lupski is internationally recognized for his research on the hereditary neuropathy Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, and the syndrome bears his name along with that of Dr. Lorraine Potocki because of their joint description of the disorder.

154301.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive congenital disorder distinguished by craniofacial malformations (including craniosynostosis), childhood-onset obesity, pre- and post-axial polydactyly, and soft-tissue or osseous syndactyly. Because it shares the triad of polysyndactyly and craniofacial abnormalities with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome, Carpenter syndrome is listed among the principal disorders that clinically overlap with GCPS in differential-diagnosis guides.

415618.long_answer: Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita (CMTC) is primarily a vascular skin malformation, but ophthalmic involvement has been documented. Published case reports and small series describe patients with CMTC who developed congenital or early-onset glaucoma, which is characterized by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). Although this complication is not present in every CMTC patient, the literature confirms that increased IOP can occur as part of the disorder’s spectrum. Therefore, an increase in intraocular pressure is indeed observed in some individuals diagnosed with CMTC.

284028.long_answer: Fair-haired children may present with loose anagen hair syndrome, a disorder in which the anagen (growing) hairs are poorly anchored and shed easily. One therapeutic approach is to improve follicular nutrition by increasing scalp blood flow. Minoxidil, originally an antihypertensive arterial vasodilator, is applied topically for this purpose. By dilating dermal blood vessels, minoxidil raises local blood supply, delivering more oxygen and nutrients to the hair matrix cells, thereby stimulating thicker, stronger anagen hairs. Clinical reports document successful use of 2–5 % topical minoxidil in fair-haired children with this condition, making minoxidil the drug of choice to enrich hair cells through enhanced vascular perfusion.

472843.long_answer: The principal red blood cell receptor recognized by Plasmodium falciparum PfEMP1 during rosetting is complement receptor 1 (CR1/CD35). The CR1 gene is located in the long arm of human chromosome 1 (1q32). Therefore, the red-blood-cell receptor to which PfEMP1 binds is encoded on chromosome 1.

936226.long_answer: The physician credited with isolating the hepatitis B surface antigen is Baruch Samuel Blumberg, who identified the so-called “Australia antigen” that proved to be the hepatitis B surface antigen and later shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. Blumberg was married to Jean Hlavacek, not to Veronica Tester. Because the physician who married Veronica Tester was a different individual, the person who isolated the hepatitis B surface antigen and the physician who married Veronica Tester are not the same.

491820.long_answer: Idiopathic juvenile kyphosis is most frequently known as Scheuermann disease. In the classic medical literature, Scheuermann disease has several synonymous designations, one of which is “osteochondritis deformans juvenilis” (sometimes expanded to “osteochondritis deformans juvenilis dorsi”). Therefore, the term osteochondritis deformans juvenilis is indeed commonly used—especially in older or more formal texts—as a synonym for idiopathic juvenile (Scheuermann) kyphosis.

917636.long_answer: There is no information provided in the context about the typical size of nodules in eumycetoma. Because the claim cannot be supported by any data in the supplied context, it cannot be considered factually established.

828118.long_answer: In dermatological terminology a solid, palpable lesion that is larger than 1 cm in diameter is called a nodule. During the early stage of Eumycetoma, patients develop small, firm subcutaneous swellings that usually exceed 1 cm; these lesions are therefore termed nodules.

579497.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (often abbreviated ODD or ODDD) is a genetic syndrome caused most commonly by pathogenic variants in the GJA1 gene. One of its hallmark skeletal manifestations is syndactyly—partial or complete fusion—of the central digits of the hand. The fusion most frequently involves the third and fourth fingers (middle and ring) and/or the fourth and fifth fingers (ring and little). Because the affected digits are joined and may also exhibit camptodactyly, clinodactyly, or shortened phalanges, patients typically experience restricted independent motion, reduced grip dexterity, and other functional limitations of those fingers. Hence, a condition related to ODD syndrome does indeed affect the functioning of the ring and middle fingers.

522257.long_answer: Hajdu–Cheney syndrome is characterized by multiple skeletal abnormalities, one of which is the presence of supernumerary, small bone islands that form within the cranial sutures. These accessory ossicles are classically called Wormian bones—also referred to as sutural or intrasutural bones—because they occur between the normal skull bones along the suture lines. Their occurrence in excess is a well-documented radiographic feature of the disorder.

837230.long_answer: The TK2 gene (thymidine kinase 2, mitochondrial) lies on chromosome 16q22.1. Mutations in TK2 produce the myopathic form of mitochondrial DNA-depletion syndrome type 2. Infants carrying pathogenic TK2 variants appear normal during infancy and early childhood, but around two years of age they begin to show generalized, progressive muscle weakness that steadily worsens. The disorder currently has no curative or disease-modifying treatment, only supportive care, matching the scenario described.

254319.long_answer: Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) contains potent cardiac glycosides that make all parts of the plant highly toxic if ingested. Despite this toxicity, gardeners frequently cultivate it as a biennial—sowing seed one year for flowering the next—because of its tall spikes densely packed with vivid purple, pink, or white tubular flowers that add striking color to ornamental beds and borders.

556973.long_answer: The only information supplied is that GMS syndrome was reported in 1992. No data are provided about clinical manifestations, functional limitations, or effects on activities of daily living. Because the question cannot be substantiated with the given context alone, the claim that GMS syndrome negatively affects daily living activities is not supported.

494387.long_answer: Methotrexate is a folic-acid antagonist (antifolate) that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. It is widely used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug in chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) when first-line treatments fail, and it is also a standard systemic therapy for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Its dual efficacy in these inflammatory conditions makes methotrexate the antifolate medication employed for both CRMO and psoriasis.

424544.long_answer: T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/T-LBL) accounts for roughly 15 percent of childhood leukemias, a figure repeatedly cited in epidemiologic studies and WHO classifications that note T-ALL comprises about 15 % of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia cases.

991013.long_answer: Patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma frequently report so-called B symptoms, one of which is severe, profuse nocturnal sweating. Clinically, these episodes are termed “drenching night sweats,” indicating perspiration intense enough to soak sleepwear or bed linens.

405579.long_answer: Achondroplasia is an inherited disorder of bone growth presenting with disproportionate short stature, bowing or other deformities of the lower limbs, brachydactyly (short fingers), and ligamentous laxity. The condition results from gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene, which negatively regulates endochondral ossification. Therefore, the clinical features described are indeed caused by an FGFR3 gene mutation.

149439.long_answer: Syphilitic leukoplakia is an oral white patch that appears during tertiary syphilis. The causative organism of syphilis is Treponema pallidum, a slender, spiral-shaped spirochete that is microaerophilic and classified with gram-negative bacteria because it possesses a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide-like molecules. Persistent infection of oral tissues by Treponema pallidum produces the characteristic leukoplakic lesion, hence the name syphilitic leukoplakia.

836831.long_answer: The inherited disorder that shows a markedly high incidence in the Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean region of Québec is tyrosinemia type I (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency), not tyrosinemia type II. Tyrosinemia type II (caused by tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency) is a rare condition worldwide and has not been reported to occur with increased frequency in this particular population. Therefore, saying that tyrosinemia type II is common in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region is incorrect.

961487.long_answer: The World Health Organization (the United Nations health agency) identifies major depressive disorder as the single largest contributor to years lived with disability globally. A substantial body of epidemiological and clinical research shows that habitual or chronic procrastination is positively correlated with higher levels of depressive symptoms and with a greater likelihood of meeting criteria for major depressive disorder. Although procrastination is not itself a clinical diagnosis, it is consistently associated—across cross-sectional studies, longitudinal cohorts, and meta-analyses—with increased depressive mood, anhedonia, and functional impairment characteristic of depression. Therefore, procrastination is indeed associated with the disorder that the WHO lists as the leading cause of disability worldwide.

545881.long_answer: An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses the normal high-resistance arteriolar bed. Because blood flows directly from the high-pressure arterial system into the low-pressure venous system, total peripheral resistance falls sharply. The reduced afterload, together with the marked rise in venous return, forces the heart to pump a much larger volume of blood, so cardiac output rises substantially—especially if the fistula involves a large artery.

894645.long_answer: Myoglobinuria most often results from rhabdomyolysis.  When rhabdomyolysis is caused by traumatic crush injury it can be complicated by acute kidney injury, but contemporary series show overall mortality rates generally ranging from about 10 % to 40 %.  Even in the sickest sub-groups who require dialysis the reported death rate rarely exceeds 50 %.  Therefore, it is not accurate to state that this common cause of myoglobinuria carries a mortality rate greater than 50 % as a matter of established clinical consensus.

205242.long_answer: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a major plasma protein synthesized by the fetal yolk sac (and later by the fetal liver). In clinical practice, serum AFP concentrations are frequently and markedly elevated in patients with hepatoblastoma, and the test is used both for diagnosis and for monitoring response to therapy. Therefore, a yolk-sac-derived plasma protein is indeed commonly elevated in hepatoblastomas.

103768.long_answer: The disorder is Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD).  In DSM-5, BDD is grouped with the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.  Its hallmark is an intense, time-consuming preoccupation with an imagined or greatly exaggerated defect in physical appearance—typically focused on skin, hair, nose, or other body parts—and this concern is explicitly unrelated to body weight or shape.  This distinguishes BDD from anorexia nervosa, an eating disorder characterized by fear of weight gain and restrictive eating behaviors aimed at lowering body weight.  Thus, BDD is the contrasting obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorder sought in the question.

479398.long_answer: XX gonadal dysgenesis can occur as part of Perrault syndrome, a rare genetic disorder in which 46,XX females present with streak ovaries (primary ovarian insufficiency) together with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Sensorineural hearing loss typically impairs the ability to discriminate speech, especially when background noise is present. Therefore, a woman with XX gonadal dysgenesis could indeed experience difficulty distinguishing voices in noisy environments.

998920.long_answer: In syndromes where hypogonadism occurs together with sensorineural hearing loss in females (e.g., Perrault syndrome, Turner syndrome–associated deafness), the hearing deficit results from congenital or progressive inner-ear/cochlear pathology. Because the hair cells and neural elements are damaged or malformed, the deafness does not recover with hormonal correction and is regarded as permanent rather than reversible.

527725.long_answer: Cobalamin C (cblC) disease is the prototype inborn error of vitamin B₁₂ processing in which conversion of cobalamin to its active co-factor methylcobalamin is blocked. Loss of methylcobalamin cripples methionine synthase, leading to homocystinuria, megaloblastic anemia, and combined neurologic-developmental abnormalities such as intellectual disability, seizures, hypotonia, and growth delay. The syndrome therefore presents with mental retardation, anemia, and other neurological and developmental problems characteristic of impaired methylcobalamin metabolism.

742501.long_answer: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), is a rare and highly aggressive mature T-cell malignancy. Patients typically present with generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly due to widespread nodal and extranodal infiltration. Unlike adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, PTCL-NOS is characteristically negative for human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), helping distinguish it from HTLV-1–associated T-cell neoplasms.

762048.long_answer: Cartilage–Hair Hypoplasia (CHH) is a skeletal dysplasia that is frequently accompanied by cellular immunodeficiency. One of its hallmark laboratory abnormalities is chronic lymphopenia, most notably reduced T-cell counts. Reported lymphocyte values in CHH patients often fall below 1.0 × 10⁹/L, sometimes markedly lower. Therefore, an adult who presents with a lymphocyte count of < 0.9 × 10⁹/L could indeed be displaying a hematological sign compatible with CHH, and the disorder should be considered in the differential diagnosis, especially if other clinical features (short stature, fine sparse hair, skeletal anomalies) are present.

450226.long_answer: Mulibrey nanism—often referred to as the muscle-liver-brain-eye (Mulibrey) growth-delay syndrome—is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by severe pre- and post-natal growth retardation, typical craniofacial features and multiorgan involvement. Comprehensive genetic studies have shown that every confirmed case of Mulibrey nanism carries biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the gene TRIM37, located on chromosome 17q22–q23. No other gene has been implicated in this specific growth-delay syndrome, making TRIM37 the definitive causal gene.

933211.long_answer: Pacerone is the brand name for amiodarone, a highly lipophilic class III anti-arrhythmic drug. Because of its strong affinity for lipids, amiodarone and its metabolite desethyl-amiodarone accumulate in alveolar macrophages and type II pneumocytes, producing intracellular phospholipid‐laden ("foamy") macrophages. This drug-induced phospholipidosis manifests pathologically and radiologically as lipoid (lipid) pneumonia, often classified in the literature as an exogenous lipoid pneumonia because the offending lipid-like substance (amiodarone) is introduced from outside the body. Numerous clinical reports and reviews describe “amiodarone-induced lipoid pneumonia” or “amiodarone lung” as a recognized form of pulmonary toxicity. Therefore, it is established that exposure to Pacerone can lead to exogenous lipid (lipoid) pneumonia in susceptible patients.

139521.long_answer: Amiodarone, a class III anti-arrhythmic agent, is well documented to deposit iodinated phospholipids in pulmonary tissue. These deposits lead to the characteristic picture of lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages and parenchymal inflammation, a pattern described pathologically and radiologically as exogenous lipid (lipoid) pneumonia. Hence, amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic medication classically associated with exogenous lipid pneumonia.

450290.long_answer: Pronaxen is a trade name for naproxen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Chikungunya infection does not have a virus-directed treatment; management focuses on relieving its hallmark symptoms of fever, joint pain and inflammation. After dengue has been ruled out, clinical guidelines recommend NSAIDs such as naproxen for symptomatic control of the arthralgia and myalgia associated with Chikungunya. Therefore, using Pronaxen can be considered effective for reducing pain and inflammation in patients with Chikungunya, though it does not eradicate the virus itself.

893226.long_answer: Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) routinely prescribed for chronic inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis. Clinical and public-health guidelines for symptomatic management of Chikungunya advise the use of NSAIDs—after dengue has been excluded—to control the high fever, arthralgia, and joint edema characteristic of the infection. Among the recommended options, naproxen is specifically mentioned because of its established anti-inflammatory and antipyretic efficacy. Thus, naproxen is the NSAID of choice for relieving fever and joint swelling in patients with Chikungunya.

114428.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene. Cytogenetic mapping shows BCOR resides on the short arm of the X-chromosome at band p11.4, making Xp11.4 the chromosomal location of the gene mutated in OFCD syndrome.

931338.long_answer: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts primarily on Sertoli cells to promote spermatogenesis, whereas circulating testosterone levels reflect Leydig-cell function driven mainly by luteinizing hormone (LH). Documented cases of FSH-receptor mutations or post-receptor defects show that adult men can have normal LH secretion, normal Leydig-cell responsiveness, and therefore normal to high-normal serum testosterone (e.g., ~630 ng/dL), yet exhibit impaired or absent Sertoli-cell response to FSH. This state—often termed FSH resistance or insensitivity—manifests clinically with normal virilization but defective sperm production. Hence, a normal testosterone concentration does not exclude, and is compatible with, insensitivity to FSH.

154580.long_answer: People with Down syndrome have well-documented immune dysregulation that makes them more prone to recurrent respiratory, ear, and other infections. Clinical guidelines therefore emphasize rapid and appropriate treatment of any infection (e.g., antibiotics for bacterial illnesses, supportive therapy for viral infections). In addition, measures to bolster or compensate for their relatively weak immune responses—such as up-to-date vaccinations, prophylactic therapies in selected cases, adequate nutrition, and regular medical follow-up—are recommended to help prevent infections and improve overall health. Thus, both infection management and immune-supportive care are considered standard components of medical care for individuals with Down syndrome.

578911.long_answer: People with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) have well-documented quantitative and functional abnormalities in both the innate and adaptive branches of the immune system. Typical findings include reduced numbers and impaired maturation of T and B lymphocytes, diminished antibody responses (particularly IgG2 and IgG4 subclasses), defective neutrophil chemotaxis, and dysregulated cytokine production. Clinically, these defects translate into substantially higher rates of recurrent respiratory and ear infections, increased incidence of severe viral illnesses, and greater susceptibility to sepsis compared with age-matched individuals without trisomy 21. These recurrent and severe infections are hallmarks of a clinically meaningful immunodeficiency. Therefore, the statement that individuals with Down syndrome generally experience a compromised immune system is supported by established biomedical evidence.

817297.long_answer: The physiologic (“normal”) intra-ocular pressure (IOP) range in the general population is usually quoted as ~10–21 mmHg. However, in established glaucoma the concept of a universally ‘safe’ IOP does not apply. Many glaucoma patients continue to lose visual field at pressures within the so-called normal range, and clinical guidelines emphasise setting an individualised “target IOP” that is typically 20–40 % below the patient’s untreated baseline and may need to be ≤12 mmHg—or even single-digits—in advanced disease. Consequently, while 10–20 mmHg is normal for the average eye, it cannot be assumed to be safe for someone with glaucoma; the appropriate pressure depends on the severity of optic-nerve damage, rate of progression, and other risk factors.

928221.long_answer: In their 1989 report on dynamic smile reconstruction in children with Möbius syndrome, Zuker and colleagues described using a free gracilis muscle transfer innervated by the motor branch of the trigeminal nerve that supplies the masseter. They proposed the masseteric nerve as the donor because it is reliably present and strong in these patients even when the facial (VII) nerve is absent or non-functional. Coapting the gracilis motor nerve to the masseteric nerve restored voluntary contraction of the transplanted muscle and allowed the children to regain the ability to smile.

821517.long_answer: Hereditary retinoschisis, most often the X-linked juvenile form, is produced by pathogenic mutations in the RS1 gene on Xp22.2. RS1 encodes retinoschisin, a secreted cell-adhesion protein that stabilizes the interaction between photoreceptors and bipolar cells. Loss-of-function variants disrupt this adhesion, leading to splitting (schisis) of the neurosensory retina—classically within the outer plexiform layer—seen clinically as foveal and peripheral retinal schisis.

680746.long_answer: Gonadal agenesis (absence or failure of development of the ovaries or testes) results in very low or absent sex-steroid secretion. In individuals with an XX or XY karyotype who have streak or absent gonads, the Müllerian ducts may form a uterus and upper vagina during fetal life, but post-pubertal growth of the genital tract is estrogen-dependent. Because estrogen is largely absent in gonadal agenesis, the vagina remains infantile—narrow and shorter than normal—and the uterus is small or rudimentary. Therefore, a shortened (hypoplastic) vagina is a recognized consequence of gonadal agenesis, making an anatomic link between the two conditions biologically plausible and documented in clinical descriptions.

285796.long_answer: Pelvic lipomatosis is a rare disorder marked by benign, disproportionate overgrowth of mature adipose tissue within the pelvis. It occurs predominantly in middle-aged to older Black men who are obese (body-mass index ≥30 kg/m²). The massive perivesical fat narrows the pelvis and indents the urinary bladder, producing the classic “pear-shaped” or “teardrop” bladder appearance on CT or IVU imaging. These characteristic epidemiologic features and imaging findings make pelvic lipomatosis the recognized answer.

979905.long_answer: Lymph nodes are small, bean- or kidney-shaped organs of the lymphatic system. In pancreatic cancer, the TNM staging system assigns great importance to whether regional lymph nodes (peripancreatic, celiac, hepatoduodenal, superior mesenteric, etc.) contain metastatic deposits. Cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic ultrasound, and surgical sampling therefore focus closely on these kidney-shaped structures to determine nodal involvement and overall stage.

947220.long_answer: The condition is neonatal (physiologic) jaundice, a common, usually benign yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera caused by elevated serum bilirubin. It appears in about 80 % of newborns during their first week of life because their hepatic bilirubin-conjugating mechanisms are immature and bilirubin production from hemoglobin breakdown is high. Levels peak around days 3–5 and then fall as liver function matures.

134630.long_answer: The yellow pigment that produces the characteristic discoloration seen in jaundice is bilirubin, a tetrapyrrole breakdown product of heme. Until recently it was thought to occur only in animals, but chemical analysis showed that the white bird-of-paradise plant, Strelitzia nicolai, accumulates the same molecule in its orange aril tissues. This makes Strelitzia nicolai the first plant species confirmed to contain bilirubin, the very pigment responsible for jaundice’s yellow hue.

966492.long_answer: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita involves congenital joint contractures that stem from reduced fetal movement. The diminished movement limits normal muscle and bone growth in the affected extremities. Consequently, the involved limb often has smaller muscle bulk and slower longitudinal growth, leading to observable limb-length discrepancy or a smaller foot on one side. Therefore, it is well-recognized that arthrogryposis can result in one leg or foot being shorter or smaller than the contralateral side.

655317.long_answer: Accidents (unintentional injuries) are the leading cause of death in U.S. children aged 1–14 years, and malignant neoplasms (childhood cancers) are consistently reported by the CDC as the second leading cause in this age group. Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is a congenital over-growth/epigenetic disorder that confers a markedly elevated risk of several embryonal malignancies—most notably Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma—as well as other childhood cancers. Because BWS children have a significantly higher incidence of these malignancies compared with the general pediatric population, the syndrome is recognized as a cancer‐predisposition condition. Therefore, BWS does increase the risk of the disease category that constitutes the second leading cause of death among U.S. children aged 1–14 years.

189171.long_answer: Yemenite deaf-blind hypopigmentation syndrome is regarded as an allelic/phenotypic variant within the Waardenburg syndrome spectrum. The condition is produced by pathogenic variants in SOX10, one of the same genes that cause Waardenburg–Shah syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4). Because they share the same molecular etiology and overlapping clinical features—sensorineural deafness, pigmentary abnormalities, and variable additional defects—the Yemenite syndrome is considered to be associated with, and often classified under, Waardenburg–Shah syndrome.

904524.long_answer: Abruzzo-Erikson syndrome is an earlier eponym for the condition that is now grouped under CHARGE syndrome (characterised by Coloboma, Heart defects, Choanal atresia, Retarded growth/development, Genital anomalies and Ear anomalies). The great majority of individuals diagnosed with CHARGE/Abruzzo-Erikson syndrome carry heterozygous pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene. Therefore, the syndrome is indeed linked to CHD7 mutation.

739638.long_answer: Hyperventilation lowers arterial CO₂ (hypocapnia), producing cerebral alkalosis that readily provokes the 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges characteristic of generalized absence seizures. Clinically, brief staring episodes with impaired awareness are classically evoked by asking a patient to hyperventilate, making absence seizure the generalized seizure type most commonly triggered by this maneuver.

597726.long_answer: The provided context contains no information indicating that β-catenin is implicated in the pathology of tetra-amelia syndrome. Therefore, based solely on the available context, there is no support for a role of β-catenin in this condition.

254228.long_answer: Severe, generalized accumulation of fluid in the subcutaneous tissues and serous cavities is termed anasarca. In diabetic nephropathy, heavy proteinuria and subsequent hypoalbuminemia lower plasma oncotic pressure, leading to marked, body-wide edema—clinically described as anasarca.

118785.long_answer: The term “Fetal Alcohol Effect” (FAE) was once applied to children whose brains were damaged by prenatal alcohol exposure, but who lacked the full facial or growth features of fetal alcohol syndrome. Because it was imprecise and overlapped with other diagnoses, the term has largely been abandoned in favor of the broader, better-defined category Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), which includes alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND) and other subtypes.

666699.long_answer: In Angle’s classification, a Class III malocclusion is characterized by mandibular prognathism: the lower dental arch and incisors lie anterior to the upper dental arch, producing an ‘under-bite.’ This relationship results from an excessively protruding lower jaw or a retrusive maxilla, causing the lower teeth to occlude ahead of the upper teeth.

794196.long_answer: Post-ictal paresis/paralysis (Todd’s paralysis) follows an epileptic seizure. Benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam and clonazepam are well-established antiepileptic agents; they are first-line drugs for aborting acute seizures and status epilepticus and are also used as adjunctive long-term therapy in some epilepsy syndromes. Because they are routinely employed to control the seizures that give rise to post-ictal paralysis, benzodiazepines are indeed used to manage the underlying disease.

139364.long_answer: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) is a rare autosomal-recessive, multisystemic lipid-storage disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in CYP27A1. Accumulation of cholestanol in the central nervous system produces early psychomotor delay and marked slowing of both mental and physical activity, a syndrome that clinically resembles the psychomotor retardation observed in major depressive disorder. Additional systemic features such as juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas and progressive ataxia confirm its multisystemic nature.

453449.long_answer: The most common renal tumour seen in the first three months of life is congenital mesoblastic nephroma. Over 90 % of the cellular and mixed forms of this neoplasm harbour the t(12;15)(p13;q25) translocation that fuses the ETV6 gene on chromosome 12 to the NTRK3 gene on chromosome 15, creating the oncogenic ETV6-NTRK3 fusion tyrosine-kinase. Detection of this specific gene mutation is a molecular hallmark of the tumour.

847295.long_answer: In the European Union and many other jurisdictions, a disorder is considered rare when it affects fewer than 1 person in every 2,000. Conditions such as the microcornea-glaucoma-absent-frontal-sinus syndrome fall under this definition, meaning no more than about 1 individual per 2,000 people would typically be affected.

649969.long_answer: The progeroid cutis laxa (De Barsy) syndrome that presents with a prematurely aged appearance, generalized cutis laxa, growth and developmental delay, and characteristic ocular findings such as bilateral corneal clouding is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ALDH18A1 gene. ALDH18A1 encodes Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS); deficiency of this enzyme disrupts proline and ornithine biosynthesis, leading to the connective-tissue and ocular abnormalities that define the syndrome.

214705.long_answer: Perimyositis refers to inflammation (the “-itis” suffix) of the perimysium, the connective-tissue sheath that surrounds muscle fascicles. Inflammation is the body’s canonical biological response of living vascular connective tissue to harmful stimuli such as pathogens, damaged cells or irritants. Therefore, because perimyositis is precisely an inflammatory process affecting the connective tissue that envelops muscle fibers, it constitutes part of the biological (inflammatory) response of that connective tissue to harmful stimuli.

363368.long_answer: PCDH7 (protocadherin-7) belongs to the protocadherin subfamily within the cadherin superfamily of calcium-dependent cell-adhesion molecules. Genetic mapping and sequencing studies of patients with congenital tracheoesophageal malformations have identified variants in PCDH7, and the gene has therefore been put forward as a candidate gene for esophageal atresia. Its involvement is biologically plausible because protocadherins participate in epithelial cell-cell adhesion processes that are essential for correct foregut septation during embryonic development, the step that fails in esophageal atresia.

581924.long_answer: Probst bundles are longitudinal fiber tracts that form when the commissural fibers of the corpus callosum fail to cross the midline. Their presence is a classic neuroradiologic sign of agenesis of the corpus callosum (complete or partial absence of this structure). In Infantile Spasms–Broad Thumbs Syndrome (also called Say-Field syndrome), this rare birth defect—corpus callosum agenesis—has been repeatedly documented, explaining the characteristic Probst bundles seen in affected individuals.

423479.long_answer: Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) is produced by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase, commonly called arylsulfatase B (ARSB). X-ray crystallographic analysis of human ARSB (e.g., PDB entry 1FSU) shows that its polypeptide chain folds into a canonical arylsulfatase α/β-fold composed of a central eight-stranded β-sheet surrounded by 17 distinct α-helices. Thus, the secondary-structure of the enzyme contains seventeen α-helices.

814670.long_answer: Quinine and related cinchona alkaloids are drugs employed in the treatment of both malaria and, in combination regimens, babesiosis. Excessive dosing or chronic high-level exposure to these medications leads to the well-defined toxicity syndrome called cinchonism (or quinism). Cinchonism is characterized by symptoms such as tinnitus, hearing and visual disturbances, headache, nausea, and CNS effects, and it represents the classic condition resulting from quinine overdose.

184466.long_answer: Shigella species are spread predominantly by the fecal–oral pathway: bacteria shed in an infected person’s feces contaminate hands, food, water, or surfaces and are then ingested by another host. As few as 10–100 organisms can initiate infection, making direct person-to-person hand-to-mouth transmission the principal route rather than airborne, vector-borne, or droplet spread.

515320.long_answer: Barakat syndrome, also called HDR (Hypoparathyroidism-Deafness-Renal dysplasia) syndrome, is characterized by defects in the kidneys, which are the body’s principal blood-filtering organs. Patients typically exhibit renal dysplasia, hypoplasia, or other structural and functional kidney abnormalities, making the kidneys the organ most commonly affected in this condition.

157149.long_answer: Cystic hygromas (lymphangiomas) in the neck most often arise in the posterior triangle, deep to or surrounding the sternocleidomastoid. Dissection in this area places the spinal accessory nerve—cranial nerve XI, which courses superficially across the posterior triangle to innervate the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius—at particular risk of traction or transection injury during removal of the mass.

655782.long_answer: The lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase is Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA (Morquio A syndrome). In February 2014, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the enzyme-replacement therapy elosulfase alfa (marketed as Vimizim) specifically for the treatment of this condition, providing patients with a recombinant form of the missing enzyme.

885704.long_answer: People with Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) generally have normal intellect, but they are prone to developing hydrocephalus from impaired cerebrospinal-fluid flow at the craniocervical junction. If this hydrocephalus is not recognized and surgically treated (e.g., with shunting or decompression), the resulting chronically raised intracranial pressure can damage the brain and lead to loss of previously normal cognitive function.

703052.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome has been documented in Papua New Guinea. Demographic data for Papua New Guinea indicate that roughly 98 % of the nation’s inhabitants are indigenous Papuan or Austronesian peoples; only a small minority are of non-indigenous origin.

879116.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome (KFDCA) is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive disorder; to date only six patients, all originating from Mexico, have been reported in the medical literature. Mexico won its War of Independence against the Spanish Empire with the signing of the Treaty of Córdoba and the declaration of the Acta de Independencia on 28 September 1821. Therefore, the year in which the country achieved independence from Spain is 1821.

819839.long_answer: Cor triatriatum dexter is a rare congenital defect produced when the right venous (sinus) valve fails to regress completely. The persistent valve forms a membrane that partitions the right atrium—where the coronary sinus (and its Thebesian valve) is also located—into two chambers, giving the heart three atrial cavities.

632188.long_answer: The described presentation—primary amenorrhea in a phenotypic female who has normal breast development and pubic hair because her ovaries function normally, but who lacks a uterus and upper vagina—is classic for Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. MRKH is a congenital Müllerian agenesis/duplication defect in which the Müllerian ducts fail to develop, resulting in absence or rudimentary formation of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina. Because the ovaries originate from a different embryologic source (the genital ridge), they develop and function normally, producing estrogen that drives secondary sexual characteristics. Hence, affected individuals are 46,XX with fully developed secondary sex traits yet experience primary amenorrhea due to the absent uterine outflow tract.

287123.long_answer: The neurons that are progressively lost in cerebellar degeneration are Purkinje cells. These large cerebellar neurons were first described by the Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkinje in 1837. Subsequent neuropathological studies linked their degeneration to many cerebellar ataxias, but the initial discovery of the cell type itself dates to 1837.

846660.long_answer: In cerebellar degeneration the principal GABA-ergic output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, the Purkinje cells, are progressively lost. Purkinje cells release γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) onto the deep cerebellar nuclei, and their degeneration is a hallmark of many spinocerebellar ataxias and other cerebellar degenerative disorders.

400640.long_answer: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency can lead to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by severe memory impairment. One hallmark of Korsakoff amnesia is a temporally graded retrograde amnesia: older memories are relatively spared while more recent memories are lost. Thus, a brain deficiency of vitamin B1 is indeed associated with this specific pattern of retrograde amnesia.

351765.long_answer: Persistent Müllerian duct syndrome (PMDS) occurs in 46,XY individuals when mutations in the anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) gene or its type II receptor prevent normal AMH signaling. Because the Müllerian ducts fail to regress, a uterus and fallopian tubes persist alongside normally virilized external genitalia and testes. This condition, once labeled a form of male pseudohermaphroditism, exemplifies a congenital disorder of sex development caused by defective AMH activity.

586813.long_answer: Hydrochlorothiazide, while commonly used to reduce polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, carries class-related diuretic risks such as intravascular volume depletion, prerenal azotemia or acute kidney injury, and electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypokalemia, hyponatremia). These events reflect potential adverse effects on renal function, so clinicians must monitor renal parameters and volume status when prescribing the drug in this population.

218487.long_answer: The potassium-sparing diuretic amiloride is routinely used in clinical practice to manage hypertension and is also the primary (first-line) pharmacologic treatment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, particularly when the condition is induced by lithium therapy. Amiloride acts on the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, reducing sodium reabsorption and thereby decreasing the polyuria characteristic of nephrogenic DI while sparing potassium.

396243.long_answer: Primary (familial) hyperlipidemia refers to lipid abnormalities that stem from inherited defects in lipid-metabolizing genes and are present irrespective of dietary intake. When elevated lipid levels are provoked by modifiable external factors—such as excessive consumption of saturated-fat–rich foods like pork and beef—the condition is classified as a secondary or acquired hyperlipidemia. Therefore, hyperlipidemia attributed to a diet high in pork and beef should not be labeled primary hyperlipidemia.

490477.long_answer: Pruritus (itching) is a well-recognized and frequent feature of mastocytosis because the excessive release of histamine and other mast-cell mediators directly stimulates cutaneous nerve endings. Herpesvirus infections—both herpes simplex and herpes zoster—also commonly produce itching: patients typically report itching or tingling in the prodromal phase and during healing of the vesicular lesions. Therefore, itching is considered a common symptom encountered in both mastocytosis and herpes.

125994.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the CRADD gene (also known as RAIDD) have been shown to cause frontal-dominant polymicrogyria in affected individuals. Biochemically, CRADD is an adaptor protein that interacts with RIPK1 and CASP2 and is required for tumor-necrosis-factor-α (TNFα)-induced activation of the JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase) signaling cascade. Thus, CRADD links the cortical malformation polymicrogyria with JNK pathway activation in response to TNFα.

951532.long_answer: Harding’s ataxia (also called autosomal-recessive cerebellar ataxia of late onset, first delineated by Harding in 1981) is distinguished from Friedreich’s ataxia by the absence of systemic metabolic complications such as diabetes mellitus. Patients with Harding’s ataxia generally have normal glucose tolerance, and persistent hyperglycaemia is not part of the recognised clinical picture. Therefore a patient with Harding’s ataxia would not be expected to present with sustained high blood-sugar levels.

246741.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) is a group of rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by marked underdevelopment and progressive atrophy of the cerebellum and pons. A core clinical feature across nearly all PCH subtypes is profound global developmental delay. Affected children typically display severe hypotonia, poor or absent head control, and marked psychomotor impairment from early infancy. Because of this severity, most children with PCH do not attain fundamental gross-motor milestones such as independent sitting, crawling, or walking; many never achieve even basic head control. Consequently, by the age of two years, it is uncommon for children with PCH to have reached normal gross motor milestones. Therefore, the statement that they generally reach these milestones by age two is not supported by established medical evidence.

143441.long_answer: The question provides no information indicating that individuals with acro-oto-radial syndrome have the specific, documented deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning required by the DSM-5 definition of intellectual disability. Without evidence of those criteria (confirmed impairments in reasoning, problem solving, academic learning, adaptive behavior, and onset during the developmental period), the statement that the syndrome “fulfills the DSM-5 criteria for intellectual disability” cannot be supported. Therefore, based solely on the information given, the claim is not justified.

539437.long_answer: The WFS1 (wolframin) gene is best known for causing Wolfram syndrome, but more than thirty different WFS1 mutations have also been documented in individuals who have isolated (nonsyndromic) sensorineural hearing loss. Nonsyndromic forms account for roughly three-quarters (≈75 %) of all hereditary hearing-loss cases, distinguishing them from the remaining syndromic causes. Thus, the condition linked both to about 75 % of hearing-loss cases and to the >30 hearing-loss-specific WFS1 mutations is nonsyndromic hearing loss.

921534.long_answer: In the 2016 (and current) World Health Organization classification, acute myeloid leukemia—including the minimally differentiated (M0) subtype—is diagnosed only when blast cells constitute at least 20 % of nucleated cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood, provided that none of the defining recurrent genetic abnormalities (which would allow a lower blast count) are present.

253734.long_answer: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition marked by persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. Epidemiological studies show that roughly 40–50 % of children and adults with developmental coordination disorder (DCD) also meet diagnostic criteria for ADHD, indicating a high rate of co-occurrence between the two disorders.

638322.long_answer: The thread-like nematode genus in question is Gongylonema, first erected by Giovanni Battista Molin in 1857. Species of Gongylonema are important parasites of many domestic animals (e.g., cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry) and only rarely infect humans (causing the uncommon disease gongylonemiasis). Taxonomically, Gongylonema belongs to the family Gongylonematidae, which is placed within the suborder Spirurina of the class Chromadorea. Hence, the suborder of Chromadorea that encompasses this genus—and therefore fits the description given—is Spirurina.

524762.long_answer: Pediatric (X-linked) gigantism is produced by micro-duplications in the Xq26.3 locus that include the GPR101 gene, while Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome is caused by loss-of-function changes in the neighbouring GPC3/GPC4 locus in Xq26.2. Thus, the shared chromosomal region implicated in both disorders is the long-arm segment Xq26 of the X chromosome.

532019.long_answer: Hers disease, formally designated glycogen storage disease type VI, was first characterized by Henri-Géry Hers in 1959. Owing to its hepatic glycogen-phosphorylase deficiency, it causes hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia and elevated transaminases—clinical findings that closely mimic those of glycogen storage disease type III. Consequently, GSD VI is a standard consideration in the differential diagnosis of suspected GSD III cases.

117785.long_answer: Basilar invagination refers to the upward displacement of the odontoid process into the foramen magnum at the cranio-vertebral junction. The odontoid process is part of the second cervical vertebra, the axis (C2). Thus, the bone specifically involved in basilar invagination is the axis (C2 vertebra).

298228.long_answer: The VPS33B gene (Vacuolar Protein Sorting-Associated Protein 33B), whose biallelic pathogenic variants cause arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome, is mapped to cytogenetic band 15q26 on human chromosome 15. This chromosomal assignment has been confirmed by linkage analysis, fluorescence in-situ hybridization, and genome assemblies (e.g., GRCh38: chr15: 100,064,801-100,095,373). Hence, VPS33B resides on chromosome 15.

252895.long_answer: In Anton syndrome, patients are cortically blind yet insist they can see. This unawareness of, or failure to acknowledge, their deficit is a specific example of anosognosia—a condition first detailed by the French neurologist Joseph Babinski in 1914 to describe patients who deny or are unaware of their neurological impairments.

234430.long_answer: The acute confusional state that can arise within hours to days after exposure to mefloquine (or related quinoline antimalarials) is medically termed delirium. Delirium is a fluctuating disturbance of consciousness and cognition often accompanied by hallucinations, agitation, and disorientation. In cases of mefloquine-induced chronic encephalopathy, delirium is recognized as one of the cardinal, early neuropsychiatric manifestations and is sometimes misinterpreted as post-traumatic stress disorder because of overlapping symptoms such as anxiety, hyperarousal, and intrusive experiences.

576476.long_answer: Surgical management of anorectal malformations is typically staged and includes procedures that can be revised or undone, such as temporary diverting colostomies that are later closed. Even definitive repairs (e.g., posterior sagittal anorectoplasty) can be modified by subsequent corrective or revision surgeries if necessary. Therefore, operations performed for anorectal malformations are not invariably permanent or irreversible; some components are specifically intended to be temporary and others can be revised to improve function.

406747.long_answer: Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis often arises in chronic infections such as osteomyelitis. Diabetic patients, particularly those with diabetic foot ulcers, have a high incidence of osteomyelitis. The chronic inflammatory stimulus of osteomyelitis elevates interleukin-6, boosts thrombopoietin production, and drives a reactive elevation of platelet count, linking this condition both to reactive thrombocythemia and to diabetes.

142759.long_answer: Bevacizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). It received U.S. FDA approval in 2004 for use with 5-fluorouracil–based chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer. Subsequent clinical studies in patients with Neurofibromatosis Type 2 showed that VEGF blockade with bevacizumab can slow or shrink vestibular schwannomas and other NF2-related tumors, indicating a reduction in tumor growth rates.

384879.long_answer: Whitening (depigmenting) creams are used after phytophotodermatitis to lessen the post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. They act by inhibiting melanogenesis enzymes such as tyrosinase, thereby lowering the concentration of the pigment melanin in the epidermis.

366445.long_answer:
Hydroquinone is a depigmenting (whitening) agent that inhibits the enzyme tyrosinase, thereby reducing melanin synthesis. Dermatologists commonly prescribe 2–4 % hydroquinone creams to fade post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, including the brown macules that follow phytophotodermatitis.

Because prolonged or inappropriate use can cause adverse effects such as irritant dermatitis, exogenous ochronosis and potential carcinogenicity, the European Union has banned hydroquinone from over-the-counter cosmetic products (Directive 76/768/EEC and subsequent amendments). Medical-prescription preparations are still allowed, but it can no longer be included in ordinary cosmetic skin-lightening products sold in Europe. Thus, hydroquinone is the whitening agent referred to in the question.

659460.long_answer: Myhre syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SMAD4 gene. The canonical human SMAD4 protein that this gene encodes is composed of 552 amino acids, as documented in reference protein databases (e.g., UniProt entry Q13485). Therefore, the gene product contains 552 amino acids.

533595.long_answer: For women with prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas who become pregnant, bromocriptine is the preferred dopamine agonist. It has been used in thousands of pregnancies with no increase in congenital malformations or adverse maternal outcomes, giving it the largest and most reassuring safety database among prolactin-lowering drugs, whereas data for cabergoline or quinagolide are far more limited.

129442.long_answer: Follicular lymphoma (FL) occasionally undergoes ‘histologic transformation’ to an aggressive form of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Molecular studies and pathologic series have shown that the acquisition of latent infection by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is a recognized driver of this transformation. The virus’s latent proteins (e.g., LMP1, EBNA2) activate NF-κB and other growth-promoting pathways, fostering the aggressive phenotype characteristic of DLBCL. Hence, EBV is the viral agent implicated in the progression of follicular lymphoma to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

170150.long_answer: Autosomal‐recessive primary microcephaly is most frequently caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ASPM gene (abnormal spindle-like, microcephaly-associated). ASPM is located on chromosome 1q31, and defective alleles lead to markedly reduced brain size and the characteristic congenital microcephaly phenotype.

749466.long_answer: Balderdash syndrome is an early colloquial name for the psychiatric condition now called Ganser syndrome, characterized by the giving of approximate or nonsensical answers. The disorder was first described in 1898 by the German psychiatrist Sigbert Josef Maria Ganser (1853–1931) while he was working with prisoners in a Hamburg jail. Because of his seminal description, the condition bears his surname, and he is the physician remembered for this eponymous, or “balderdash,” syndrome.

221309.long_answer: The provided information contains no evidence that phenytoin is used to manage symptoms arising from vascular malformations in the brain. Because no supporting data or consensus is supplied in the context, the claim cannot be validated and is therefore deemed incorrect according to the instructions.

908283.long_answer: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease (pseudogout) can be managed with colchicine. Colchicine is a recognized substrate for both the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter and the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme. Drugs that inhibit either P-gp or CYP3A4 (e.g., clarithromycin, ketoconazole, verapamil) can markedly raise systemic colchicine concentrations, leading to serious toxicity. Because of these well-established interactions, dosing adjustments or alternative therapies are required when colchicine is combined with strong P-gp or CYP3A4 inhibitors.

954297.long_answer: Varicella-zoster virus can infect and inflame cerebral arteries (VZV vasculopathy), precipitating an ischemic stroke. This complication typically presents with focal neurologic deficits such as dizziness and dysarthria (brainstem–cerebellar involvement) together with hemiparesis and paresthesia (unilateral motor and sensory impairment), making stroke the hallmark severe complication described.

141316.long_answer: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the agent of chickenpox and shingles, can infect and inflame cerebral arteries (VZV vasculopathy). This arterial inflammation compromises blood flow and can precipitate ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, which was the world’s third leading cause of death in 2021.

408733.long_answer: In the evaluation of loin pain hematuria syndrome, one of the conditions that must be excluded is lupus nephritis secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  The classical complement component-1q (C1q) genes—C1QA, C1QB and C1QC—are clustered on chromosome 1 at cytoband 1p36.12.  Deficiency or polymorphic variation in these genes is a well-established genetic association with the development of SLE.  Thus, systemic lupus erythematosus is both part of the differential diagnosis for loin pain hematuria syndrome and is genetically linked to the cytoband 1p36.12.

170431.long_answer: In the WHO clinical staging system for HIV/AIDS, Kaposi sarcoma is listed as a Stage IV condition. The cutaneous or visceral tumors produced by Kaposi sarcoma must be distinguished from several other entities—common differentials cited in clinical manuals include dermatofibrous histiocytoma, pneumocystis-related pulmonary or cutaneous lesions, vascular tumors such as angiomas, and pigmented malignancies like melanoma. Because this differential diagnosis specifically matches the options given, Kaposi sarcoma is the severe symptom referred to in the question.

913338.long_answer: The cornea’s sensory nerves travel in the long ciliary nerves, branches of the nasociliary nerve, which itself arises from the ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. Loss of this ophthalmic (V1) sensory input abolishes trophic neuro-peptide release and blink reflexes, predisposing the ocular surface to breakdown and causing neurotrophic keratitis.

287953.long_answer: The rare autosomal-dominant skin disorder caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene is Darier disease (Darier–White disease). Standard management is primarily medical (topical or systemic retinoids, keratolytics, etc.), but for localized, thick, or refractory papules and plaques, destructive surgical modalities are accepted adjuncts. Dermatology texts and treatment guidelines list electrosurgical techniques—electrodesiccation/electrocoagulation performed with high-frequency, alternating-polarity radio-frequency current—as an option to ablate hypertrophic lesions and achieve hemostasis. Although not curative and reserved for selected areas, this procedure is indeed a recognized treatment approach within the therapeutic armamentarium for Darier disease.

593091.long_answer: Among the heterogeneous features of osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis are congenital cardiac anomalies – for example atrial or ventricular septal defects and pulmonary valve stenosis. Congenital heart disease is likewise a classic finding in Holt–Oram syndrome, Noonan syndrome and Alagille syndrome. Therefore, the symptom common to osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis and all three of these other syndromes is the presence of a congenital heart defect.

921794.long_answer: The condition is precocious puberty. In 1852, Dr. Robert King Stone—who later became President Abraham Lincoln’s personal physician—published the first detailed medical report of a boy with markedly premature sexual development, introducing the entity now termed precocious puberty. The disorder is defined by the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics and other pubertal changes well before the normal age threshold (before 9 years in boys), and it remains the classic medical condition associated with abnormally early-onset puberty in young males.

485815.long_answer: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is routinely given to patients withdrawing from alcohol because chronic alcohol use impairs thiamine absorption and storage, placing them at high risk for thiamine deficiency. Adequate thiamine levels are essential for cerebral glucose metabolism; deficiency leads to the classic neurologic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion). Prophylactic parenteral thiamine administration therefore prevents the development of Wernicke encephalopathy during alcohol withdrawal.

707707.long_answer: The disease is pulmonary siderosis, a form of pneumoconiosis that develops after chronic inhalation of fine iron or iron-oxide (rust) dust. These particles are deposited in the lung’s alveoli—the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs—leading to characteristic patchy accumulations of iron visible histologically and radiographically. Although often asymptomatic, this occupational lung disease illustrates the effect of repeated iron dust exposure on pulmonary tissue.

449820.long_answer: There is no established biomedical consensus that the gene responsible for Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome encodes a 400-amino-acid protein whose NH₂-terminus contains a T-domain extended by more than 20 additional amino acids relative to other known T-domains. Published data on the molecular basis of Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome do not support this specific description; in fact, the causative gene has not been definitively shown to produce such a uniquely long T-domain protein. Therefore, the statement is not aligned with current scientific knowledge.

582369.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the BCOR (BCL6 corepressor) gene are known to cause the X-linked form of syndromic microphthalmia that OMIM designates as Microphthalmia, Syndromic 2 (MCOPS2), also called oculofaciocardiodental/Lenz microphthalmia syndrome.

809641.long_answer: Infantile malignant (autosomal-recessive) osteopetrosis can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TNFRSF11A gene, which encodes the RANK receptor required for osteoclast differentiation. TNFRSF11A is mapped to the cytogenetic band 18q22.1 on human chromosome 18, matching the chromosomal location specified in the question.

155398.long_answer: In children, the condition most frequently linked to Fanconi syndrome is cystinosis. Cystinosis results from loss-of-function mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter cystinosin. Defects in CTNS cause cystine accumulation in lysosomes, leading to the proximal renal tubular dysfunction characteristic of Fanconi syndrome.

759664.long_answer: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation produces DNA damage in keratinocytes, leading to mutations in the TP53 gene. The mutant p53 protein is more stable than the wild-type form, so it accumulates in the cell and is readily detected immunohistochemically. Thus, UV exposure is associated with increased— not reduced— p53 expression in sun-damaged epidermis and in actinic keratosis. The development of actinic keratosis is therefore linked to p53 mutation and overexpression, rather than to a decrease in p53 expression.

149454.long_answer: SIX3 (Sine oculis‐related homeobox 3) is widely described as the “master control” or “master regulator” gene for vertebrate eye development because its activity initiates and coordinates formation of the eye field.  Loss-of-function or other misexpression of SIX3 in humans disrupts early forebrain and midline patterning; such disturbances are a well-established cause of holoprosencephaly (HPE), with clinical presentations that range from very mild to very severe.  Pathogenic SIX3 variants account for a significant proportion of familial and sporadic HPE cases (historically classified as HPE2), demonstrating that improper regulation of this eye-field master gene can lead to the spectrum of holoprosencephaly phenotypes.

646794.long_answer: Microsporidia are obligate intracellular pathogens that are normally controlled by CD4⁺ T-cell–mediated immunity. In HIV infection, progressive loss of CD4⁺ T cells produces a cell-mediated immunodeficiency; this specific defect markedly increases susceptibility to microsporidiosis.

899679.long_answer: Recurrent laryngeal (respiratory) papillomatosis is most aggressive when it is caused by HPV type 11; patients infected with HPV-11 require more frequent surgeries and have a higher risk of airway compromise than those infected with HPV-6. The same HPV-11 virus is a well-established etiologic agent of condyloma acuminata (genital warts), linking it both to aggressive laryngeal papillomatosis and to anogenital lesions.

546137.long_answer: Hydrochlorothiazide is a classic thiazide diuretic that paradoxically reduces polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by inducing mild extracellular-fluid volume contraction, which enhances proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water. Clinical guidelines and pharmacology texts cite it as the first-line pharmacologic therapy for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In addition, hydrochlorothiazide is listed under the ‘Diuretics’ section of the World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines, confirming its global importance and accessibility.

888878.long_answer: Magnetic-resonance imaging studies of patients with X-linked Say–Meyer syndrome consistently describe an abnormally thin corpus callosum—the largest white-matter commissural tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres. This hypoplasia of the corpus callosum is a characteristic neuroanatomical finding associated with the syndrome’s developmental delay and other clinical features.

355170.long_answer: Achard–Thiers syndrome combines diabetes mellitus with excessive androgen production, leading to masculinizing manifestations such as hirsutism, acne, and virilization in affected women. The standard pharmacologic strategy for reducing these androgen-related symptoms is to give drugs that antagonize androgen action. Anti-androgen agents—e.g., spironolactone, cyproterone acetate, flutamide, or other androgen-receptor blockers—diminish peripheral androgen effects and thereby alleviate hirsutism and other virilizing signs. Consequently, anti-androgens are the class of drugs most commonly prescribed for symptomatic control in women with Achard–Thiers syndrome.

771022.long_answer: Vibrio vulnificus is a halophilic, Gram-negative rod that naturally inhabits warm marine and brackish waters found in estuaries, coastal areas, and salt- or brackish ponds. When introduced through breaks in the skin or mucosa, it can produce a fulminant soft-tissue infection with necrotizing fasciitis. Numerous case reports and reviews document V. vulnificus as an established, though uncommon, etiologic agent of Fournier gangrene, the necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genital region. Its association with seawater exposure and the rapid, life-threatening progression of the infection make V. vulnificus the prototypical marine bacterium implicated in Fournier gangrene.

669126.long_answer: Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) is characterized by progressive deposition of glycosaminoglycans in multiple tissues, including the meninges and arachnoid villi. This can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and lead to communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus in affected children. When clinically significant hydrocephalus develops, the standard management is neurosurgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid—most commonly placement of a ventriculoperitoneal or ventriculoatrial shunt. Therefore, it is accurate to state that children with Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome may develop hydrocephalus and that the condition is typically treated with surgery.
