348471.long_answer: Neutral lipid storage myopathy (NLSD) is pathologically defined by the excessive accumulation of neutral lipids (primarily triacylglycerol) in skeletal-muscle fibers. Muscle-biopsy specimens show numerous cytoplasmic fat droplets that are readily demonstrable with lipid-specific stains (e.g., Oil Red O) and on ultrastructural examination. For electron microscopy, proper fixation with osmium tetroxide preserves the hydrophobic lipid content, allowing the discrete round lipid droplets to be visualized clearly within the myofiber cytoplasm. Consequently, the presence of intramyocellular neutral-lipid droplets and their detection by electron microscopy after osmium tetroxide treatment are well-established diagnostic features of NLSD. Therefore, the statement accurately reflects current biomedical understanding.

982027.long_answer: Thalidomide exposure during early pregnancy is indeed a well-established and historically prominent cause of phocomelia. However, management of phocomelia focuses on the malformed or absent limbs (e.g., limb-lengthening procedures, orthopedic surgery, prosthetics, physical and occupational therapy). Surgical intervention on the facial bones is not a recognized or standard treatment for this limb malformation. Therefore, while the causal link to thalidomide is correct, the stated treatment is not; taken together, the overall statement is inaccurate.

525642.long_answer: Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (the phenotype seen in pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a) is classically associated with sensorineural deafness, mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, and characteristic skeletal abnormalities such as short 4th/5th metacarpals and metatarsals, brachydactyly, and other malformations of the bones of the fingers and toes.

483615.long_answer: Blue-cone monochromacy involves the two highly homologous X-linked cone-opsin genes, OPN1LW (long-wave/red) and OPN1MW (medium-wave/green).  Across their coding regions these genes are almost identical, but they differ in a set of fixed, gene-specific nucleotide positions—commonly termed dimorphic (or “dismorphic”) sites.  Comparative sequencing has shown that there are 15 such dimorphic sites, which account for all of the consistent amino-acid differences between the L- and M-cone pigments.  Hence, the two homologous genes differ at 15 dimorphic sites.

682791.long_answer: Paul Tessier, a pioneering French cranio-facial surgeon, introduced the first corrective operations for orbital hypertelorism in the 1960s and later devised the widely adopted Tessier craniofacial cleft classification, which includes the spectrum of congenital bifid-nose malformations.

665260.long_answer: The chromosomal disorder Down syndrome (trisomy 21), first described by the physician John Langdon Down, markedly increases the likelihood of developing acute myeloid leukemia—especially the megakaryoblastic (AML-M7) subtype. Children with Down syndrome have a several-hundred–fold higher incidence of AML compared with the general population, making this congenital condition a well-recognized risk factor for the disease.

414459.long_answer: Gliosarcoma is a rare malignant brain tumor that the 2007 World Health Organization (WHO) classification lists as a histologic subtype (variant) of glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumor. Epidemiologic data compiled by the U.S. National Cancer Institute’s SEER program show that patients with gliosarcoma have an exceptionally poor prognosis, with a reported five-year relative survival rate of about 5.6 %. These features—rarity, classification under glioblastoma in the 2007 WHO system, and the specific 5.6 % five-year survival figure—identify gliosarcoma as the tumor described in the question.

356129.long_answer: The folate-antagonist antimetabolite methotrexate, first synthesized in 1947 by Subbarao and colleagues, is widely accepted as the first-line agent for primary intraocular (vitreoretinal) lymphoma. High-dose systemic methotrexate or intravitreal methotrexate injections achieve cytotoxic folate depletion in malignant lymphocytes and have become the standard initial therapy recommended in oncology and ophthalmology guidelines for this disease.

227907.long_answer: When ocular inflammation is suspected to be a masquerade syndrome and infectious or autoimmune uveitis has been excluded, molecular analysis of the vitreous humor is performed. Detection of the MYD88 L265P point mutation (a leucine-to-proline substitution at codon 265 of the MYD88 gene) strongly supports the diagnosis of primary vitreoretinal lymphoma, the classic masquerade condition, and guides appropriate oncologic management.

788541.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is marked by a characteristic coarse, thickened facial appearance. The same coarse facial features are a well-recognised hallmark of the Rasopathies—disorders caused by mutations in the Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway such as Costello and cardio-facio-cutaneous syndromes. This shared craniofacial phenotype is the main clinical similarity between Fryns-Aftimos syndrome and conditions stemming from Ras/MAPK signaling defects.

295910.long_answer: The adrenal cortex gives rise to adrenocortical adenomas, which are the most frequent benign tumors found in the adrenal glands. A large proportion of these tumors, especially cortisol-producing adenomas, harbor activating mutations in genes that regulate the cyclic AMP (cAMP)–dependent protein kinase A (PKA) pathway—for example, somatic mutations in PRKACA or inactivating mutations in GNAS or PRKAR1A. These molecular alterations lead to constitutive PKA signaling, driving cell proliferation and hormone excess. Because of both their prevalence and their well-established link to dysregulated cAMP-PKA activity, adrenocortical adenomas represent the prototypic benign adrenal tumor associated with cAMP-dependent protein kinase A signaling.

731031.long_answer: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that shuttles electrons between complexes I/II and III in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. Humans synthesize CoQ10 endogenously, and additional amounts are obtained from dietary sources such as oily fish, meat, and nuts. Supplemental CoQ10 has been shown in controlled clinical studies to improve myocardial energy production, reduce oxidative stress, and enhance ejection fraction in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, thereby helping to treat the resultant heart failure.

660741.long_answer: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a mitochondrial co-factor sold as a dietary supplement rather than an FDA-approved drug. Small clinical studies in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and other forms of congestive heart failure have shown that supplemental CoQ10 can improve myocardial energy production, ejection fraction, and functional status. Because of these observed benefits, clinicians sometimes recommend CoQ10 to individuals with dilated cardiomyopathy who are experiencing heart failure, even though the supplement has not yet received FDA approval for this indication.

683309.long_answer: In angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), the reactive B-cell population is very often infected by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). The prototypical and most common disease caused by EBV is infectious mononucleosis (“mono,” glandular fever). Thus, the virus present in the B-cells of AITL is the same agent that commonly produces infectious mononucleosis.

725163.long_answer: The described condition is adermatoglyphia, sometimes nick-named the “immigration delay disease.” It is an extremely rare autosomal-dominant disorder reported in only about ten families worldwide. Affected individuals are born without epidermal ridges (fingerprints) and often develop transient neonatal blisters and facial milia. Genetic studies have shown that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations affecting an alternative, skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene on chromosome 4 are responsible for the phenotype.

857333.long_answer: Jens Christian Skou first described the sodium-potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) in 1957. This membrane transporter hydrolyses ATP to exchange intracellular Na⁺ for extracellular K⁺ and therefore depends critically on an adequate ATP supply. In Hashimoto’s encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis), autoantibodies directed against α-enolase interfere with glycolysis, reducing cellular ATP production. With diminished ATP, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is one of the first ion transporters to fail, leading to neuronal ionic imbalance and contributing to the encephalopathic manifestations of the disorder.

207452.long_answer: L-carnitine serves two clinically useful functions in certain inborn errors of metabolism such as propionic acidemia or related organic acidemias. 1) It facilitates mitochondrial β-oxidation by shuttling long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane, thereby supporting cellular energy production. 2) More importantly for propionic acidemia, L-carnitine conjugates with accumulated toxic acyl-CoA intermediates (e.g., propionyl-CoA) to form acyl-carnitines that are water-soluble and can be excreted in the urine. This lowers intracellular propionic acid and related metabolite levels, regenerates free CoA, and helps prevent secondary mitochondrial dysfunction. Consequently, L-carnitine supplementation is a standard adjunctive therapy in managing metabolic crises and chronic treatment of propionic acidemia and similar disorders, confirming that it enhances energy metabolism while mitigating toxic metabolite buildup.

421078.long_answer: L-carnitine is routinely supplemented in propionic acidemia because it shuttles long-chain fatty acyl groups across the mitochondrial inner membrane via the carnitine shuttle, allowing β-oxidation and ATP generation while also forming propionyl-carnitine that can be excreted, thereby lowering toxic propionyl-CoA levels.

153240.long_answer: In the 2016 study that examined the prenatal‐ultrasound characteristics of Limb Body Wall Complex, the investigators documented that the malformation could already be recognised during the first-trimester scan; the earliest case in their series was identified at 11 weeks of gestation. Thus, the study concluded that Limb Body Wall Complex can first be detected at 11 weeks.

831634.long_answer:
The aortopulmonary space (often referred to as the aortopulmonary window) contains lymph nodes and loose connective tissue situated between the aortic arch and the main pulmonary artery. Any pathological process that produces lymph-node enlargement or soft-tissue masses in the mediastinum can therefore manifest in this space.  
• Infections (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infections, bacterial lymphadenitis) can cause reactive or suppurative enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes, including those in the aortopulmonary window.  
• Autoimmune or granulomatous disorders such as sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or rheumatoid nodules can similarly lead to nodal or soft-tissue involvement in this region.  
• Malignancies—whether primary mediastinal tumors (lymphoma) or metastatic disease (e.g., lung, breast, melanoma)—commonly produce aortopulmonary window lymphadenopathy or mass lesions.  
Therefore, infectious, autoimmune, and neoplastic conditions are all well-recognized causes of abnormal findings in the aortopulmonary space.

925519.long_answer: The congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD) deficiency blocks conversion of 17α-hydroxypregnenolone to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, leading to markedly elevated 17α-hydroxypregnenolone levels. Because both androgen and glucocorticoid synthesis are impaired, XY fetuses are undervirilized and XX fetuses may be virilized by accumulated Δ5 steroids, producing ambiguous genitalia in both genetic sexes.

728614.long_answer: Bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II (BMPR2) is the principal gene in which pathogenic variants cause heritable/primary pulmonary (arterial) hypertension.  Separate families carrying heterozygous BMPR2 mutations have also been reported with the skeletal malformation brachydactyly type A2, characterised by shortening of the middle phalanges of the index (and often little) fingers.  Thus, BMPR2 is the gene that is etiologically linked to both primary pulmonary hypertension and type A2 brachydactyly.

879885.long_answer: Equinophobia is classified as a specific phobia.  The first-line, evidence-based ‘talk therapy’ for specific phobias is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).  In CBT, a therapist helps the person identify and challenge distorted thoughts about horses and gradually confront the feared stimulus through controlled exposure, relaxation training and cognitive restructuring.  Numerous clinical guidelines (e.g., American Psychiatric Association, NICE) recommend CBT as the most effective psychotherapy for treating specific phobias such as equinophobia.

695539.long_answer: Oxymetholone is an anabolic androgenic steroid that stimulates proliferation and differentiation of hematopoietic progenitor cells, thereby enhancing the growth and maturation of red cells, neutrophils and platelets. Because these effects can partially counter the pancytopenia characteristic of Fanconi anemia, oxymetholone is routinely employed as a supportive (non-curative) pharmacologic therapy for patients with this disorder.

106578.long_answer: Fanconi anemia–associated bone-marrow failure can be managed temporarily with pharmacologic agents. Androgens (e.g., oxymetholone) are often combined with hematopoietic growth factors that are naturally occurring glycoproteins capable of stimulating the proliferation, differentiation, and maturation of blood-cell precursors. This class of glycoproteins is collectively termed colony-stimulating factors (CSFs), which include agents such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Administering CSFs alongside androgens can transiently improve cytopenias until definitive therapy (e.g., hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation) is undertaken.

593161.long_answer: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—the first-line pharmacologic treatment for active axial spondyloarthritis—work by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and thereby reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Renal prostaglandins normally help maintain adequate renal blood flow, especially under conditions of decreased effective circulating volume. By lowering prostaglandin levels, NSAIDs can constrict the afferent arteriole and diminish renal perfusion, increasing the risk of acute kidney injury or worsening chronic kidney disease. This renal safety concern is well documented for commonly used agents such as naproxen, ibuprofen, indomethacin, diclofenac and celecoxib, all of which are considered first-line options in axial spondyloarthritis management.

139280.long_answer: Ackerman syndrome has occasionally been reported in association with juvenile open-angle glaucoma. This form of glaucoma is rare, arises between childhood and early adulthood, and is classically inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern, matching the description in the question.

716881.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (also known as acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by craniosynostosis, polysyndactyly, brachydactyly, soft-tissue syndactyly, obesity, and other malformations. Pathogenic biallelic mutations in the small GTP-binding protein gene RAB23 (located on chromosome 6p12) have been identified as a major molecular cause of this syndrome. Thus, Carpenter syndrome is the RAB23-related condition classically associated with brachydactyly.

782966.long_answer: The definitive, disease-modifying therapy frequently employed for life-threatening bone-marrow disorders such as acute leukemia, lymphoma, myelodysplastic syndromes, and certain solid-tumor malignancies is hematopoietic stem-cell (bone marrow) transplantation. In this procedure a patient’s diseased or dysfunctional marrow is ablated with high-dose chemotherapy and/or total-body irradiation, then replaced by infusion of healthy hematopoietic stem cells obtained from a compatible donor (allogeneic) or from the patient previously collected (autologous). The new stem cells migrate to the marrow cavities and re-establish normal blood-cell production. Although usually reserved for malignant or otherwise fatal marrow failure states, the same transplant technique is also considered for selected patients with severe, transfusion-dependent sideroblastic anemia when conventional medical therapy is ineffective or complications such as iron overload threaten survival, because successful engraftment can permanently correct the underlying erythroid defect.

910648.long_answer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles that house hydrolytic enzymes responsible for degrading glycosaminoglycans, sphingolipids, and other macromolecules. Beyond their classic catabolic role, lysosomes participate in regulated secretion, plasma-membrane repair, apoptosis, nutrient and energy sensing, and multiple cell-signaling pathways. When specific lysosomal enzymes that break down glycosaminoglycans are genetically deficient, undegraded ‘mucopolysaccharides’ accumulate inside lysosomes, producing the group of lysosomal storage disorders collectively known as the mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler, Hunter, Sanfilippo syndromes). Thus, malfunction of lysosomes underlies the pathogenesis of mucopolysaccharidoses.

558304.long_answer: MPI-CDG (Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation type Ib) is caused by pathogenic variants in the MPI gene, which encodes the human phosphomannose isomerase enzyme. The canonical human phosphomannose isomerase protein (UniProt accession P34949) is composed of 406 amino acid residues. Therefore, the enzyme whose mutations lead to MPI-CDG contains 406 amino acid residues.

656674.long_answer: In Joubert syndrome the eyelid drooping (ptosis) is attributed to weakness or dysfunction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, the striated muscle that normally lifts the upper eyelid. Impairment of this muscle prevents adequate eyelid elevation, producing the characteristic ptosis seen in affected patients.

151378.long_answer: The cerebral cortex is the expansive outer layer of the cerebrum and constitutes the largest site of neural integration in the central nervous system, processing and integrating sensory, motor, and associative information. Epileptic seizures arise when cortical neurons exhibit synchronous, excessive, and abnormal electrical discharges; thus, the cerebral cortex is the primary brain region implicated in the generation of epileptic activity.

838174.long_answer: Seizures that can accompany encephalitis are commonly managed with anticonvulsant (antiepileptic) drugs. This heterogeneous class of agents—including medications such as phenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate and others—acts by stabilizing neuronal membranes and inhibiting the excessive, rapid firing of neurons that underlies seizure activity. Their shared ability to dampen aberrant neuronal excitability makes anticonvulsants the standard pharmacological approach for seizure control in encephalitis patients.

514385.long_answer: L-glyceric acidemia (also called L-glyceric aciduria or primary hyperoxaluria type II) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GRHPR gene, which encodes glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase. Defective GRHPR impairs the conversion of hydroxypyruvate to D-glycerate and glyoxylate to glycolate, leading to accumulation and systemic elevation of L-glycerate. This condition is distinct from D-glyceric acidemia, which involves a different enzymatic defect (glycerate kinase/GLYCTK).

430378.long_answer: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—agents such as ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin, and other COX inhibitors—are widely used for analgesia and to control inflammation. By inhibiting renal prostaglandin synthesis, they reduce renin release and aldosterone secretion, impair renal potassium excretion, and can precipitate hyperkalemia, especially in patients with renal impairment or those taking other potassium-raising drugs.

643490.long_answer: In the autosomal-recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophies caused by loss of any sarcoglycan (α, β, γ or δ)—classified as LGMD 2C, 2D, 2E and 2F—absence of the sarcoglycan subunit destabilises the entire dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. This secondary destabilisation can lead to a reduced or patchy dystrophin signal on immunohistochemistry even though the dystrophin gene itself is intact. Therefore, the sarcoglycan-deficient limb-girdle muscular dystrophies are the forms that may show decreased dystrophin staining without dystrophin mutations.

796776.long_answer: A retrovirus that targets and weakens the immune system—such as Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)—reduces host immunologic defenses in the oral cavity. Immunosuppression impairs the ability to control bacterial and fungal biofilms that normally coexist in the gingival sulcus. Clinical and epidemiologic studies show that people with HIV have higher prevalence and severity of periodontal conditions (e.g., linear gingival erythema, necrotizing gingivitis/periodontitis, rapid attachment loss) compared with immunocompetent individuals. Therefore, by compromising immune surveillance and inflammatory regulation, an immune-attacking retrovirus can indeed increase the risk of periodontal disease.

490774.long_answer: The human F2 gene encodes coagulation factor II, commonly known as prothrombin. Prothrombin is the zymogen precursor that is proteolytically cleaved to generate the active serine protease thrombin, a central enzyme in the coagulation cascade responsible for converting fibrinogen to fibrin and activating several other clotting factors. Extensive genetic, biochemical and clinical studies have firmly established that mutations in the F2 gene alter prothrombin levels or function, leading to bleeding disorders or thrombophilia, confirming that F2 specifically encodes prothrombin (coagulation factor II).

100860.long_answer: The confirmation of complete mirror-image reversal of the heart and visceral organs in situs inversus totalis is typically obtained with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI produces detailed cross-sectional images without using ionizing radiation and has even been applied to the study of ancient mummies, making it a suitable non-ionizing modality for both archaeological imaging and modern clinical assessment of organ position.

883181.long_answer: Habermann’s disease (pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, or PLEVA) presents with crops of vesicular, crusted or necrotic papules that closely resemble the lesions of chicken-pox, the highly contagious infection produced by the varicella-zoster virus. Because chicken-pox is far more common and often the first condition physicians think of when they see scattered vesicles and crusts, PLEVA is frequently misidentified as varicella, at least initially, until biopsy or the clinical course clarifies the diagnosis. Thus, in routine clinical practice, Habermann’s disease is indeed often (i.e., commonly) misdiagnosed as chicken-pox, the contagious disease caused by the varicella virus.

457983.long_answer: Vitamin A is essential for normal differentiation of epithelial tissues. When the body lacks vitamin A, epithelial cells lose their ability to mature properly and instead become hyper-keratinized, a change clinically referred to as hyperkeratosis or follicular keratosis. This process involves excessive synthesis and deposition of keratin—a scleroprotein—within the affected epithelial layers. The resulting overproduction and accumulation of keratin is a well-documented hallmark of vitamin A deficiency, manifesting in dry, rough skin, keratinised conjunctival plaques (Bitot spots), and other keratinisation disorders. Therefore, the statement that keratin can be overproduced in cases of vitamin A deficiency is consistent with established biomedical knowledge.

253003.long_answer: Deferiprone is an orally active iron-chelating agent (marketed as Ferriprox) that received its first marketing authorisation in the European Union in August 1999 for the treatment of transfusional iron overload in patients with thalassaemia major. Because it can be taken by mouth and effectively lowers body iron stores, deferiprone is also employed in patients with hereditary haemochromatosis who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to regular phlebotomy, providing an alternative means of reducing excess iron.

722273.long_answer: Color vision depends on cone photoreceptors whose visual pigments contain 11-cis-retinal, a metabolite of vitamin A. When dietary vitamin A is insufficient, the supply of retinal to both rod and cone cells falls, disrupting regeneration of cone opsins and impairing their ability to differentiate wavelengths. Clinically, marked vitamin A deficiency can therefore produce an acquired color vision defect in addition to its better-known night blindness.

803647.long_answer: Alzheimer’s disease accounts for roughly 60–70 % of dementia cases worldwide. Recent research has detected the oral pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis—bacteria commonly implicated in gingivitis and periodontitis—and its neurotoxic gingipain enzymes in the brains and cerebrospinal fluid of Alzheimer’s patients, linking this bacterium to the neurodegenerative process characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease.

147361.long_answer: Lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 gene. The definitive way to establish whether an individual carries one of these variants is to sequence the coding region of FOXC2. The sequencing method first described in 1977 by Frederick Sanger and colleagues—the dideoxy chain-termination or Sanger sequencing test—directly reads the nucleotide sequence of DNA and therefore can reveal the presence or absence of FOXC2 mutations, confirming or excluding the diagnosis of lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome.

151952.long_answer: Infliximab is a chimeric (mouse-human) IgG1 monoclonal antibody that specifically binds to tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and neutralizes its biological activity. Although primarily approved for Crohn’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory disorders, infliximab has been used off-label to treat refractory cases of collagenous colitis, taking advantage of its TNF-α–blocking action to reduce mucosal inflammation.

814637.long_answer: The GLB1 gene encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-galactosidase. Pathogenic variants in GLB1 cause GM1 gangliosidosis (infantile, juvenile and adult forms) and Morquio-B disease. The other major category, GM2 gangliosidosis (which includes Tay-Sachs disease, Sandhoff disease and GM2 activator deficiency), is produced by defects in different genes—HEXA, HEXB and GM2A, respectively. Thus, GLB1 is responsible for GM1 gangliosidosis only, not for both GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses.

504058.long_answer: The protein is GAIP-interacting protein, C-terminus 1 (GIPC1, also called synectin). Human GIPC1 is composed of 333 amino acids, has an apparent molecular mass of ~36 kDa, and contains a single centrally positioned PDZ domain (residues ≈101-185). Biochemical studies demonstrated that GIPC1 binds to the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif of the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR), making it the scaffold protein that satisfies all features described in the question.

571688.long_answer: The stethoscope is the acoustic medical device physicians place on the chest or other body surfaces to perform auscultation—listening to internal sounds from the heart, lungs, intestines, and blood flowing through arteries and veins. In 1887, French physicians M. Cuffer and M. Barbillon used a stethoscope during auscultation to describe the characteristic mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that occurs in patients with mitral valve prolapse. This landmark observation established the stethoscope as an essential tool for diagnosing valvular heart disorders as well as a broad range of cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal conditions.

902852.long_answer: The nuclear gene SDHA encodes the 664-amino-acid flavoprotein subunit of mitochondrial complex II. Pathogenic variants in SDHA produce isolated or combined mitochondrial complex II deficiency. SDHA is mapped to chromosome 5 (region 5p15), so the causative gene for CII deficiency resides on chromosome 5.

244933.long_answer: The TP53 gene (commonly referred to as p53) is a classic tumor-suppressor gene situated at chromosome 17p13.1—the short (p) arm of chromosome 17. Its genomic locus spans roughly 20 kilobases. Loss-of-function mutations or deletions of TP53 are frequently documented in malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs), contributing to defective cell-cycle control and genomic instability characteristic of these aggressive sarcomas.

559411.long_answer: The condition is Early Myoclonic Encephalopathy (EME), an epileptic encephalopathy that begins in the neonatal period or within the first three months of life. It is distinguished by fragmentary, erratic myoclonic jerks and violent myoclonic spasms, leading to frequent, drug-resistant seizures and severe developmental impairment.

986088.long_answer: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the DMD gene located at Xp21 on the X chromosome. Several X-linked forms of hereditary spastic paraplegia (e.g., SPG1 / L1CAM at Xq28 and SPG2 / PLP1 at Xq22) also map to genes on the X chromosome. Therefore, both conditions involve mutations in genes situated on the X chromosome.

960525.long_answer: Petrolatum (commonly called petroleum jelly or white petrolatum) is an occlusive barrier whose melting point generally falls between 40 °C and 70 °C. It is widely recommended in dermatology for managing xeroderma because it forms an impermeable film that reduces transepidermal water loss. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration lists petrolatum as an approved over-the-counter skin protectant active ingredient, confirming its recognized safety and effectiveness for this purpose.

229400.long_answer: Hypergammaglobulinemic purpura (also called Waldenström’s purpura) is an uncommon form of recurrent purpura characterized by elevated serum immunoglobulins. Epidemiologic studies show a marked female predominance—about 85 % of reported cases occur in women—making it both rare and distinctly more frequent in the female population.

686876.long_answer: A 2016 global nutrition review by UNICEF, WHO and the World Bank estimated that about 52.9 million children under five years of age were affected by wasting—acute malnutrition manifested by low weight-for-height and loss of muscle and fat tissue.  Wasting is recognised as being associated with a variety of disorders that impair energy storage or utilisation, including glycogen-storage disease type VI (Hers’ disease), in which impaired hepatic glycogen breakdown can lead to poor growth and loss of body mass.  Thus, the condition linked to Hers’ disease and reported to affect roughly 52.9 million young children worldwide in 2016 is wasting (acute malnutrition).

571170.long_answer: The AI variant that shows characteristically enlarged (taurodont) pulp chambers and an apically displaced furcation is the hypomaturation–hypoplastic type associated with taurodontism, traditionally classified as Type IV amelogenesis imperfecta.

920528.long_answer: Van den Ende–Gupta syndrome (VDEGS) is an autosomal-recessive malformation syndrome that was first described in 1992 in two siblings born to consanguineous Arab parents—the only cases known at that time, making it an exceptionally rare genetic disorder.  Core manifestations include characteristic facial features (blepharophimosis, narrow beaked nose, everted lower lip) and multiple skeletal anomalies such as radial-head dislocation, camptodactyly, slender ribs, hypoplastic scapulae and, very commonly, congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).  Subsequent reports have confirmed the strong association of VDEGS with clubfoot, and mutations in the SCARF2 gene have been identified as its molecular cause.

353993.long_answer: Species that have produced hallucinatory intoxication in people on Réunion Island—such as spinefoots (Siganus spp.) and sea chubs (Kyphosus spp.)—are primarily shallow-reef herbivores. They are most commonly encountered on coral or rocky substrates in the first few metres below the surface, generally between about 1 m and 30 m, only occasionally extending to roughly 40–60 m. They are not characteristically or predominately distributed at depths of 50–100 m. Therefore the depth range given in the question does not reflect their typical habitat.

651642.long_answer: Arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene (or the related VIPAS39). VPS33B encodes a member of the Sec1/Munc18 family that forms part of the class C Vps tethering complex. This protein regulates the docking and fusion of intracellular transport vesicles with their target membranes, thereby ensuring correct trafficking of proteins to apical, endosomal and lysosomal compartments. In other words, the gene mediates vesicle-mediated protein sorting within the cell.

706424.long_answer: Werner syndrome accelerates age-related changes, including early loss of bone mineral density. This premature bone demineralization leads to osteoporosis, a disorder in which bones become porous and fragile, markedly increasing the risk of fractures. Osteoporosis is likewise the leading cause of fragility fractures in the general elderly population, making it the common complication that links Werner syndrome to the high incidence of broken bones in older adults.

776758.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I, also called sialidosis, is caused by an inherited deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase. Because its primary defect involves a lysosomal hydrolase and leads to intralysosomal accumulation of undegraded substrates, it is classified within the broader group of inherited metabolic conditions known as lysosomal storage disorders.

971405.long_answer: The RELN gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein reelin, is located on chromosome 7q22.1. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in RELN disturb the reelin signaling pathway that guides neuronal migration and cortical layering. Such mutations are a well-documented cause of autosomal-recessive lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia and have also been reported in patients whose brains are markedly smaller (microlissencephaly), demonstrating that defective RELN can underlie both conditions.

619326.long_answer: In the single infant described with Cortés-Lacassie syndrome, progressive renal failure developed secondary to the metabolic defect. The authors of the case report noted that early liver transplantation (to correct the underlying enzymatic defect) or, alternatively, dialysis to remove the accumulating metabolites could potentially have halted or delayed the advance of this renal failure.

793771.long_answer: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of the Hepatitis B virus was awarded to Dr. Baruch S. Blumberg in 1976. Blumberg completed his medical training at Columbia University’s College of Physicians and Surgeons, receiving his M.D. in 1951. Thus, the university where he earned his medical degree is Columbia University.

687426.long_answer: Michels syndrome is a craniosynostosis-containing malformation syndrome in which the premature fusion occurs at the coronal sutures—the paired fibrous joints that run transversely between the frontal and parietal bones of the skull. Early closure of these sutures produces the brachycephalic skull shape and associated mid-face and orbital findings characteristic of the disorder.

627609.long_answer: Two parts of the statement are incorrect. (1) Yellow fever is not “one of only two” viral-hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) with a vaccine. In addition to yellow fever, licensed or routinely used human vaccines now exist for several other VHFs—e.g., Ebola virus disease (Ervebo, 2019), dengue (Dengvaxia, 2015), Argentine hemorrhagic fever (Candid #1, used since the 1990s in Argentina), and Kyasanur Forest disease in India. Thus yellow fever is not uniquely one of just two VHFs with an available vaccine. (2) While the World Health Organization states that a single dose of the 17D yellow-fever vaccine provides lifelong protection for immunocompetent persons, this does NOT apply to symptomatic HIV-positive individuals. Because the vaccine is live-attenuated, it is contraindicated in patients with advanced or symptomatic HIV infection or severe immunosuppression (typically CD4 < 200 cells/µL); those who are eligible but immunocompromised may mount a weaker response and may require re-vaccination or repeated serologic testing. Therefore the claim that one dose confers lifelong immunity “even in symptomatic HIV-positive individuals” is not supported by current medical consensus.

238212.long_answer: The provided context contains no information indicating that the early symptoms of psittacosis resemble those of an infection with Salmonella enterica Typhi. Without evidence in the context to support such a similarity, the statement cannot be considered factually correct based solely on the given information.

421218.long_answer: Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in the LYST (LYSosomal Trafficking regulator) gene. The defect disrupts normal formation, trafficking, and release of lysosome-related organelles, including melanosomes in melanocytes. Because the abnormal, oversized melanosomes cannot be properly processed or transferred to keratinocytes, affected individuals show partial oculocutaneous albinism (light skin, silvery hair, and photophobia). This hypopigmentation reflects an intrinsic defect in the handling—and thus the effective production/distribution—of melanin. Therefore, individuals with Chédiak–Higashi syndrome do indeed have a defect that ultimately impairs melanin production/distribution.

453784.long_answer: Reduced resistance of skeletal muscle to passive stretching is the clinical definition of hypotonia. Hypotonia is a well-recognized manifestation of several organic acidemias (e.g., propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric, glutaric acidemia type I), frequently appearing in the neonatal period or during metabolic decompensation. It is attributed to metabolic encephalopathy, hyperammonemia, and other biochemical derangements characteristic of these disorders. Therefore, stating that reduced muscle resistance to stretching is one of the symptoms of organic acidemias is consistent with established medical knowledge; it is not incorrect to argue this.

264282.long_answer: Behçet’s disease shows a strong genetic association with the HLA-B51 allele. HLA-B51 is a class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) surface molecule encoded at the B locus on chromosome 6, and carriers have a markedly increased risk of developing Behçet’s disease compared with non-carriers.

442105.long_answer: Profuse sweating (hyperhidrosis) is one of the cardinal autonomic manifestations of Shapiro syndrome, accompanying its characteristic paroxysmal hypothermia. In contrast, autoimmune encephalopathy (e.g., Hashimoto’s encephalopathy or antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis) is chiefly characterized by subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms—confusion, seizures, cognitive decline, behavioral change—while autonomic features such as sweating are uncommon and not part of the core clinical picture. Therefore, sweating cannot be considered a common symptom shared by both conditions.

361204.long_answer: The Italian scientist Bartolomeo Gosio first isolated mycophenolic acid, from which the modern immunosuppressant agents mycophenolate mofetil / mycophenolate sodium are derived and widely used in solid-organ transplantation. A well-recognized and relatively frequent adverse effect of these mycophenolate preparations is bone-marrow suppression, manifesting clinically as leukopenia (decreased white-blood-cell count); neutropenia and other cytopenias are routinely monitored for in treated transplant patients. Therefore, a decrease in white blood cells is indeed a common adverse reaction to this drug.

132747.long_answer: Leydig cell hypoplasia is caused by inactivating mutations of the luteinizing-hormone/chorionic-gonadotropin (LH/CG) receptor that is expressed almost exclusively on fetal and adult Leydig cells. The primary consequence is underdevelopment of Leydig cells and markedly reduced testosterone production. Sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, which line the seminiferous tubules and provide structural and metabolic support for germ cells, do not express the LH/CG receptor and are not the direct cellular target of the mutation. Although the resultant androgen deficiency can secondarily impair spermatogenesis, the disorder does not directly damage or alter the function of Sertoli cells themselves. Therefore, Leydig cell hypoplasia does not directly affect the sustentacular cells in human testes.

412427.long_answer: In hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, multiple arteriovenous malformations create low-resistance shunts that divert blood away from capillary beds. This reduces effective organ perfusion. To maintain adequate systemic perfusion and blood pressure, the heart compensates by pumping a larger volume of blood per minute—i.e., it increases its cardiac output (via higher heart rate and/or stroke volume). This sustained elevation in cardiac output characterizes the high-output state often seen in patients with extensive AV malformations.

278085.long_answer: Bardet-Biedl syndrome is genetically heterogeneous, with each causative gene defining a numbered subtype of the disorder. Pathogenic variants in the BBS1 gene cause the phenotype classified as Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 1 (BBS1). Hence, mutations in the BBS1 gene are specifically associated with BBS type 1.

131415.long_answer: Petrolatum (petroleum jelly) is widely used as an over-the-counter topical emollient to treat xeroderma (dry skin) because it forms an occlusive barrier that reduces transepidermal water loss. The same substance—listed as white petrolatum or petroleum jelly—is the principal lubricating ingredient in many commercial hairball remedies for domestic cats, where it helps the ingested hair pass through the gastrointestinal tract.

406222.long_answer: Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI) is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC7A7 gene, which encodes the light-chain subunit (y+LAT1) of the heterodimeric cationic-amino-acid transporter system y+L. This transporter functions as an obligate heterodimer composed of the SLC7A7 light chain non-covalently linked to the heavy-chain subunit 4F2hc/CD98, which is encoded by the SLC3A2 gene. The physical association between SLC7A7 and SLC3A2 is required for correct trafficking to the plasma membrane and for transporter activity. Therefore, the gene responsible for LPI (SLC7A7) directly interacts with the SLC3A2 gene product, making the statement correct.

709773.long_answer: The epidemic disease that first appeared in November 2002 was Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). The initial cluster was reported in Guangdong Province, China, and the illness rapidly spread internationally during 2002-2003. Clinically, SARS is caused by the SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and is marked by high fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and laboratory findings that commonly include leukopenia with pronounced lymphocytopenia. These hematologic abnormalities, together with its sudden emergence and global transmission, define the SARS epidemic that began in November 2002.

859993.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an iminostilbene anticonvulsant that acts primarily by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. It was first synthesized and characterized in Basel, Switzerland, by the company J. R. Geigy in the 1950s, and has since become a widely used medication for epilepsy, trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder. Among its rare but serious adverse effects is the development of severe cutaneous reactions, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell’s syndrome). Because of this well-documented association, carbamazepine is the anticonvulsant most commonly linked to Lyell’s syndrome in clinical reports and pharmacovigilance data.

527304.long_answer:
Extensive epidemiologic and experimental evidence shows that exposure to ionizing radiation increases the incidence of several malignancies, including both brain tumors and chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). 

1. Brain cancer: Survivors of therapeutic cranial irradiation for conditions such as tinea capitis or childhood leukemia, as well as atomic-bomb survivors and patients who received high-dose diagnostic/therapeutic radiation to the head, have a clearly elevated risk of primary brain tumours (e.g., gliomas, meningiomas). This association has been consistently reproduced and accepted as causal by authoritative bodies such as the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the U.S. National Academies’ BEIR committees.

2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML): Ionizing radiation is a well-documented leukemogenic agent. Cohorts of atomic-bomb survivors, radiotherapy patients, and occupationally exposed workers show an increased incidence of CML that rises with cumulative radiation dose. CML is one of the classic hematologic malignancies listed among the radiation-induced cancers by the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) and other expert reviews.

Because ionizing radiation is an established, dose-related risk factor for both primary brain cancers and CML, the statement is correct.

284704.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by mutations in the NBN gene, which resides on human chromosome 8. Chromosome 8 in the current human reference genome spans roughly 145 million nucleotide base pairs, so the chromosome containing the causal gene comprises about 145 Mb of DNA.

935298.long_answer: The setting sun sign results from impaired up-gaze caused by pressure on the dorsal midbrain and is classically associated with conditions that raise intracranial pressure—most commonly infantile hydrocephalus or lesions such as tectal tumors. Agenesis of the corpus callosum, by itself, does not produce dorsal midbrain compression or the characteristic oculomotor disturbance needed to create the setting sun phenomenon. Therefore, a patient who has isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum would not be expected to exhibit the setting sun sign unless a separate, pressure-producing pathology (e.g., hydrocephalus) were also present.

614616.long_answer: Hereditary Non-polyposis Colorectal Cancer (now commonly called Lynch syndrome) was first systematically described by Prof. Henry T. Lynch. In 1992 the American Cancer Society honored Prof. Lynch with a major society award (reported in contemporary ACS and medical-society press releases as the American Cancer Society Distinguished Service Award/Medal of Honor). Thus, the professor who originally characterized HNPCC did receive an American Cancer Society award in 1992, confirming the statement as accurate.

182905.long_answer: Type 1 diabetes mellitus arises from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells and, when present prior to conception, exposes the embryo to maternal hyperglycaemia during early organogenesis. This markedly elevates the incidence of major fetal malformations compared with other forms of diabetes or normoglycaemic pregnancies.

602194.long_answer: Ionizing radiation is defined by its ability to carry enough energy to remove (ionize) electrons from atoms and molecules. Sources such as therapeutic X-rays, γ-rays, and radiation from atomic bomb explosions deliver this high-energy radiation. Large epidemiologic studies of survivors of atomic bombings, patients who received cranial radiotherapy, and workers exposed occupationally have consistently shown increased incidences of gliomas, meningiomas, and other central nervous system tumors. Because of this clear dose-related association, ionizing radiation is recognized by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and other health authorities as a proven environmental risk factor for brain cancers.

439326.long_answer: Papillorenal (renal-coloboma) syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in the PAX2 gene. PAX2 is one of the nine human genes that share the conserved paired-box DNA-binding domain, placing it within the Paired box (PAX) transcription factor gene family.

684640.long_answer: The described disorder is Bloom syndrome, an autosomal-recessive condition especially frequent in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. It presents with marked pre- and postnatal growth deficiency (short stature), photosensitive skin changes, genomic instability leading to a greatly elevated risk of a broad spectrum of cancers, and features that can resemble premature aging. Bloom syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the BLM gene on chromosome 15q26.1, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase crucial for DNA repair and genomic stability. Identification of pathogenic variants in BLM confirms the diagnosis.

974208.long_answer: Hodgkin lymphoma makes up roughly 10 % of all lymphoma cases. About 40–50 % of Hodgkin lymphoma tumors contain Epstein-Barr virus genomes, indicating a frequent association with EBV infection.

486804.long_answer: Brachydactyly type A1 (BDA1) is caused by pathogenic variants in the Indian hedgehog gene (IHH). IHH encodes one of the three mammalian Hedgehog ligands and functions at the center of the Hedgehog signaling pathway that regulates chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation during endochondral ossification. Disruption of this pathway through IHH mutations specifically produces the characteristic shortening of the middle phalanges seen in BDA1, making this form of brachydactyly directly linked to Hedgehog signaling.

421230.long_answer: Hemophilia A is a classic X-linked bleeding disorder caused by deficient or defective coagulation factor VIII. Lack of factor VIII impairs the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade, leading to prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and the characteristic bleeding tendency seen in affected individuals.

655589.long_answer: Paragonimiasis is the tissue-fluke infection produced by Paragonimus species (most often Paragonimus westermani). Although the adult worms characteristically lodge in the lungs, aberrant migration occurs in a substantial proportion of patients. Epidemiologic series show that 10 – 24 % of documented Paragonimus infections involve ectopic sites, most commonly the brain or spinal cord, giving rise to cerebral (neurologic) paragonimiasis. When the parasite lodges in the central nervous system it can provoke seizures, focal deficits, intracranial inflammation and, on occasion, thrombotic complications such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – a rare form of stroke produced by clotting of the brain’s dural venous sinuses. Therefore, the parasitic disease whose central-nervous-system involvement is seen in roughly 10–24 % of affected individuals and is linked to CVST is paragonimiasis.

329502.long_answer: The rare genetic disorder linked to an extra copy of DNA on the long (q) arm of chromosome 15 is called Dup15q syndrome, also known as chromosome 15q11-q13 duplication syndrome or isodicentric 15 syndrome. In this condition, individuals carry an additional duplicated segment (either interstitial or as an isodicentric supernumerary chromosome) involving 15q11.2-q13. The dosage increase of genes within this region disrupts neurodevelopment, leading to features such as hypotonia, developmental delay, seizures, autism spectrum behaviors, and varying degrees of intellectual disability. Thus, duplication of 15q material underlies the intellectual impairment characteristic of Dup15q syndrome.

666402.long_answer: Parastremmatic dwarfism is classified among the TRPV4-related skeletal dysplasias.  The cardinal pathological features are profound abnormalities of bone development: marked shortening and bowing of the long bones, platyspondyly, kyphoscoliosis, and characteristic dense, striated metaphyseal bone on radiographs.  Although some individuals may have limited range of motion because of the bony deformities themselves, generalized soft-tissue contractures (shortening of muscles, tendons, skin and surrounding soft tissues) are not considered a defining or major component of the disorder.  Such contractures are hallmarks of conditions like arthrogryposis, not parastremmatic dwarfism.  Therefore, the statement that soft-tissue shortening leading to joint stiffness is a major aspect of parastremmatic dwarfism is incorrect.

779986.long_answer: Mowat-Wilson syndrome is frequently accompanied by epilepsy or other seizure disorders in a large proportion of affected individuals. Because seizures are common, routine electroencephalography (EEG) in these patients often reveals focal or generalized epileptiform discharges or other abnormalities. Therefore, anticipating an abnormal EEG in someone with Mowat-Wilson syndrome is consistent with the clinical experience reported in the literature; expecting such findings is not incorrect.

362433.long_answer: Mowat–Wilson syndrome is a congenital disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ZEB2 gene. Along with distinctive facial features, Hirschsprung disease, intellectual disability, and agenesis of the corpus callosum, a high proportion of affected individuals develop recurrent, unprovoked seizures. The neurological disorder defined by such recurrent seizures is epilepsy, making epilepsy a common comorbidity in people with Mowat–Wilson syndrome.

799254.long_answer: Pseudo-IUGR (also called constitutional smallness) is reserved for fetuses who are small for gestational age but otherwise healthy, with no underlying pathological process; their small size represents a normal variant. Primordial dwarfism, in contrast, is a genetic growth-failure syndrome that produces marked, proportionate intrauterine growth restriction due to an intrinsic fetal pathology. Because the growth restriction arises from a disease process within the fetus, it is classified as true symmetrical (type I) IUGR, not as pseudo-IUGR. Therefore, a fetus affected by primordial dwarfism is not considered pseudo-IUGR.

739348.long_answer: Keloid disorder is characterized by an abnormal fibroproliferative response to virtually any cutaneous injury, including surgical incisions. A heart transplant involves a median sternotomy, chest-tube sites, vascular access lines and repeated endomyocardial biopsy sites—each representing dermal injury. Although transplant recipients receive systemic immunosuppression, these drugs do not eliminate the underlying genetic/biologic propensity for keloid formation. Case reports and small series document keloid development in transplant patients who had a pre-existing tendency. Therefore, individuals with keloid disorder remain at risk—and may in fact have a heightened risk—of developing keloids after a heart transplant. The statement claiming they are “not at risk” is incorrect.

647379.long_answer: Bejel (also called endemic syphilis) is caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum. It is a non-venereal treponemal infection found mainly in dry, hot regions of the Middle East and in many parts of northern and western Africa. Because it is produced by a subspecies of the same bacterium that causes sexually transmitted syphilis (T. pallidum subspecies pallidum), the two diseases are microbiologically and antigenically very closely related. Therefore, the statement that Bejel is endemic in many African countries and is closely related to sexually transmitted syphilis is accurate, so it is not false.

259072.long_answer: Peyronie’s disease is characterized by the development of fibrous plaques within the tunica albuginea of the penis. These plaques can cause abnormal penile curvature, pain, and interfere with normal blood flow and tissue elasticity, often resulting in erectile dysfunction—defined as the inability to achieve or maintain an erection with sufficient rigidity for satisfactory sexual activity.

422677.long_answer: The well-established fragile sites on the X chromosome are FRAXA at Xq27.3 (associated with the FMR1 gene and Fragile X syndrome) and FRAXE at Xq28; other, much rarer sites such as FRAXF are mapped to Xq22. A fragile site at Xq27.2 is not part of the recognized catalog of cytogenetically confirmed fragile sites. Therefore, stating that a fragile site is located specifically at Xq27.2 is not supported by the established scientific consensus.

854124.long_answer: Hematopoiesis (also spelled haemopoiesis) is the fundamental physiological process by which all new blood cellular elements—erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets—are continuously produced from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. This process takes place primarily in the bone marrow, the tissue that is commonly biopsied in suspected Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) to look for characteristic macrophage (histiocyte) infiltration and hemophagocytosis. Thus, hematopoiesis is the key process occurring in the bone marrow that generates new blood cells.

224062.long_answer: The SPAST gene, encoding the microtubule-severing AAA ATPase spastin, is the major cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia. Pathogenic variants in SPAST (also called SPG4) explain roughly 40–50 % of all genetically resolved HSP cases, reflecting its central role among AAA protein family members in axonal maintenance.

679390.long_answer: Deferiprone (brand name Ferriprox) is an oral iron-chelating agent. It received its first marketing authorization from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 1999 for the treatment of iron overload in patients with thalassemia major. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval 12 years later, in 2011. Because deferiprone removes excess iron from the body, it is also employed in managing iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis when standard phlebotomy is unsuitable. Thus, deferiprone fits the description of a medication approved by the FDA for thalassemia major 12 years after EMA approval and also used to treat hemochromatosis.

167352.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome type A is caused by pathogenic variants in the ERCC8 gene, which is located on chromosome 5q12. In contrast, Cockayne syndrome type B results from pathogenic variants in the ERCC6 gene, situated on chromosome 10q11.23. Because only the type A gene lies on chromosome 5 while the type B gene is on chromosome 10, it is incorrect to state that the genes responsible for both types are located on chromosome 5.

559664.long_answer: Besides SNRIs, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the other class of reuptake inhibitors shown to raise extracellular serotonin by blocking the serotonin transporter. This elevation of synaptic serotonin reduces anxiety-related symptoms and has been demonstrated to alleviate hypochondriasis (illness anxiety disorder) in clinical studies.

437386.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies have consistently shown that men with diabetes mellitus experience markedly higher rates of erectile dysfunction (impotence) than men without diabetes. Large population-based analyses indicate that the prevalence of erectile dysfunction in diabetic men is approximately 3.5 times greater than in nondiabetic men, largely because chronic hyperglycemia accelerates vascular and neuropathic damage that impairs penile blood flow and nitric-oxide–mediated smooth-muscle relaxation. Therefore, the sexual dysfunction that is 3.5 times more common in men with diabetes mellitus is erectile dysfunction.

771231.long_answer: Ischiopatellar dysplasia (also called small-patella syndrome) is an autosomal-dominant skeletal malformation characterized by hypoplastic or absent patellae, pelvic and foot anomalies. Genetic studies have shown that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the TBX4 gene are responsible for this disorder. TBX4 encodes a T-box transcription factor that is critically required for embryonic hindlimb development; it is expressed in the developing hindlimb bud and in the allantois, the embryonic structure that gives rise to the umbilical cord and umbilicus. Disruption of TBX4 therefore affects both hindlimb morphogenesis and umbilical formation, explaining the clinical features of ischiopatellar dysplasia when the gene is mutated.

654558.long_answer: Lenz–Majewski syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PTDSS1 gene, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1 (PSS1). PSS1 catalyzes the base-exchange reaction that converts phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylserine. The constitutively active mutant enzyme drives excessive synthesis of its product, leading to cellular accumulation of the phospholipid phosphatidylserine.

955705.long_answer: Infliximab (a chimeric anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody) has regulatory approval for Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis. Collagenous colitis – a form of microscopic colitis – is usually managed with antidiarrhoeal agents, budesonide, and occasionally immunomodulators such as azathioprine or methotrexate. Although a few case reports and small series describe off-label use of infliximab in patients with severe, treatment-refractory collagenous colitis, these anecdotal experiences have not led to formal guideline recommendations or regulatory approval. Therefore, infliximab is not an established or officially indicated therapy for collagenous colitis.

954659.long_answer: Trichothiodystrophy manifests with brittle hair, ichthyotic skin, nail abnormalities, and neurologic deficits—all structures that originate from the embryonic ectoderm. Because the disorder predominantly involves these ectoderm-derived tissues, it is considered an ectodermal dysplasia.

378607.long_answer: Polysaccharides of the glycosaminoglycan family are grouped into four major classes—hyaluronan, chondroitin/dermatan sulfates, heparin/heparan sulfate, and keratan sulfate—according to the composition and linkage pattern of their repeating core disaccharide units. Hence, four types are recognized on the basis of core disaccharide structure.

753323.long_answer: The most prevalent form of arthritis is osteoarthritis. Synovial fluid from an osteoarthritic joint is classified as “non-inflammatory”: it remains clear (transparent) and shows only a slight straw-yellow tint. This clear, lightly yellow appearance helps distinguish it from the turbid, more intensely colored fluid seen in inflammatory or infectious arthritides.

512370.long_answer: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (idiopathic brachial neuritis) and hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy characteristically injure branches of the brachial plexus, with the axillary nerve being one of the nerves most often involved. The axillary nerve exclusively supplies the deltoid, a thick, triangular muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder. Consequently, weakness, pain, and atrophy of the deltoid are common clinical findings in both disorders, making the deltoid the muscle most likely to be affected.

714294.long_answer: Moyamoya disease 2 (MYMY2) was first linked to a missense change in the RNF213 gene: a G→A transition at nucleotide 14576 that replaces arginine with lysine at position 4810 of the protein (commonly written p.R4810K, also described as p.R4859K in a longer isoform). This founding East-Asian mutation was the initial genetic alteration proven to cause autosomal-dominant Moyamoya disease 2.

970294.long_answer: The parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by kissing bugs, causes Chagas disease. In chronically infected individuals who later become immunosuppressed by HIV, reactivation of T. cruzi most commonly produces a severe meningoencephalitis. This is marked by intense inflammation and the formation of necrotizing, pus-filled abscesses within the brain parenchyma, visible on imaging and confirmed histologically. Hence, the organ affected is the brain.

632138.long_answer: Ocular toxoplasmosis, caused by infection with the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii, is the classic infectious cause of chorioretinitis. It produces focal necrotizing lesions in the retina and choroid, and patients most often present with painless, unilateral loss of vision or blurred vision—a decrease in visual acuity in one eye. This presentation makes toxoplasmosis the prototypical infectious etiology of chorioretinitis described in ophthalmology and infectious-disease texts.

678399.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type 0 results from deficiency of hepatic glycogen synthase (GYS2), an ~80 kDa enzyme that catalyzes transfer of glucose from UDP-glucose to glycogen. Glycogen synthase belongs to the broad glycosyltransferase protein family, enzymes that transfer sugar moieties to acceptor molecules. Thus, the relevant general protein family is the glycosyltransferases.

776831.long_answer: In 2015, researchers used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector to introduce a normal copy of the Transmembrane Channel-Like 1 (TMC1) gene into the inner-ear hair cells of Tmc1-deficient ‘Beethoven’ and knockout mice. Because mutations in TMC1 cause the human nonsyndromic hearing‐loss forms DFNB7/11 (recessive) and DFNA36 (dominant), supplying the correct TMC1 protein restored mechanotransduction currents and produced measurable improvements in auditory brain-stem responses, demonstrating partial recovery of hearing in these genetically deaf animals.

314843.long_answer: In hereditary spastic paraplegia, an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern means the disease-causing gene is located on the X chromosome and is recessive. Because males have only one X chromosome, a single mutated copy causes the disorder, so they are affected. Females have two X chromosomes; when only one carries the mutation, the normal copy on the other X usually prevents disease expression, making them asymptomatic carriers who can pass the mutation to their sons.

502680.long_answer: Activated protein C (APC) resistance in hereditary thrombophilia is most commonly caused by the Factor V Leiden mutation, a single-nucleotide substitution in the F5 gene. The F5 (coagulation factor V) gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 1 at position 1q23. Therefore, the gene mutated in the prevalent hereditary form of APC resistance resides on chromosome 1.

334677.long_answer: Langer–Giedion syndrome (trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II) is produced by a microdeletion on the long arm of chromosome 8, specifically encompassing bands q24.11 through q24.13. Loss of this 8q24.1 segment, which includes the TRPS1 and EXT1 genes, contrasts with Warkany syndrome 2, where an entire extra copy of chromosome 8 is present.

815861.long_answer: The disorder is Combined Malonic and Methylmalonic Aciduria (CMAMMA), an autosomal-recessive condition caused by loss-of-function mutations in the mitochondrial enzyme ACSF3. ACSF3 is an acyl-CoA synthetase that activates malonate and methylmalonate by forming their thioester linkage with coenzyme A. Deficiency blocks this step, leading to accumulation of both malonic and methylmalonic acids. CMAMMA is differentiated from classic methylmalonic acidemia because plasma shows a relatively low methylmalonic-to-malonic acid ratio, whereas classic MMA has markedly elevated methylmalonic acid with little or no rise in malonic acid.

438711.long_answer: The World Health Organization and UNICEF recommend zinc supplementation (10–20 mg daily for 10-14 days) for children suffering from acute gastroenteritis because it shortens the duration and severity of diarrhoeal episodes and reduces subsequent morbidity. Zinc is an essential trace element required for over 300 enzymatic reactions, DNA and protein synthesis, and immune function. Adequate zinc status is critical during both prenatal development (organogenesis, neural and immune system formation) and postnatal growth (linear growth, cognitive development, immune competence). Thus, zinc fulfills both criteria mentioned: it is routinely given as a supplement in paediatric gastroenteritis and is indispensable for normal prenatal and postnatal development.

672653.long_answer: Major depressive disorder—commonly referred to as depression—is characterized by a sustained low mood, loss of interest or pleasure in normally enjoyable activities (anhedonia), and other cognitive and somatic symptoms. Numerous epidemiological and clinical studies demonstrate that individuals with depression have a higher prevalence and incidence of systemic arterial hypertension, likely mediated by dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, autonomic imbalance, and inflammatory pathways.

256957.long_answer: The disorder is Grover disease, also called transient acantholytic dermatosis. It was first described in 1975 by American dermatopathologist Dr. Ralph W. Grover. Histologically, Grover disease shows focal acantholysis—the loss of intercellular desmosomal connections between keratinocytes—exactly the feature seen in pemphigus vulgaris and notably absent in bullous pemphigoid, making this microscopic finding a key diagnostic clue.

259365.long_answer: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD) is well-known for its cardiac involvement, especially conduction-system disease originating in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Sinus-node dysfunction frequently presents as persistent sinus bradycardia—a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute—and may progress to atrioventricular block or other arrhythmias. Because this slow resting heart rate is a recognized part of the EDMD cardiac phenotype, stating that a resting heart rate of <60 bpm is one of its cardiac manifestations is accurate, not incorrect.

144821.long_answer: Eosinophilic folliculitis is strongly associated with HIV infection and is most often seen in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), a condition marked by progressive loss of CD4⁺ T-cells and consequent immune system failure.

232559.long_answer: The condition is HIV-associated eosinophilic folliculitis.  It presents with intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and pustules centered on hair follicles, most often on the face, scalp, neck, upper chest and back.  The lesions appear in patients with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease, typically when CD4 counts are low.  HIV is a member of the lentivirus genus, so the eruption is ultimately caused by infection with a lentivirus and is therefore tightly linked to advanced HIV/AIDS.

853329.long_answer: Barth syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TAZ gene, which encodes the mitochondrial phospholipid-remodeling enzyme tafazzin. Restoring or replacing functional TAZ is therefore the main molecular target in experimental treatments such as AAV-mediated gene therapy and mRNA replacement aimed at correcting the cardiolipin defect and reversing the cardiomyopathy seen in Barth syndrome.

866039.long_answer: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is caused by an autosomal-dominant deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase encoded by the HMBS gene on chromosome 11. The enzymatic block leads to accumulation of ALA and PBG, producing episodic neuro-visceral attacks—abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric changes—without the cutaneous photosensitivity seen in other porphyrias, making AIP the classic hepatic porphyria that fits the described features.

290551.long_answer: Individuals with xeroderma pigmentosum avoid sunlight to limit UV-induced DNA damage, which markedly reduces cutaneous synthesis of vitamin D. Consequently they often take vitamin D supplements. The metabolically active (hormonally active) form of vitamin D in the body is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol—also known as calcitriol—which exerts the biological effects of the vitamin on calcium and phosphate homeostasis.

166341.long_answer: The first recognized clinical case of uniparental disomy (reported by Spence et al., 1988) involved maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 in a patient with cystic fibrosis. Human chromosome 7 contains about 159 million base pairs; as detailed in genome reference data (e.g., NCBI, Genetics Home Reference), this amount corresponds to roughly 5 percent of the total DNA present in human cells. Therefore, the duplicated chromosome in that landmark UPD case represents about 5 % of the cellular DNA.

352067.long_answer: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is an autosomal-recessive disorder that can result from mutations in more than 40 different genes encoding components of motile cilia (e.g., DNAH5, DNAI1, CCDC39, CCDC40). Defective ciliary structure or function impairs mucociliary clearance throughout the respiratory tract, leading to chronic sinusitis, recurrent otitis media, and persistent lower-airway infections such as bronchiectasis. The hallmark pathophysiology is abnormal mucociliary clearance, which explains the lifelong pattern of chronic respiratory infections seen in affected individuals.

667770.long_answer: Hay-Wells (AEC) syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the TP63 gene. TP63 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q27-q29), so the mutated gene responsible for Hay-Wells syndrome is located on chromosome 3.

408853.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type X is caused by a deficiency of the cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase (protein kinase A). This enzyme normally phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn activates glycogen phosphorylase to promote glycogen breakdown. When PKA is deficient, this signaling cascade is blunted, leading to impaired glycogenolysis, hepatic glycogen accumulation, and the clinical picture of GSD X.

829837.long_answer: The triad of gait instability, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence defines normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). The standard first-line management for NPH is surgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid with a ventriculoperitoneal (or equivalent CSF) shunt, which can substantially improve gait, cognition, and bladder control.

969034.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the coding region of the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene are an established cause of holoprosencephaly (HPE). Limb malformations such as polydactyly or polysyndactyly, however, are typically produced by gain-of-function alterations confined to a distant limb-specific enhancer of SHH (the ZRS) or by mutations in downstream pathway genes such as GLI3 or GLI2. Pathogenic variants that simultaneously give rise to both holoprosencephaly and polysyndactyly have not been documented in the biomedical literature, and this dual phenotype is not part of the accepted clinical spectrum of SHH coding-sequence mutations. Therefore, a single SHH mutation is not considered a recognized cause of the combined presentation of polysyndactyly and holoprosencephaly.

473053.long_answer: Grebe-type chondrodysplasia (also called acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type) is a very rare skeletal dysplasia distinguished by marked shortening of the limbs while the trunk is relatively spared. Reported adults with this condition generally reach a stature well below 147 cm (4 ft 10 in), often under 120 cm. Despite the severe skeletal abnormalities, neurological development is normal and no intellectual disability is associated with the disorder. Therefore, the statement that Grebe-type chondrodysplasia typically results in an adult height of less than 147 cm while leaving intelligence unaffected is consistent with the established clinical description of the condition.

583155.long_answer: In type I (distal) renal tubular acidosis, the α-intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct fail to secrete hydrogen ions via their H⁺-ATPase/H⁺-K⁺-ATPase pumps. This defect prevents adequate acidification of the urine, leading to accumulation of acid in the body and the characteristic metabolic acidosis of distal RTA.

736626.long_answer:
All three factors listed are recognized causes of microcephaly.

1. MacDermot-Winter syndrome (also termed blepharophimosis-ptosis-microcephaly syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder whose core diagnostic triad includes congenital microcephaly, characteristic eyelid malformations, and developmental delay. Thus, microcephaly is an intrinsic feature of the syndrome.

2. Prenatal alcohol exposure, particularly the spectrum encompassed by fetal alcohol syndrome, disrupts brain growth during gestation. A consistent hallmark of this teratogenic exposure is reduced head circumference at birth and throughout childhood, i.e., microcephaly.

3. Vertically transmitted (congenital) infections—classically grouped as TORCH (toxoplasmosis, “other” such as syphilis and Zika, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) and similar pathogens—can cross the placenta, injure the developing fetal brain, and result in structural abnormalities, including microcephaly. Recent outbreaks of congenital Zika infection dramatically underscored this causal link.

Therefore, MacDermot-Winter syndrome, prenatal alcohol exposure, and vertically transmitted infections are all established etiological factors capable of causing microcephaly.

459609.long_answer: The larynx is the organ that contains the vocal cords. When laryngeal carcinoma spreads hematogenously, the lungs are by far the most frequent site of distant metastases, reflecting both vascular drainage patterns and the high susceptibility of pulmonary tissue to lodging of circulating tumor cells. Clinical series consistently report the lung as the initial and predominant organ involved in distant spread from laryngeal cancer.

778748.long_answer: Haploinsufficiency is the situation in which loss or inactivation of one allele reduces gene dosage so much that the remaining normal allele cannot supply enough functional product to preserve the wild-type phenotype, leading to a detectable abnormal trait.

795817.long_answer: The described condition is the Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon, a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis. In this anomaly, voluntary movements of the jaw (chewing, opening, lateral excursion) produce an involuntary, rhythmic elevation of the upper eyelid. It results from aberrant connections between branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and the oculomotor nerve that innervates the levator palpebrae superioris. Clinically, it is seen as ptosis at rest with a sudden ‘wink’—an upward jerk of the eyelid—whenever the jaw moves, fitting the description given.

665185.long_answer: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), caused by the zoonotic coronavirus SARS-CoV first detected in Guangdong, China in late 2002, typically presents with fever, pneumonia and marked lymphocytopenia. Clinical series from the 2002–2003 outbreak reported that a drop in circulating lymphocyte counts was one of the characteristic hematological findings in SARS patients.

496183.long_answer: The cells first identified in the bursa of Fabricius (an avian organ absent in mammals) are B lymphocytes.  In X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia), mutations in the gene encoding Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) lead to markedly reduced or absent BTK protein levels in B-cell precursors.  The deficiency of this specific tyrosine kinase blocks B-cell maturation, causing the characteristic disorder.
