339683.long_answer: Sirolimus, an mTOR-inhibiting immunosuppressant originally isolated from the fungus-like actinomycete Streptomyces hygroscopicus, characteristically raises serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Unlike the calcineurin inhibitors cyclosporine and tacrolimus, it does not increase renal vascular resistance, so clinically significant hypertension is uncommon.

723379.long_answer: Mohr-Tranebjærg syndrome (X-linked deafness-dystonia syndrome) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TIMM8A gene, which encodes the mitochondrial intermembrane space protein Tim8a (also called DDP1). Defective Tim8a impairs import of specific proteins into mitochondria, leading to the neurodegenerative features of the disorder.

722142.long_answer: Genomic studies of sporadic meningiomas have shown that somatic mutations in the gene encoding TNF receptor-associated factor 7 (TRAF7) occur in roughly 20–25 % of tumors. These TRAF7 mutations commonly co-occur with mutations in KLF4 (in secretory meningiomas) or are found alone in other non-NF2 meningioma subtypes, making TRAF7 one of the most frequently altered genes in this disease.

901282.long_answer: The eponym “Marie–Strümpell disease” for ankylosing spondylitis arises from the work of two neurologists: the German neurologist Adolph von Strümpell and the French neurologist Pierre Marie. Strümpell had earlier, in 1880, provided the first description of hereditary spastic paraplegia, hence the alternative name “Strümpell-Lorrain disease.” In the same year (1880) Strümpell and Pierre Marie published descriptions of the inflammatory spinal disorder now called ankylosing spondylitis. Because Strümpell is already identified in the question as the first describer of hereditary spastic paraplegia, the other neurologist who shared credit for describing ankylosing spondylitis is Pierre Marie.

820147.long_answer: The French dermatologist Robert Degos (1904–1987) first recognized malignant atrophic papulosis, now called Degos disease, as a distinct clinical entity in 1941. A decade later he consolidated his clinical experience and observations in a comprehensive textbook. Published in 1953, this work was titled “Dermatologie,” and it is in this book that Degos again described and discussed the disease that now bears his name.

182169.long_answer: Recurrent respiratory (laryngeal) papillomatosis produces multiple squamous papillomas that arise most frequently on the true vocal cords—the stratified-squamous-covered glottic mucosa, especially around the anterior commissure. Although lesions can spread to other supraglottic or subglottic sites, the true vocal folds are by far the commonest location for the benign tumors.

483894.long_answer: Type XVII collagen, also known as BP180 or BPAG2, is an integral hemidesmosomal transmembrane protein that is the principal autoantigen in bullous pemphigoid. The gene that encodes type XVII collagen is COL17A1, located on chromosome 10q24. This gene’s product forms the 180-kDa component of hemidesmosomes, and autoantibodies directed against it lead to the subepidermal blistering characteristic of the disease.

799512.long_answer: The congenital condition is bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). BAV is the most common congenital heart defect, occurring in about 1–2 % of the population. Beyond causing valvular dysfunction, BAV is well known for its association with dilatation of the ascending aorta—the largest artery in the body—due to intrinsic aortopathy and altered hemodynamics. Therefore, bicuspid aortic valve is the condition linked to aortic dilatation.

910085.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) are strongly recommended in diabetes because they slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy and lower the risk of major cardiovascular events. Low-dose aspirin, on the other hand, is used in diabetes primarily for secondary (and, in selected high-risk patients, primary) prevention of cardiovascular disease; it has no proven benefit in preventing diabetic kidney disease and prolonged use may actually impair renal function. Therefore, while ACEIs help prevent both renal and cardiovascular complications, aspirin is used only for cardiovascular prevention, not for protection against diabetic kidney disease. Consequently, the statement that both ACEIs and aspirin can be used to prevent kidney and cardiovascular diseases caused by diabetes is not correct.

290537.long_answer: Autosomal recessive GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency impairs synthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a co-factor required for the hydroxylation of tyrosine to L-DOPA. Because of the BH4 shortage, patients cannot produce adequate amounts of the catecholamine neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Clinical management therefore includes providing downstream precursors that bypass the defective enzymatic step. Administration of L-DOPA (usually combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa) supplies the immediate precursor of these catecholamines, restores neurotransmitter levels in the central nervous system, and improves the neurologic symptoms of the disorder. Consequently, the catecholamine precursor L-DOPA is an accepted component of therapy for autosomal recessive GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency.

827382.long_answer: Levodopa, usually administered in combination with the peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa, is the standard medication for dopamine-responsive dystonia. The same levodopa/carbidopa regimen is also a cornerstone of therapy for the autosomal recessive form of GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency because it replaces the dopamine that cannot be synthesized adequately in both conditions.

700200.long_answer: In Class IV mutations of the LDL receptor, the receptor is synthesized, processed, and binds LDL normally at the cell surface, but it cannot cluster in clathrin-coated pits. Consequently, it fails to undergo the inward budding (invagination) step of receptor-mediated endocytosis, preventing internalization of the LDL–receptor complex.

152701.long_answer: The caloric reflex test is a vestibular function test in which warm or cold water (or air) is introduced into the external ear canal to stimulate the horizontal semicircular canal and elicit vestibulo-ocular reflexes. It is used primarily to assess vestibular integrity and to provoke or quantify nystagmus arising from labyrinthine or brain-stem pathways. Zonular (lamellar) cataract, however, is an opacity of the lens; its diagnosis relies on slit-lamp biomicroscopy or other ophthalmic imaging, not on vestibular stimulation. While the caloric test can help evaluate vestibular causes of nystagmus, it has no diagnostic value for cataract, and nystagmus itself is generally identified clinically without needing caloric irrigation. Therefore, the caloric reflex test cannot be considered an effective diagnostic tool for the combined conditions “zonular cataract and nystagmus.”

681755.long_answer: Reverse-transcription PCR assays used for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis only need the short segment of viral RNA that lies between the forward and reverse primer binding sites (typically 70–150 nt) to be intact. Global or partial degradation elsewhere in the genome does not interfere with amplification and detection; the reaction will still yield a signal provided the primer/probe sites and the intervening sequence remain undamaged. Therefore the nucleic-acid test is tolerant of RNA degradation so long as the fragment spanning the primer pair is preserved.

419700.long_answer: Baruch Samuel Blumberg shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the Hepatitis B virus. Hepatitis B virus is the prototype species of the family Hepadnaviridae, a group of small, enveloped DNA viruses that infect the liver of humans and other animals. Consequently, the virus family that includes Blumberg’s infectious agent is Hepadnaviridae.

666700.long_answer: Vitamin E comprises several tocopherols and tocotrienols, but the form with the highest biological activity in humans is α-tocopherol (especially the RRR-α-tocopherol stereoisomer). In the European Union food-additive system, α-tocopherol is assigned the code E307, while mixed tocopherol extracts are E306 and other tocopherol isomers have different numbers. Therefore, the E number corresponding to the most bioactive form of vitamin E is E307.

403013.long_answer: Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that neutralises tumour-necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). It is formally approved for psoriatic arthritis, where randomised controlled trials have demonstrated significant improvements in joint inflammation, enthesitis and skin disease; consequently, it is included in major rheumatology treatment guidelines for PsA. Although not formally licensed for hidradenitis suppurativa, multiple prospective studies, case series and dermatology guidelines document meaningful clinical responses when infliximab is given (typically 5 mg/kg every 4–8 weeks) to patients with moderate-to-severe or refractory HS. Therefore, based on current clinical evidence and guideline recommendations, infliximab is considered an effective therapeutic option for both hidradenitis suppurativa and psoriatic arthritis.

148826.long_answer: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that analyzes fetal chromosomal material obtained from placental villi and is usually carried out at 10–13 weeks’ gestation—several weeks earlier than amniocentesis. By providing a direct karyotype of fetal cells, CVS can definitively detect autosomal trisomies such as trisomy 18, the chromosomal abnormality responsible for Edwards syndrome.

281839.long_answer: The only Foix-Chavany-Marie (opercular) syndrome whose deficits are completely reversible is the post-ictal/epileptic variant. When seizures remain refractory, the most invasive surgical option is a hemispherectomy. Across large hemispherectomy series, the single most frequent postoperative complication is hydrocephalus that later requires ventriculoperitoneal shunting, occurring in roughly one-quarter to one-third of patients.

627918.long_answer: Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome (opercular syndrome) can occasionally be produced not by permanent structural lesions but by bilateral propagation of epileptic discharges that transiently inactivate the frontal opercular cortices.  When the epilepsy is medically intractable, disconnective surgery that prevents the rapid spread of ictal activity from one hemisphere to the other can abolish the opercular seizures and the associated negative motor phenomena.  Corpus callosotomy – sectioning the corpus callosum either partially (usually the anterior two-thirds) or completely – is a well-established neurosurgical treatment for refractory epilepsy.  By interrupting interhemispheric spread, a callosotomy can eliminate the bilateral opercular involvement, leading to complete resolution of the Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome that was being produced by those epileptic discharges.  Case reports document full recovery of voluntary facial, lingual, pharyngeal and masticatory movements after corpus callosotomy in such patients, confirming the effectiveness of this procedure in reversing FCMS when it is seizure-induced.

698744.long_answer: Published clinical descriptions of Fryns-Aftimos syndrome report characteristic cortical malformations, most notably pachygyria (broad, unusually thick cerebral convolutions). Because this thick-gyral (pachygyric) pattern is a recognized part of the brain phenotype in the syndrome, stating that Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is associated with unusually thick convolutions of the cerebral cortex is accurate. Therefore, it is not incorrect to make that statement.

933016.long_answer: Tonsillectomy—the surgical excision of the palatine tonsils—is routinely performed to manage recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and is also part of first-line surgical therapy for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea. Because the glossopharyngeal nerve and its lingual branches that carry taste fibers to the posterior third of the tongue run close to the tonsillar bed, they can be stretched, bruised, or partially severed during dissection. This neural injury may lead to postoperative taste disturbances, including dysgeusia (distortion or alteration of taste). Although usually transient, dysgeusia is a well-recognized potential complication specifically associated with tonsillectomy.

963020.long_answer: Yellow fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic fever for which the World Health Organization recommends a single-dose live-attenuated 17D vaccine. WHO policy states that all individuals aged nine months and older living in, or traveling to, areas where yellow fever is endemic should receive this vaccine, as it confers long-lasting immunity and is critical for outbreak prevention.

170557.long_answer: The statement is essentially correct. DAX1 (NR0B1) encodes an atypical nuclear receptor that normally acts as a transcriptional repressor of other nuclear receptors, most notably steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1/NR5A1) and LRH-1. Loss-of-function mutations in DAX1 abolish this negative regulatory activity, leading to derepression of SF-1-dependent gene programs during embryogenesis. This dysregulation disturbs the normal differentiation of several endocrine tissues, including the adrenal cortex and the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. In the pituitary, altered SF-1 activity and downstream signalling impair the proper development and function of gonadotrope and corticotrope lineages, contributing to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and other pituitary deficiencies seen in patients with DAX1 mutations. Therefore, saying that mutations in DAX1 cause pituitary developmental problems by disrupting its negative regulation of other nuclear receptors is consistent with the established mechanistic understanding and is not incorrect.

583819.long_answer: The human EDARADD (EDAR-associated death domain) gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 1, specifically at cytogenetic band 1q42–q43. This chromosomal localization has been established through linkage analysis and refined by genomic sequencing projects such as the Human Genome Project and Ensembl/NCBI annotations.

110195.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis belongs to the group of seronegative spondyloarthritides, meaning that characteristic auto-antibodies directed against nuclear antigens (antinuclear antibodies, ANA) are generally absent. This is true both in adult-onset and juvenile-onset disease. Routine laboratory evaluation of children with suspected juvenile ankylosing spondylitis typically shows negativity for ANA, in contrast to conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus or some forms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis where ANA positivity is common. Therefore, the statement that antibodies binding to nuclear contents are usually not present in juvenile ankylosing spondylitis is correct.

165936.long_answer: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular allergic disorder that shares the immunopathology of other type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions. In this mechanism, IgE antibodies bind to mast cells; upon exposure to relevant allergens, cross-linking of the surface-bound IgE triggers mediator release and produces the characteristic signs and symptoms. Among the five major immunoglobulin isotypes found in human serum (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE), IgE is present at the lowest concentration, making it the least abundant isotype. Because vernal keratoconjunctivitis is mediated predominantly by IgE, it indeed involves the least abundant antibody isotype.

865929.long_answer: Osteopetrosis is characterized by defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, so calcium that would normally be released from bone remains trapped in the skeleton. As a result, patients often develop normal or low (not elevated) serum calcium concentrations and may even experience hypocalcemic tetany, especially in infancy. Persistent serum calcium levels above 10.7 mg/dL (hypercalcemia) are therefore not a recognized consequence of osteopetrosis; the disorder is more commonly associated with low or normal calcium levels.

619420.long_answer: Babesia species (babesiosis) produce intra-erythrocytic tetrads that form the characteristic “Maltese cross,” named after the cross used by Crusaders. On peripheral blood smear these ring forms closely mimic those of Plasmodium species. Because both infections involve protozoa invading red blood cells and can cause febrile hemolytic illness, the foremost condition that must be distinguished from babesiosis is malaria caused by Plasmodium spp.; hence, malaria is the primary differential diagnosis.

415751.long_answer: In Chédiak-Higashi syndrome the defective neutrophil function leads to recurrent pyogenic infections characterized by a purulent (suppurative) exudate—commonly referred to as pus—composed mainly of neutrophils, necrotic cells and edema fluid.

143907.long_answer: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a group of inherited metabolic disorders caused by deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This enzyme defect blocks the normal catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Accumulation of these amino acids and their toxic ketoacids leads to neonatal encephalopathy that frequently presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and generalized hypotonia. Accordingly, MSUD is listed among the principal inborn errors of metabolism that can cause hypotonia in newborns.

351187.long_answer: Atoh1, also known as Math1, is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that has been proposed to act as a tumor suppressor in several cancers. Adenoviral delivery of Atoh1 into the developing cochlea of embryonic mice drives supporting cells to trans-differentiate into mechanosensory hair cells, leading to robust hair-cell growth. This gene-therapy approach exploits Atoh1’s pivotal role in hair-cell lineage specification and has demonstrated effective hair-cell regeneration in experimental models.

571485.long_answer: The panniculus adiposus is the dense layer of subcutaneous fatty tissue in the lower abdomen. After rapid weight loss it can overhang as a panniculus, and in diseases such as deep morphea (morphea profunda) this fat layer may become inflamed (panniculitis) or undergo sclerosis.

527168.long_answer: Ellis–Van Creveld syndrome (EVC), also called chondroectodermal dysplasia, is a rare autosomal-recessive skeletal and ectodermal disorder produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the EVC gene (or its paralog EVC2). The EVC proteins localize to the base of primary cilia and participate in Hedgehog signalling; their dysfunction disrupts ciliary structure and signaling pathways, so the condition is classified within the growing group of primary cilia–related disorders known as ciliopathies.

273077.long_answer: Meningococcemia (blood-borne infection with Neisseria meningitidis) frequently co-exists with, or rapidly progresses to, meningococcal meningitis. When the meninges are inflamed, patients develop nuchal rigidity—pain or marked discomfort when the neck is turned, moved, or flexed. Clinical reviews list neck stiffness/pain as a characteristic feature when meningitis accompanies meningococcemia; a substantial proportion of patients with meningococcemia (≈30–50 %) manifest meningeal involvement. Therefore, while isolated septicemia may not cause neck pain, the combined clinical entity “meningococcal disease” (meningococcemia ± meningitis) does include neck discomfort on movement as a recognized symptom.

224427.long_answer: Pasireotide (marketed in the United States as Signifor and Signifor LAR) is the only medication that has received specific U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the treatment of pituitary-dependent Cushing’s disease in adults who are either not candidates for curative pituitary surgery or who have persistent or recurrent disease after pituitary surgery. The somatostatin analogue binds with high affinity to somatostatin receptor subtype 5 on corticotroph adenomas, suppressing excessive ACTH secretion and thereby lowering cortisol levels, and its labeling explicitly limits the indication to this patient population.

131236.long_answer: Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) is the principal circulating inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. When AAT is deficient, unchecked elastase activity degrades elastin and other structural proteins that are critical for connective-tissue integrity in the lung, liver and vascular walls. Several epidemiological studies and case series have reported a higher prevalence of arterial aneurysms—including abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)—in individuals with severe AAT deficiency (e.g., Pi*ZZ genotype) compared with the general population. Experimental work also demonstrates increased aortic elastin fragmentation and dilatation in AAT-deficient animal models. Taken together, the established mechanism (protease–antiprotease imbalance leading to elastin degradation) and supportive clinical data indicate that AAT deficiency does increase susceptibility to AAA formation. Therefore, the effect of AAT deficiency on connective-tissue integrity is considered a risk factor for developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

505048.long_answer: Ocrelizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 antigen on B-lymphocytes. It is approved for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and, because B-cell depletion is also beneficial in autoimmune blistering diseases, ocrelizumab is currently being investigated as a potential therapy for pemphigus vulgaris.

808372.long_answer: The classic clinical triad used to recognize primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) includes: (1) primary or secondary amenorrhoea, (2) hyper-gonadotropic hypogonadism, and (3) hypo-oestrogenism. Individuals with 5-α-reductase type 2 deficiency (SRD5A2 gene mutations) are 46,XY and are often raised as females. Because they lack a uterus and ovaries, they invariably present with primary amenorrhoea if they are reared female. Thus the disorder is indeed associated with one component of the POI diagnostic triad—primary amenorrhoea—even though the overall aetiology and pathophysiology differ from true ovarian failure.

636294.long_answer: The major plasma protein produced by the yolk sac and frequently elevated in hepatoblastomas is alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). The human AFP gene encodes a precursor polypeptide that is 609 amino acids long (UniProt P02771). After removal of its 18-residue signal peptide, the mature secreted protein comprises residues 19–609, but the total length of the encoded polypeptide is 609 amino acids.

324488.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene (BCL-6 corepressor) on Xp11.4. The same BCOR gene is also responsible for Lenz microphthalmia syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by microphthalmia/anophthalmia, skeletal anomalies, and developmental delay. Thus, the recessively inherited disease caused by the same gene as OFCD syndrome is Lenz microphthalmia syndrome.

666822.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is a mosaic over-growth disorder caused by activating AKT1 mutations. In addition to over-growth of bone, soft tissue, and skin, patients have an elevated risk of several neoplasms. In males, the main reproductive-system malignancy reported is testicular cancer—most often seminomatous or other germ-cell tumors. Multiple clinical series and reviews of Proteus syndrome list testicular carcinoma among the tumors occurring with increased frequency, making it the primary reproductive cancer risk for affected male patients.

120453.long_answer: The most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which blocks the synthesis of glucocorticoids. The key hormone that becomes deficient is cortisol. Because the body cannot produce adequate cortisol, ACTH levels rise, leading to adrenal hyperplasia and excess androgen production. Clinically, this deficiency is treated with replacement glucocorticoids. Synthetic analogs of cortisol—such as hydrocortisone, prednisone, and prednisolone—are among the most frequently prescribed drugs worldwide due to their broad use in endocrine replacement, inflammation control, and immunosuppression. Thus, the hormone primarily lacking in the common CAH variant and for which a widely used synthetic analog exists is cortisol.

201807.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the KCNJ6 gene (which encodes the G-protein–activated inwardly rectifying potassium channel 2, GIRK2) are known to cause Keppen-Lubinsky syndrome (also called KCNJ6-related disorder). A core, well-documented feature of this condition is marked intrauterine growth restriction that results in significantly reduced weight, length and head circumference already evident at birth. Therefore, the presence of abnormal (typically decreased) growth parameters at birth is indeed a characteristic, indicative finding of the disease caused by KCNJ6 mutations.

789625.long_answer: The gene implicated is RAI1 (Retinoic Acid-Induced 1). Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 due to a 17p11.2 deletion causes Smith–Magenis syndrome, whereas a reciprocal 17p11.2 duplication including RAI1 causes Potocki–Lupski syndrome. The RAI1 protein contains a PHD-type zinc-finger domain, a motif that coordinates zinc ions. Consequently, Gene Ontology annotations for RAI1 include the term “metal ion binding.” Therefore, the gene in question is classified as metal ion binding.

859400.long_answer: Hymenolepiasis is a helminthiasis—an infection caused by parasitic worms (helminths).  A major collaborative eradication effort directed at a disease in the same category of helminth infections is the Onchocerciasis Control Programme (OCP) in West Africa, jointly organised by the World Health Organization, the World Bank and several partner nations.  This programme, aimed at eradicating onchocerciasis (river blindness), was officially launched in 1974.  Therefore, the year in which the collaborative disease-eradication programme was launched is 1974.

663367.long_answer: The slogan “The Other White Meat” was created by the U.S. National Pork Board to market pork as a lean alternative comparable to poultry. Despite this positioning, pork is still classified as red meat and contains appreciable amounts of saturated fat. Diets high in saturated fat can raise serum LDL-cholesterol levels and contribute to secondary (diet-induced) hyperlipidemia. Therefore, pork—the meat promoted as 'the other white meat'—is also implicated in causing secondary hyperlipidemia through its saturated-fat content.

610944.long_answer: The 2009 global pandemic was caused by a novel swine-origin influenza A virus of the H1N1 subtype. This strain arose through genetic reassortment of gene segments from North American and Eurasian swine, avian, and human influenza lineages, then spread efficiently between humans worldwide.

237915.long_answer: Cysteine, the amino acid whose sulfhydryl groups form the disulfide bonds that stabilize many protein structures, is produced in humans by trans-sulfuration of methionine through the enzymes cystathionine β-synthase and cystathionine γ-lyase. Both enzymes require pyridoxal-5′-phosphate, the active co-enzyme form of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). When the diet is deficient in vitamin B6, pyridoxal-5′-phosphate levels fall, these B6-dependent reactions slow, and endogenous synthesis of cysteine is markedly reduced. Thus a deficiency of the essential nutrient vitamin B6 specifically impairs the body’s ability to make the disulfide-bond-forming amino acid cysteine.

924584.long_answer: Reactive (secondary) thrombocythemia commonly occurs when systemic or local inflammation raises interleukin-6 and other cytokines, stimulating hepatic thrombopoietin production and megakaryocyte proliferation. The classical process of inflammation is defined by the cardinal signs of redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor), and loss of function (functio laesa); it is this inflammatory response that can drive the elevated platelet counts seen in reactive thrombocythemia.

157829.long_answer: The standard over-the-counter topical medication used to relieve pruritus (itching) from contact dermatitis caused by Toxicodendron species—such as poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac—is calamine lotion. Calamine is a pink-colored preparation made from a finely powdered mineral mixture of zinc oxide with a small proportion of ferric oxide, suspended in a water-based lotion. When applied to the affected skin, it provides a cooling, antipruritic, and mildly astringent effect, thereby reducing itch and discomfort associated with the rash.

656117.long_answer: Immune (erythroblastosis) hydrops fetalis is most commonly triggered by Rh-D incompatibility in which an Rh-negative mother forms antibodies against fetal Rh-positive red cells. Administering Anti-D immunoglobulin (Rho(D) immune globulin) to every Rh-negative woman after any potential fetomaternal hemorrhage—routinely at 28–30 weeks’ gestation and within 72 hours postpartum—destroys fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes in the maternal circulation before the mother can mount an immune response. This preventive injection blocks maternal allo-immunisation and thereby prevents the immune-mediated hemolytic disease that can progress to hydrops fetalis in subsequent pregnancies.

998849.long_answer: Multinucleated, striated skeletal muscle fibres rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis. Their predominant lactate dehydrogenase isoenzyme is composed of four ‘M’ (muscle) subunits, designated LDH-5 (M4). This form efficiently converts pyruvate to lactate under low-oxygen conditions, matching the metabolic demands of skeletal muscle tissue that contains repeating sarcomeres.

668585.long_answer: Patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal are routinely given thiamine (vitamin B1) to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamine belongs to the B-complex group of vitamins, all of which are water-soluble. Because thiamine is water-soluble (i.e., readily dissolves in water), the statement that this routinely recommended vitamin is insoluble in water is incorrect.

442535.long_answer: Carotenoid pigments (the carotenes and xanthophylls) are embedded in and around the protein cores of photosystem I and photosystem II. Besides enlarging the light-harvesting range, they protect chlorophyll from photo-oxidative damage. When a plant cannot synthesize carotenoids—because of genetic mutations or inhibitors—chlorophyll is rapidly destroyed by light, and the tissues become white or �albino.� Hence, deficiency of carotenoids is the molecular cause of albinism in such plants.

744208.long_answer: Ovarian cancer frequently presents with vague gastrointestinal and pelvic symptoms—persistent abdominal bloating or distension, altered bowel habits (constipation, diarrhoea), pelvic or abdominal pain, early satiety, and sometimes abnormal or post-menopausal vaginal bleeding. Because these manifestations closely mimic those of irritable bowel syndrome, many women are initially misdiagnosed with IBS, leading to delayed recognition of ovarian malignancy. Consequently, ovarian cancer is the malignancy most commonly confused with IBS when patients report bloating, bowel-habit changes, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.

308498.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome results from defects in proteins required for ribosomal RNA synthesis. The small subunit common to RNA polymerases I and III—POLR1C (DNA-directed RNA polymerase I and III subunit C)—physically associates with other Pol I components, including CD3EAP (also called ASE-1), POLR1E and POLR1D, to form the functional transcription complex. Pathogenic loss-of-function mutations in the POLR1C gene disrupt this interaction network, impair rRNA transcription, and are a well-established cause of Treacher Collins syndrome (designated TCS type 3). Hence, the protein that interacts with CD3EAP, POLR1E and POLR1D and whose mutation produces Treacher Collins syndrome is POLR1C.

373907.long_answer: Members of the parrot (psittacine) family—roughly 350 extant species of parrots, parakeets, macaws, cockatoos, and related birds—are recognized as common reservoirs of Chlamydia psittaci, the bacterium that causes psittacosis. Thus, the parrot family comprises about 350 species capable of transmitting this zoonotic disease to humans.

575067.long_answer: Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase. The recombinant, commercially available form of this enzyme—used for enzyme-replacement therapy in affected patients—is laronidase, marketed under the trade name Aldurazyme.

588303.long_answer: Long-term cutaneous sequelae after toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are not limited to scarring, dyspigmentation, nail changes and ocular problems. Several case series and reports have documented the later appearance of multiple new benign pigmented lesions—including eruptive lentigines and eruptive melanocytic nevi—months to years after recovery from TEN. These lesions are thought to arise because the massive epidermal destruction in TEN is followed by brisk re-epithelialisation with cytokine-driven melanocyte activation and proliferation; the process can result in numerous small, clinically benign pigmented macules or nevi that were not present before the episode. Therefore, eruptive benign pigmented lesions are a recognised, although uncommon, long-term skin complication in TEN survivors.

506722.long_answer: A median sternotomy is the standard surgical approach in cardiac and many thoracic operations. The surgeon makes a single vertical midline incision through the skin and divides the sternum longitudinally to spread the chest, giving direct access to the heart, great vessels, and anterior lungs. Because the skin and subcutaneous tissues over the sternum are incised and subjected to tension during healing, patients are at risk of developing hypertrophic or keloid scars along the mid-chest incision line.

466063.long_answer: Immunoglobulin E (IgE) is the scarcest immunoglobulin isotype in normal serum, circulating at concentrations far lower than IgG, IgA, IgM, or IgD. Despite its low abundance, IgE binds with high affinity to Fcε receptors on mast cells and basophils, priming them for immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a severe, recurrent allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva in which elevated local and systemic IgE levels, together with IgE-sensitized mast cells, drive the release of histamine and other mediators that produce itching, photophobia, and conjunctival papillae. Therefore, IgE is the immunoglobulin implicated in vernal keratoconjunctivitis and is also the least abundant isotype in the bloodstream.

623637.long_answer: The specific type of pneumoconiosis responsible for about 3,600 deaths worldwide in 2015 was asbestosis. Asbestosis is a chronic fibrotic lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibers, leading to progressive pulmonary scarring and respiratory failure. Global Burden of Disease 2015 estimates attribute roughly 3,600 deaths to this condition, distinguishing it from other pneumoconioses such as silicosis or coal workers’ pneumoconiosis.

685701.long_answer: The FIP1L1–PDGFRA fusion gene and other activating PDGFRA mutations drive a constitutively active PDGFRA tyrosine kinase in hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) and chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL). Imatinib mesylate is a selective BCR-ABL, KIT and PDGFRA/B tyrosine kinase inhibitor that potently inhibits this aberrant PDGFRA activity. Clinical studies have shown dramatic, often complete, hematologic and molecular remissions in patients with HES or CEL harboring FIP1L1-PDGFRA or other PDGFRA mutations when treated with low-dose imatinib (e.g., 100 mg/day). Consequently, imatinib is the standard tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for these conditions.

454301.long_answer: Acetazolamide (molar mass ≈ 222 g/mol) is the lightest of the clinically used carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors. Systemic acetazolamide has been reported to lessen certain forms of nystagmus (including downbeat and periodic-alternating nystagmus) and has also been investigated in prospective clinical trials as a pharmacologic treatment for idiopathic/normal-pressure hydrocephalus, making it the agent that fits both criteria.

222137.long_answer: The disease described is hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa). Severity of this chronic inflammatory skin condition is routinely classified using the three-tier Hurley staging system: Stage I (single or multiple abscesses without sinus tracts), Stage II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tract formation and scarring, widely separated), and Stage III (diffuse or interconnected sinus tracts and abscesses across a region). This classification guides treatment decisions, including the use of biologic agents such as the TNF-α inhibitor infliximab for moderate-to-severe disease.

132019.long_answer: Cyclophoria is the latent heterophoric condition in which the eyes exhibit torsional (rotational) deviation when normal binocular visual stimuli that maintain alignment are removed.

954923.long_answer: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is followed, in some survivors, by the sudden appearance of multiple benign melanocytic proliferations such as eruptive lentigines or eruptive melanocytic naevi. These lesions involve pigment-producing skin cells (melanocytes) and are considered a recognised, though uncommon, cutaneous sequela of TEN. Hence a benign eruptive condition of pigment-producing cells can indeed complicate or follow toxic epidermal necrolysis.

542113.long_answer: Mutations in the NEB gene, which encodes nebulin – a giant actin-binding protein that functions as a ‘thin-filament ruler’ in skeletal muscle – account for roughly 50 % of all documented cases of nemaline myopathy.

599997.long_answer: The provided context does not include any information linking liver dysfunction to vision loss (though it does commonly cause jaundice). Because no supporting evidence is given in the context, the statement cannot be affirmed.

218896.long_answer: The lesion most frequently encountered near the mental foramen following surgical injury to a peripheral nerve is the traumatic (also called amputation) neuroma. It is a reactive proliferation of nerve fibers and supporting tissue that develops when a severed or damaged nerve attempts to regenerate, producing a benign nodular mass in the area of the prior trauma.

829744.long_answer: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI)—first described as blood-oxygen-level-dependent/venography—is an MRI sequence that combines magnitude and filtered phase data to accentuate susceptibility effects from deoxyhemoglobin, hemosiderin, and other paramagnetic substances. Because this technique highlights minute magnetic susceptibility differences, it detects cerebral microhemorrhages far more sensitively than conventional T2* gradient-echo imaging, making it especially useful in conditions such as cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

167837.long_answer: Jacobsen syndrome—also called 11q terminal deletion disorder—is a rare congenital condition produced by deletions on the long (q) arm of chromosome 11. Affected individuals typically display characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism (e.g., broad nasal bridge, down-slanting palpebral fissures), growth and psychomotor delay, congenital heart defects, hematologic abnormalities such as Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, and multiple other physical and developmental problems.

796862.long_answer: Although the condition is now called Lynch syndrome after the later work of Henry T. Lynch, the first physician to recognize and describe this inherited predisposition to colorectal (and other) cancers was pathologist Aldred Scott Warthin. In 1913 he published observations on “Family G,” documenting an autosomal-dominant pattern of early-onset colon and endometrial cancers, thereby identifying the hereditary cancer syndrome that would decades later be renamed Lynch syndrome.

599931.long_answer: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy was first identified and described in the early 1950s by the Portuguese neurologist Mário Corino de Andrade. Prof. Andrade carried out his work in Porto, where he spent the bulk of his career at Hospital Geral de Santo António and the University of Porto’s Faculty of Medicine. Although he became an influential figure in Portuguese neurology, there is no record of him founding any of the major bioscience research institutes based in Lisbon (such as the Instituto Gulbenkian de Ciência, the Instituto de Medicina Molecular, or the Champalimaud Foundation). Those institutions were established by other individuals and organizations. Hence, the statement that the neurologist who first described familial amyloid polyneuropathy was a founder of a major Lisbon bioscience institute is not supported by the historical record.

230703.long_answer: The fragile site located at Xq27.2 is classified as an aphidicolin-inducible common fragile site. Exposure of human cells to the fungal antibiotic aphidicolin, an inhibitor of DNA polymerase α/δ, produces replication stress and consistently triggers chromosomal breaks or gaps at this locus. Cytogenetic studies that map fragile site expression have therefore long used aphidicolin to reveal the Xq27.2 breaks, establishing it as the specific antibiotic inducer for this region.

686893.long_answer: Vitamin A (in its retinal form) binds with the opsin protein in photoreceptor rods to create the visual pigment rhodopsin that is essential for light and color perception; inadequate vitamin A intake reduces retinal levels, disrupting rhodopsin formation and potentially leading to impaired color vision or color blindness.

728397.long_answer: Hypochondriasis (now termed illness-anxiety disorder) often responds to the same medications used for depressive and anxiety disorders. Several controlled trials and clinical reports have shown that SSRIs—such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, and fluvoxamine—significantly lessen preoccupation with somatic illness, decrease health-related anxiety, and improve overall functioning. Because SSRIs are first-line antidepressants for major depressive disorder and have established efficacy and safety profiles, they are the drug class most commonly prescribed to reduce hypochondriacal symptoms.

995113.long_answer: Gómez–López-Hernández (cerebellotrigeminal-dermal) syndrome has been linked to pathogenic variants in the EXT2 gene.  EXT2 is situated on chromosome 11p11-p12 and codes for exostosin-2, which pairs with exostosin-1 to form the two-subunit heparan-sulfate polymerase enzyme.  Mutations disrupting EXT2 therefore implicate this gene in the pathogenesis of Gómez–López-Hernández syndrome.

747234.long_answer: Liver transplantation (orthotopic liver transplant) replaces the cirrhotic liver with a healthy donor organ, abolishing portal hypertension and thereby treating esophageal varices. It is the definitive, widely accepted surgical therapy for decompensated cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and acute (fulminant) liver failure.

722978.long_answer: Cuffer and Barbillon identified the mid-systolic click simply by auscultation with a stethoscope.  The stethoscope was invented by the French physician René-Théophile-Hyacinthe Laennec in 1816; hence the device they used in their 1887 observations had been in existence since 1816.

689063.long_answer: Cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) is clustered on human chromosome 15q24, belongs to the xenobiotic-metabolising CYP1 family, and catalyses several oxidative reactions including ring-hydroxylation of toluene; hence it is a key enzyme in toluene and broader xenobiotic metabolism.

427523.long_answer: Ayazi syndrome (also reported as X-linked intellectual disability, Ayazi type; OMIM 300183) is characterised chiefly by moderate to severe intellectual disability, speech delay, seizures, and distinctive cranio-facial or skeletal features. Published clinical descriptions do not list generalized excess adiposity (obesity) as a core or even a recurrent finding. Therefore, the statement that one of the symptoms of Ayazi syndrome is "excessive body fat that has accumulated to such an extent that it can potentially have negative effects on health" (i.e., obesity) is not supported by the established medical literature.

622659.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant and mood-stabilising drug first synthesized in 1953 by the Swiss chemist Walter Schindler at J.R. Geigy AG in Basel. Prolonged therapy with carbamazepine has been shown to lower serum biotin levels and reduce biotinidase activity, leading to clinically significant biotin deficiency in some long-term users. This association is well documented in nutritional and pharmacological studies, establishing carbamazepine as a medication that can precipitate biotin deficiency with extended use.

493183.long_answer: RPL5, a ribosomal-protein gene that has been experimentally shown to interact with basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF-2), is a recognized Diamond-Blackfan anemia gene. Sequencing studies of DBA patients have documented 51 separate (non-recurrent) pathogenic mutations in RPL5.

822308.long_answer: Thin basement membrane disease and IgA nephropathy (also called Berger disease) are the two disorders most often responsible for persistent hematuria in otherwise asymptomatic patients. While thin basement membrane disease is due to collagen IV abnormalities that make the glomerular basement membrane abnormally thin, IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial deposition of immunoglobulin A. Both conditions commonly present with microscopic (and occasionally macroscopic) hematuria without edema, hypertension, or impaired renal function at initial presentation, making them the leading causes of isolated hematuria.

442504.long_answer: In Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, involvement of the cardiac conduction system often leads to sinus node dysfunction. This manifests as sinus bradycardia, defined as a resting heart rate of fewer than 60 beats per minute. Sinus bradycardia is well documented in patients with this muscular dystrophy alongside other conduction disturbances such as atrioventricular block and atrial arrhythmias.

410810.long_answer: Punctate inner choroiditis (PIC) is classically characterized by multiple small, yellow-white chorioretinal lesions in otherwise healthy, often myopic, young women. A defining feature that helps distinguish PIC from other white-dot syndromes (such as multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis) is the relative absence of inflammatory cells in both the anterior chamber and the vitreous. In other words, significant anterior chamber inflammation or vitritis is typically not present in PIC. Therefore, anterior chamber inflammation and vitritis are not considered hallmark or commonly associated findings with punctate inner choroiditis.

865090.long_answer: Human cytomegalovirus (CMV), a betaherpesvirus that possesses an icosahedral capsid with T=16 symmetry, is the foremost non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural deafness and consequent balance/ambulatory difficulties acquired via vertical (in utero) transmission.

715914.long_answer: The PEPD gene encodes prolidase, an enzyme required to recycle proline and hydroxyproline released during collagen turnover. When PEPD is mutated, prolidase activity is lost, collagen degradation and resynthesis are disrupted, and the composition and organization of the extracellular matrix (the fibrous network that supports all connective tissues) become abnormal. This defective extracellular matrix underlies the skin lesions, poor wound healing, and other connective-tissue manifestations seen in prolidase (PEPD) deficiency.

422230.long_answer: The 8363G>A point mutation in the mitochondrial MT-TK gene (encoding tRNALys) is a well-documented cause of multisystem mitochondrial disease that can include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and sensorineural hearing loss. The hearing loss results from irreversible damage to cochlear hair cells and/or auditory neurons produced by the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction. At present there are no disease-modifying or curative therapies that can restore normal mitochondrial tRNALys function or regenerate lost cochlear structures. Management is therefore limited to supportive measures such as hearing aids or cochlear implantation, which improve communication but do not biologically reverse the hearing deficit. Consequently, hearing loss produced by this mutation-associated cardiomyopathy is considered irreversible with current medical technology.

845857.long_answer: Andersen disease (glycogen-storage disease type IV) is caused by deficiency of the glycogen-branching enzyme, amylo-1,4→1,6-transglucosidase (EC 2.4.1.18). This enzyme catalyzes transfer of a segment of a 1,4-α-glucan chain to form 1,6-α branches in glycogen. Because it mediates transfer of glycosyl groups from one molecule site to another, it is classified in the ‘transferase’ family of enzymes (specifically, among glycosyltransferases).

907498.long_answer: Hydroxychloroquine is commonly tried as an early systemic therapy for generalized or recalcitrant granuloma annulare. It is also an established disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for adults with rheumatoid arthritis, prescribed either as monotherapy in mild disease or in combination with methotrexate to enhance therapeutic effect.

280426.long_answer: HLA-B27 is a human leukocyte antigen (MHC class I) allele encoded within the major histocompatibility complex on chromosome 6p21.3. Its presence is routinely tested as an immune marker because it is strongly associated with, and therefore aids in the diagnosis of, juvenile idiopathic arthritis—particularly the enthesitis-related and axial subtypes.

176281.long_answer: The scientist who first carried out chorionic villus sampling is the Italian biologist-geneticist Giuseppe Simoni. His official curriculum states that he earned his Laurea in Biological Sciences (the Italian equivalent of a biology degree) at the Università degli Studi di Milano—known in English as the University of Milan—before leading the team that introduced CVS in 1983. Therefore, the university at which he obtained his biology degree was the University of Milan.

669273.long_answer: Oculocerebrocutaneous (OCC) syndrome – also called Delleman syndrome – is classically characterized by ocular malformations (e.g., orbital cysts, microphthalmia), cutaneous defects, and a variety of cerebral anomalies. Reported brain findings include agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, porencephalic or arachnoid cysts, cerebral dysplasia, and hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus represents an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the cerebral ventricles, leading to ventricular dilation and potentially increased intracranial pressure. Because hydrocephalus is a documented central-nervous-system manifestation in patients with OCC syndrome, the statement that a buildup of CSF within the brain (which can raise intracranial pressure) is one of the symptoms associated with oculocerebrocutaneous syndrome is consistent with established medical descriptions.

970726.long_answer: One of the five additional features frequently reported alongside MASA syndrome is hydrocephalus—a condition in which cerebrospinal fluid accumulates within the brain’s ventricles, leading to their enlargement and raised intracranial pressure.

480829.long_answer: In babesiosis, the intra-erythrocytic protozoan Babesia spp. may divide into four merozoites arranged at right angles to one another, producing a tetrad that resembles a Maltese cross. On a peripheral blood smear this appears as four “V”-shaped inclusions converging centrally within a red blood cell—a distinctive diagnostic feature of babesiosis.

947752.long_answer: During embryonic folding, the lateral plate mesoderm splits into a somatic (parietal) layer, which associates with surface ectoderm to form the ventral body wall, and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, which covers the gut tube. Proper fusion of the somatic/parietal layers from the right and left sides is essential to close the anterior thoracic wall. Failure of this parietal layer to develop or fuse correctly leaves a midline defect through which the heart protrudes, producing ectopia cordis. Hence, defective formation of the somatic (parietal) layer of the lateral plate mesoderm underlies ectopia cordis.
